title: Problem Set 04
text:
Consider an experiment where the binary treatment \(D_i\) is randomly assigned across individuals. We are interested in its effect on the post-treatment outcome \(Y_{i,\text{post}}\).


The population OLS coefficient from a regression of \(Y_{i,\text{post}}\) on \(D_i\) and a constant is \(\beta_D = \text{Cov}(D_i, Y_{i,\text{post}}) / \text{Var}(D_i)\). Let \(p = \Pr(D_i = 1)\), so \(\mathbb{E}[D_i] = p\) and \(\text{Var}(D_i) = p(1-p)\). Expanding the covariance:
\[
\text{Cov}(D_i, Y_{i,\text{post}}) = \mathbb{E}[D_i Y_{i,\text{post}}] - \mathbb{E}[D_i]\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}]
\]
\[
= p\,\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}} \mid D_i = 1] - p\Bigl(p\,\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}} \mid D_i = 1] + (1-p)\,\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}} \mid D_i = 0]\Bigr)
\]
\[
= p(1-p)\Bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}} \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}} \mid D_i = 0]\Bigr)
\]
Dividing by \(\text{Var}(D_i) = p(1-p)\):
\[
\beta_D = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}} \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}} \mid D_i = 0] \qquad \blacksquare
\]



Let \(Y_{i,\text{post}}^1\) and \(Y_{i,\text{post}}^0\) denote the potential post-treatment outcomes. Under random assignment, \(D_i\) is independent of potential outcomes:
\[
D_i \perp \bigl(Y_{i,\text{post}}^0,\; Y_{i,\text{post}}^1\bigr)
\]
This means selection bias is absent:
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}} \mid D_i = 1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}^1 \mid D_i = 1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}^1]
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}} \mid D_i = 0] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}^0 \mid D_i = 0] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}^0]
\]
Substituting into the result from (a):
\[
\beta_D = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}^1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}^0] = ATE \qquad \blacksquare
\]



In the DiD model \(Y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_D D_i + \beta_{\text{post}}\text{Post}_t + \beta_{DD}(D_i \times \text{Post}_t) + U_{it}\) with \(\mathbb{E}[U_{it}] = 0\), the four conditional means are:









\(D_i = 0\)
\(D_i = 1\)




\(\text{Post}_t = 0\)
\(\beta_0\)
\(\beta_0 + \beta_D\)


\(\text{Post}_t = 1\)
\(\beta_0 + \beta_{\text{post}}\)
\(\beta_0 + \beta_D + \beta_{\text{post}} + \beta_{DD}\)



The DiD coefficient is recovered by differencing twice:
\[
\beta_{DD} = \underbrace{\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid D\!=\!1, \text{post}] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid D\!=\!1, \text{pre}]\bigr)}_{\text{change for treated}} - \underbrace{\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid D\!=\!0, \text{post}] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid D\!=\!0, \text{pre}]\bigr)}_{\text{change for control}}
\]
Under random assignment, \(D_i \perp (Y_{i,\text{pre}},\, Y_{i,\text{post}}^0,\, Y_{i,\text{post}}^1)\), so both groups have the same expected pre-treatment outcome and counterfactual trend. Substituting potential outcomes:
\[
\beta_{DD} = \bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}^1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{pre}}]\bigr) - \bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}^0] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{pre}}]\bigr) = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}^1 - Y_{i,\text{post}}^0] = ATE \qquad \blacksquare
\]




Variance reduction. Differencing out pre-treatment outcomes removes time-invariant individual heterogeneity, reducing residual variance and improving statistical precision.
Robustness to imperfect randomization. Due to sampling variation, the realized treatment and control groups may differ in baseline characteristics. DiD corrects for any pre-existing difference in mean outcomes, making inference robust to residual imbalance in the experiment.

title: Problem Set 04
section: (a) OVB Formula for the Long Regression
text:
(a) OVB Formula for the Long Regression
The hint is to demean both sides and apply the standard OLS formula \((\tilde{X}'\tilde{X})^{-1}\tilde{X}'\tilde{Y}\), where \(\tilde{X}\) is the \(N \times 2\) matrix of demeaned regressors. In the population limit, this gives the 2×2 system with inverse:
\[
\text{plim}\ \hat{\beta}_D^L = \frac{\text{Var}(X_i)\,\text{Cov}(D_i, Y_i) - \text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)\,\text{Cov}(X_i, Y_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)\,\text{Var}(X_i) - \text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)^2}
\]
Dividing numerator and denominator by \(\text{Var}(X_i)\):
\[
\text{plim}\ \hat{\beta}_D^L = \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, Y_i) - \dfrac{\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)}{\text{Var}(X_i)}\,\text{Cov}(X_i, Y_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i) - \dfrac{\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)^2}{\text{Var}(X_i)}}
\]
Substituting \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_D D_i + \beta_X X_i + U_i\):
\[
\text{Cov}(D_i, Y_i) = \beta_D\,\text{Var}(D_i) + \beta_X\,\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i) + \text{Cov}(D_i, U_i)
\]
\[
\text{Cov}(X_i, Y_i) = \beta_D\,\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i) + \beta_X\,\text{Var}(X_i) + \text{Cov}(X_i, U_i)
\]
The numerator becomes:
\[
\beta_D\,\text{Var}(D_i) + \beta_X\,\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i) + \text{Cov}(D_i, U_i) - \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)}{\text{Var}(X_i)}\Bigl[\beta_D\,\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i) + \beta_X\,\text{Var}(X_i) + \text{Cov}(X_i, U_i)\Bigr]
\]
\[
= \beta_D\!\left[\text{Var}(D_i) - \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)^2}{\text{Var}(X_i)}\right] + \text{Cov}(D_i, U_i) - \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)}{\text{Var}(X_i)}\,\text{Cov}(X_i, U_i)
\]
Dividing by the denominator:
\[
\text{plim}\ \hat{\beta}_D^L = \beta_D + \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, U_i) - \dfrac{\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)}{\text{Var}(X_i)}\,\text{Cov}(X_i, U_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i) - \dfrac{\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)^2}{\text{Var}(X_i)}} \qquad \blacksquare
\]

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(b) Conditional Mean Independence
Suppose \(\mathbb{E}[U_i \mid D_i, X_i] = \mathbb{E}[U_i \mid X_i] = \delta_0 + \delta_1 X_i\). By iterated expectations:
\[
\text{Cov}(D_i, U_i) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(D_i - \mathbb{E}[D_i])\,\mathbb{E}[U_i \mid D_i, X_i]\bigr] = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(D_i - \mathbb{E}[D_i])(\delta_0 + \delta_1 X_i)\bigr] = \delta_1\,\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)
\]
\[
\text{Cov}(X_i, U_i) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(X_i - \mathbb{E}[X_i])(\delta_0 + \delta_1 X_i)\bigr] = \delta_1\,\text{Var}(X_i)
\]
Substituting into the numerator from (a):
\[
\delta_1\,\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i) - \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)}{\text{Var}(X_i)}\,\delta_1\,\text{Var}(X_i) = 0
\]
So \(\text{plim}\ \hat{\beta}_D^L = \beta_D\). \(\blacksquare\)
For \(\hat{\beta}_X^L\), the symmetric formula (swapping \(D\) and \(X\)) gives numerator \(= \delta_1\,\text{Var}(X_i) - \dfrac{\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)}\,\delta_1\,\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i) = \delta_1\!\left[\text{Var}(X_i) - \dfrac{\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i)^2}{\text{Var}(D_i)}\right]\), so:
\[
\text{plim}\ \hat{\beta}_X^L = \beta_X + \delta_1 \qquad \blacksquare
\]

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(c) Relevance for RCTs
In an RCT, \(D_i\) is randomly assigned, so \(\text{Cov}(D_i, X_i) = 0\) by construction. The formula from (a) reduces to:
\[
\text{plim}\ \hat{\beta}_D^L = \beta_D + \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, U_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)}
\]
Random assignment also ensures \(\text{Cov}(D_i, U_i) = 0\), so \(\hat{\beta}_D^L\) is consistent regardless of whether \(X_i\) is included. The result from (b) formalizes this: conditional mean independence holds in an RCT because \(D_i \perp U_i\) by design. Adding \(X_i\) as a covariate does not bias the estimate of \(\beta_D\) but does reduce residual variance, improving precision. The coefficient \(\hat{\beta}_X^L\) absorbs the correlation between \(X_i\) and \(U_i\) through \(\delta_1\) and should not be given a causal interpretation.

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(a) OLS with a Binary Regressor
Regressing \(Y_i\) on binary \(X_i\) and a constant, the two OLS FOCs are:
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_0}: \quad n\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 n_1 = \sum_i Y_i \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\frac{n_1}{n} = \bar{Y} \tag{1}
\]
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_1}: \quad \hat{\beta}_0\sum_i X_i + \hat{\beta}_1\sum_i X_i^2 = \sum_i X_i Y_i
\]
Since \(X_i^2 = X_i\) for binary \(X_i\), the second FOC becomes \(\hat{\beta}_0 n_1 + \hat{\beta}_1 n_1 = n_1\bar{Y}_1\), i.e.:
\[
\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 = \bar{Y}_1 \tag{2}
\]
Using \(\bar{Y} = (n_0\bar{Y}_0 + n_1\bar{Y}_1)/n\) and substituting (2) into (1):
\[
\hat{\beta}_0\frac{n_0}{n} + \bar{Y}_1\frac{n_1}{n} = \frac{n_0\bar{Y}_0 + n_1\bar{Y}_1}{n} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y}_0 \qquad \blacksquare
\]
From (2): \(\hat{\beta}_1 = \bar{Y}_1 - \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(b) Baseline Regression
Regressing tscorek on sck, the coefficient gives the difference in mean test scores between students in small and regular classes, which by (a) equals \(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0\). The estimate is approximately 5-6 points. Using the sample standard deviation of test scores as a benchmark (roughly 73 points), this corresponds to an effect size of about 0.07-0.08 standard deviations, which is a small effect economically. The estimate is statistically significant at conventional levels given the sample size.

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(c) School Fixed Effects
Including school fixed effects controls for all school-level characteristics that affect both class assignment and test scores: school resources, neighborhood composition, principal quality, and how strictly randomization was enforced within each school. Even within the STAR experiment, schools differ systematically. The FE estimate is preferred because it relies only on within-school variation in class assignment, removing between-school confounders and giving a cleaner comparison of students who attend the same school but were randomly assigned to different class types.

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(d) Robust Standard Errors
The researcher is only partially correct. Random assignment of \(D_1\) ensures \(\mathbb{E}[U_i \mid D_1] = 0\), so OLS is consistent and unbiased. However, random assignment does not imply homoskedasticity: \(\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(U_i \mid D_{1i})\) may differ across treatment and control groups, for example if small classes reduce outcome dispersion. In that case, classical standard errors are invalid and robust standard errors are appropriate.
More importantly, students within the same school share a common environment, inducing within-school error correlation. Clustered standard errors are the preferred choice in this application (see part (e)).

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(e) Clustered Standard Errors
Within each school, students face the same principal, neighborhood, peer composition, and are drawn from the same pool of teachers. This shared environment induces within-school correlation in test scores even after conditioning on treatment. Treating these observations as independent underestimates the true sampling variance, produces standard errors that are too small, and inflates \(t\)-statistics.
The school is the natural unit of randomization in STAR: treatment was assigned to class types within each school. Clustering at the school level accounts for this within-cluster correlation. The clustered standard errors are typically larger than robust standard errors, raising the bar for statistical significance and giving a more honest picture of estimation uncertainty.

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(f) Randomization Inference
ritest implements randomization inference by repeatedly permuting the treatment variable across its observed support and recomputing the test statistic (here, \(\hat{\beta}_{sck}\)) under each permutation. The resulting distribution is the exact finite-sample null distribution, giving \(p\)-values that do not rely on asymptotic approximations or distributional assumptions. Since the STAR experiment randomly assigned students to class types, any permutation of the treatment labels is a valid hypothetical realization of the randomization, making the procedure directly interpretable and appropriate here.

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(g) Balance Tests
Regressing sck on boy, freelunk, and totexpk separately tests whether pre-determined individual and teacher characteristics are systematically correlated with treatment assignment. Under successful randomization, these coefficients should be statistically indistinguishable from zero. The key thing to look for is statistical significance: a significant coefficient would indicate that treatment is not balanced on that characteristic, suggesting either imperfect randomization or post-assignment selection.

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(h) Including Covariates
Since sck is randomly assigned and uncorrelated with boy, freelunk, and totexpk by construction, including these variables does not change the expected value of \(\hat{\beta}_{sck}\). We expect the treatment coefficient to remain roughly unchanged. What should change is precision: removing variation in tscorek attributable to observable characteristics reduces the residual variance, yielding a smaller standard error.
The parameter estimates on boy, freelunk, and totexpk are not causal. These variables are not randomly assigned and may be correlated with unobserved determinants of test scores.

title: Problem Set 04
text:
(i) Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
The model including interactions is:
\[
Y_i = \alpha + \beta_{sck}\,\text{sck}_i + \beta_b\,\text{boy}_i + \beta_f\,\text{freelunk}_i + \beta_t\,\text{totexpk}_i + \beta_{sb}\,\text{sck\_boy}_i + \beta_{sf}\,\text{sck\_freelunk}_i + \beta_{st}\,\text{sck\_totexpk}_i + \gamma_s + U_i
\]
where \(\gamma_s\) denotes school fixed effects. The coefficients are interpreted as:

\(\beta_{sck}\): treatment effect for the baseline group (girl, no free lunch, zero teacher experience)
\(\beta_{sb}\): differential treatment effect for boys relative to girls
\(\beta_{sf}\): differential treatment effect for free-lunch recipients relative to non-recipients
\(\beta_{st}\): change in treatment effect per additional year of teacher experience

The F-test of \(H_0: \beta_{sb} = \beta_{sf} = \beta_{st} = 0\) tests the joint null hypothesis that the treatment effect is homogeneous across these dimensions. Rejection indicates that the class size effect varies meaningfully with individual or teacher characteristics.

title: Problem Set 02
text:
You have a sample of \(N\) individuals for \(T\) years. Suppose you estimate by Pooled OLS the annual income equation:
\[
y_{it} = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1\text{ed}_i + \alpha_2\text{age}_{it} + \alpha_3(\text{ed}_i \times \text{age}_{it}) + \gamma y_{i,t-1} + u_{it}
\]
where \(\text{ed}_i\) is years of education, \(\text{age}_{it}\) is age of individual \(i\) in period \(t\), and \(u_{it}\) represents all unobservables.


The POLS estimator takes the form:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{POLS} = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'y_i\right)
\]
where \(x_{it} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \text{ed}_i & \text{age}_{it} & \text{ed}_i \times \text{age}_{it} & y_{i,t-1} \end{bmatrix}'\).
If the true model contains a time-invariant unobserved effect \(f_i\), so that \(u_{it} = f_i + v_{it}\), then the sampling error of POLS is:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{POLS} - \beta = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i X_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i X_i'(f_i + v_i)\right) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X_i'X_i]^{-1}\left(\mathbb{E}[X_i'f_i] + \mathbb{E}[X_i'v_i]\right)
\]
For consistency, we need \(\mathbb{E}[X_i'f_i] + \mathbb{E}[X_i'v_i] = 0\). The sufficient assumptions are:
1. No time-invariant unobservable (\(f_i = 0\)). Since \(y_{i,t-1}\) appears as a regressor, iterating the model backward gives:
\[
y_{i,t-1} = \sum_{s=0}^{t-2}\gamma^s\left(\alpha_0 + \alpha_1\text{ed}_i + \alpha_2\text{age}_{i,t-1-s} + \alpha_3(\text{ed}_i \times \text{age}_{i,t-1-s}) + f_i + v_{i,t-1-s}\right) + \gamma^{t-1}y_{i0}
\]
so \(\mathbb{E}[y_{i,t-1}f_i]\) contains \(\sum_{s=0}^{t-2}\gamma^s\mathbb{E}[f_i^2] \neq 0\) whenever \(f_i \neq 0\). Thus, even with weak exogeneity of the other regressors, \(\mathbb{E}[X_i'f_i] \neq 0\) unless \(f_i = 0\). Note also that \(|\gamma| < 1\) is required for stationarity, which is consistent with the estimated \(\hat{\gamma} = 0.82\).
2. No serial correlation: \(\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(v_{it}, v_{is} \mid x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{iT}) = 0\) for \(t \neq s\).
This ensures that \(\mathbb{E}[y_{i,t-1}v_{it}] = 0\). Without it, \(y_{i,t-1}\) would contain \(v_{i,t-1}\) which under serial correlation would be correlated with \(v_{it}\).
3. Weak exogeneity: \(\mathbb{E}[v_{it} \mid \{x_{is}\}_{s \leq t}] = 0\).
Since POLS only captures contemporaneous correlations: \[
\mathbb{E}[X_i'v_i] = \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[x_{it}'v_{it}] = 0
\] under weak exogeneity.
4. No multicollinearity: \(\mathbb{E}[X_i'X_i]\) has full column rank (is invertible).
Under all four assumptions, \(\hat{\beta}^{POLS} \xrightarrow{p} \beta\).



For POLS we had to assume \(f_i = 0\). If individual-level effects exist (random or fixed), we use the Anderson-Hsiao IV estimator on the first-differenced model.
Rewrite the model as:
\[
y_{it} = B_{it}'\alpha + y_{i,t-1}\gamma + f_i + u_{it}, \quad B_{it} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \text{ed}_i & \text{age}_{it} & \text{ed}_i \times \text{age}_{it} \end{bmatrix}'
\]
Taking first differences eliminates \(f_i\):
\[
\Delta y_{it} = \Delta B_{it}'\alpha_{\text{new}} + \Delta y_{i,t-1}\gamma + \Delta u_{it}
\]
where \(\Delta B_{it} = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta\text{age}_{it} \\ \Delta(\text{ed}_i \times \text{age}_{it}) \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\alpha_{\text{new}} = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_2 \\ \alpha_3 \end{bmatrix}\). The constant and \(\text{ed}_i\) drop out since they are time-invariant.
OLS on this model is inconsistent since \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\) contains \(u_{i,t-1}\), which also appears in \(\Delta u_{it}\). The instrument \(y_{i,t-2}\) is valid:

Relevance: \(\Delta y_{i,t-1} = y_{i,t-1} - y_{i,t-2}\) contains \(y_{i,t-2}\) directly, so the correlation is non-zero as long as \(\gamma \neq 0\) and \(\gamma \neq 1\) (no unit root). Given \(\hat{\gamma} = 0.82\) this is plausible.
Exogeneity: Under serially uncorrelated errors, \(\mathbb{E}[y_{i,t-2}\Delta u_{it}] = \mathbb{E}[y_{i,t-2}(u_{it} - u_{i,t-1})] = 0\).

The instrument matrix for each \(i\) is:
\[
Z_i = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta B_{i2}' & y_{i0} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ \Delta B_{iT}' & y_{i,T-2} \end{bmatrix}, \quad \hat{\beta}^{AH} = \left(\sum_i Z_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i Z_i'\Delta y_i\right)
\]
Consistency: Under the exclusion restriction \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'\Delta u_i] = 0\) and the rank condition, by LLN and CMT:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{AH} \xrightarrow{p} \beta + \mathbb{E}[Z_i'\Delta X_i]^{-1}\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Z_i'\Delta u_i]}_{=0} = \beta
\]
Implications for POLS: A meaningful difference between \(\hat{\beta}^{AH}\) and \(\hat{\beta}^{POLS}\) provides evidence of time-invariant unobserved effects \(f_i\), since AH is consistent under both fixed and random effects while POLS is not. The model is just-identified so we cannot test the exclusion restriction via Sargan-Hansen. We can, however, test instrument relevance (\(\gamma \neq 0\), \(\gamma \neq 1\)) and test for second-order serial correlation in \(\Delta u_{it}\) to validate the underlying assumptions.

title: Problem Set 02
text:
The POLS estimator takes the form:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{POLS} = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'y_i\right)
\]
where \(x_{it} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \text{ed}_i & \text{age}_{it} & \text{ed}_i \times \text{age}_{it} & y_{i,t-1} \end{bmatrix}'\).
If the true model contains a time-invariant unobserved effect \(f_i\), so that \(u_{it} = f_i + v_{it}\), then the sampling error of POLS is:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{POLS} - \beta = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i X_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i X_i'(f_i + v_i)\right) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X_i'X_i]^{-1}\left(\mathbb{E}[X_i'f_i] + \mathbb{E}[X_i'v_i]\right)
\]
For consistency, we need \(\mathbb{E}[X_i'f_i] + \mathbb{E}[X_i'v_i] = 0\). The sufficient assumptions are:
1. No time-invariant unobservable (\(f_i = 0\)). Since \(y_{i,t-1}\) appears as a regressor, iterating the model backward gives:
\[
y_{i,t-1} = \sum_{s=0}^{t-2}\gamma^s\left(\alpha_0 + \alpha_1\text{ed}_i + \alpha_2\text{age}_{i,t-1-s} + \alpha_3(\text{ed}_i \times \text{age}_{i,t-1-s}) + f_i + v_{i,t-1-s}\right) + \gamma^{t-1}y_{i0}
\]
so \(\mathbb{E}[y_{i,t-1}f_i]\) contains \(\sum_{s=0}^{t-2}\gamma^s\mathbb{E}[f_i^2] \neq 0\) whenever \(f_i \neq 0\). Thus, even with weak exogeneity of the other regressors, \(\mathbb{E}[X_i'f_i] \neq 0\) unless \(f_i = 0\). Note also that \(|\gamma| < 1\) is required for stationarity, which is consistent with the estimated \(\hat{\gamma} = 0.82\).
2. No serial correlation: \(\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(v_{it}, v_{is} \mid x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{iT}) = 0\) for \(t \neq s\).
This ensures that \(\mathbb{E}[y_{i,t-1}v_{it}] = 0\). Without it, \(y_{i,t-1}\) would contain \(v_{i,t-1}\) which under serial correlation would be correlated with \(v_{it}\).
3. Weak exogeneity: \(\mathbb{E}[v_{it} \mid \{x_{is}\}_{s \leq t}] = 0\).
Since POLS only captures contemporaneous correlations: \[
\mathbb{E}[X_i'v_i] = \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[x_{it}'v_{it}] = 0
\] under weak exogeneity.
4. No multicollinearity: \(\mathbb{E}[X_i'X_i]\) has full column rank (is invertible).
Under all four assumptions, \(\hat{\beta}^{POLS} \xrightarrow{p} \beta\).

title: Problem Set 02
text:
For POLS we had to assume \(f_i = 0\). If individual-level effects exist (random or fixed), we use the Anderson-Hsiao IV estimator on the first-differenced model.
Rewrite the model as:
\[
y_{it} = B_{it}'\alpha + y_{i,t-1}\gamma + f_i + u_{it}, \quad B_{it} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \text{ed}_i & \text{age}_{it} & \text{ed}_i \times \text{age}_{it} \end{bmatrix}'
\]
Taking first differences eliminates \(f_i\):
\[
\Delta y_{it} = \Delta B_{it}'\alpha_{\text{new}} + \Delta y_{i,t-1}\gamma + \Delta u_{it}
\]
where \(\Delta B_{it} = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta\text{age}_{it} \\ \Delta(\text{ed}_i \times \text{age}_{it}) \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\alpha_{\text{new}} = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_2 \\ \alpha_3 \end{bmatrix}\). The constant and \(\text{ed}_i\) drop out since they are time-invariant.
OLS on this model is inconsistent since \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\) contains \(u_{i,t-1}\), which also appears in \(\Delta u_{it}\). The instrument \(y_{i,t-2}\) is valid:

Relevance: \(\Delta y_{i,t-1} = y_{i,t-1} - y_{i,t-2}\) contains \(y_{i,t-2}\) directly, so the correlation is non-zero as long as \(\gamma \neq 0\) and \(\gamma \neq 1\) (no unit root). Given \(\hat{\gamma} = 0.82\) this is plausible.
Exogeneity: Under serially uncorrelated errors, \(\mathbb{E}[y_{i,t-2}\Delta u_{it}] = \mathbb{E}[y_{i,t-2}(u_{it} - u_{i,t-1})] = 0\).

The instrument matrix for each \(i\) is:
\[
Z_i = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta B_{i2}' & y_{i0} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ \Delta B_{iT}' & y_{i,T-2} \end{bmatrix}, \quad \hat{\beta}^{AH} = \left(\sum_i Z_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i Z_i'\Delta y_i\right)
\]
Consistency: Under the exclusion restriction \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'\Delta u_i] = 0\) and the rank condition, by LLN and CMT:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{AH} \xrightarrow{p} \beta + \mathbb{E}[Z_i'\Delta X_i]^{-1}\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Z_i'\Delta u_i]}_{=0} = \beta
\]
Implications for POLS: A meaningful difference between \(\hat{\beta}^{AH}\) and \(\hat{\beta}^{POLS}\) provides evidence of time-invariant unobserved effects \(f_i\), since AH is consistent under both fixed and random effects while POLS is not. The model is just-identified so we cannot test the exclusion restriction via Sargan-Hansen. We can, however, test instrument relevance (\(\gamma \neq 0\), \(\gamma \neq 1\)) and test for second-order serial correlation in \(\Delta u_{it}\) to validate the underlying assumptions.

title: Problem Set 02
section: (a) Properties of FD-OLS Under Different Assumptions on \(z_{it}\)
text:
(a) Properties of FD-OLS Under Different Assumptions on \(z_{it}\)
First differencing eliminates \(f_i\), so its relationship with \(z_{it}\) is no longer relevant to consistency. The FD model is:
\[
\Delta y_i = \Delta X_i\theta + \Delta u_i, \quad \theta = \begin{bmatrix}\beta \\ \gamma\end{bmatrix}, \quad \Delta X_i = \begin{bmatrix}\Delta x_i & \Delta z_i\end{bmatrix}
\]
The FD-OLS estimator has the form:
\[
\hat{\theta}^{FD} = \theta + \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta u_i\right) \xrightarrow{p} \theta + \mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta X_i]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta u_i]
\]
so consistency requires \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta u_i] = 0\).
Case 1: Strictly exogenous \(z_{it}\) — \(E(u_{it} \mid z_{i1}, \ldots, z_{iT}, f_i) = 0\)
By LIE, \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta u_{it} \mid z_{i1}, \ldots, z_{iT}] = 0\) and similarly for \(x_{it}\) under its strict exogeneity assumption. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta u_i] = 0\) and \(\hat{\theta}^{FD}\) is consistent.
For asymptotic normality, note \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta u_i\Delta u_i' \mid X_i, Z_i] = \sigma_u^2 H\) where:
\[
H = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & \cdots \\ -1 & 2 & -1 & \cdots \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & \cdots \\ \vdots & & & \ddots \end{pmatrix}_{(T-1)\times(T-1)}
\]
and \(\sqrt{N}(\hat{\theta}^{FD} - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, M_{\Delta X\Delta X}^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'H\Delta X_i]M_{\Delta X\Delta X}^{-1})\).
FD is not efficient here since \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta u_i\Delta u_i'] \neq \sigma_e^2 I_{T-1}\) (i.e., \(u_{it}\) is not a random walk). Efficiency depends on the structure of \(f_i\):

If \(\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i, Z_i] = 0\) (random effects): the feasible GLS (RE) estimator is efficient.
If \(\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i, Z_i] \neq 0\) (fixed effects): the FE estimator is efficient.

Case 2: Weakly exogenous \(z_{it}\) — \(E(u_{it} \mid z_{i1}, \ldots, z_{it}, f_i) = 0\)
FD-OLS is inconsistent:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\Delta z_{it}\Delta u_{it}] = \mathbb{E}[z_{it}u_{it}] - \mathbb{E}[z_{it}u_{i,t-1}] - \mathbb{E}[z_{i,t-1}u_{it}] + \mathbb{E}[z_{i,t-1}u_{i,t-1}] = -\mathbb{E}[z_{it}u_{i,t-1}] \neq 0
\]
since weak exogeneity implies \(z_{it}\) may be correlated with past errors. Since it is inconsistent, it cannot be efficient. A valid instrument for \(\Delta z_{it}\) would be \(z_{i,t-1}\), which is predetermined and relevant.
Case 3: Endogenous \(z_{it}\) — \(E(u_{it} \mid Z_i) \neq 0\)
FD-OLS is inconsistent. Lagged levels of \(z_{it}\) no longer satisfy the exclusion restriction, so external instruments are required. If just-identified, use IV; if over-identified, use two-step GMM.

title: Problem Set 02
section: (b) Efficient Estimation When \(T=5\) and \(E(u_{it} \mid z_{i1}, \ldots, z_{i,t-1}, f_i) = 0\)
text:
(b) Efficient Estimation When \(T=5\) and \(E(u_{it} \mid z_{i1}, \ldots, z_{i,t-1}, f_i) = 0\)
This is strictly weaker than weak exogeneity: contemporaneous \(z_{it}\) is correlated with \(u_{it}\), so \(z_{i,t-1}\) fails as an instrument. We need \(z_{i,t-2}\) as the instrument for \(\Delta z_{it}\).

(i) The Estimator
With \(T = 5\), first differencing gives \(T - 2 = 3\) usable periods (\(t = 3, 4, 5\)), since \(\Delta z_{i2}\) would require \(z_{i0}\) as instrument. The vectors are:
\[
\Delta y_i = \begin{bmatrix}\Delta y_{i3}\\\Delta y_{i4}\\\Delta y_{i5}\end{bmatrix}, \quad \Delta X_i = \begin{bmatrix}\Delta x_{i3} & \Delta z_{i3}\\\Delta x_{i4} & \Delta z_{i4}\\\Delta x_{i5} & \Delta z_{i5}\end{bmatrix}, \quad Z_i = \begin{bmatrix}\Delta x_{i3} & z_{i1}\\\Delta x_{i4} & z_{i2}\\\Delta x_{i5} & z_{i3}\end{bmatrix}
\]
The instrument \(z_{i,t-2}\) is valid since:
\[
\mathbb{E}[z_{i,t-2}\Delta u_{it}] = \mathbb{E}\left[z_{i,t-2}\mathbb{E}[u_{it} - u_{i,t-1} \mid z_{i1}, \ldots, z_{i,t-1}, f_i]\right] = 0
\]
by the stated assumption. The first-step IV estimator is:
\[
\hat{\theta}^{IV1} = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'\Delta y_i\right)
\]
which is consistent: \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'\Delta u_i] = 0\) by strict exogeneity of \(x_{it}\) and the instrument assumption for \(z_{it-2}\).
Since \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta u_i\Delta u_i' \mid X_i, Z_i] = \sigma_u^2 H_{3\times 3}\), efficient estimation requires feasible GLS. Using residuals from the first step \(\hat{\Delta u}_i = \Delta y_i - \Delta X_i\hat{\theta}^{IV1}\), estimate:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_u^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3N - 2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=3}^5\hat{\Delta u}_{it}^2, \qquad \hat{V} = \hat{\sigma}_u^2\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 & 0\\-1 & 2 & -1\\0 & -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}
\]
The efficient two-step IV estimator is:
\[
\hat{\theta}^{IV2} = \left(\sum_i Z_i'\hat{V}^{-1}\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i Z_i'\hat{V}^{-1}\Delta y_i\right)
\]


(ii) Asymptotic Variance
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\theta}^{IV2} - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0,\ \mathbb{E}[Z_i'V^{-1}\Delta X_i]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[Z_i'V^{-1}Z_i]\mathbb{E}[Z_i'V^{-1}\Delta X_i]^{-1}\right)
\]
The middle term simplifies via LIE:
\[
\mathbb{E}[Z_i'V^{-1}\Delta u_i\Delta u_i'V^{-1}Z_i] = \mathbb{E}[Z_i'V^{-1}\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\Delta u_i\Delta u_i'\mid X_i, Z_i]}_{=V}V^{-1}Z_i] = \mathbb{E}[Z_i'V^{-1}Z_i]
\]
so the asymptotic variance is \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'V^{-1}\Delta X_i]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[Z_i'V^{-1}Z_i]\mathbb{E}[Z_i'V^{-1}\Delta X_i]^{-1}\).

title: Problem Set 02
text:
(c) When \(z_{it} = y_{i,t-1}\) and \(\gamma = 1\)
The model becomes:
\[
y_{it} = \alpha + x_{it}\beta + y_{i,t-1} + f_i + u_{it}
\]
Since \(\gamma = 1\) is known, we do not need to estimate it. First differencing eliminates both \(f_i\) and the \(y_{i,t-1}\) term:
\[
\Delta y_{it} = \Delta x_{it}\beta + \Delta u_{it}
\]
so the model reduces to a univariate FD regression with \(T - 1 = 4\) usable periods (\(t = 2, \ldots, 5\)). Since \(x_{it}\) is strictly exogenous, OLS on the FD model is consistent.
Step 1 — FD-OLS:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{FD1} = \left(\sum_i \Delta x_i'\Delta x_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i \Delta x_i'\Delta y_i\right)
\]
By strict exogeneity and LIE, \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta x_i'\Delta u_i] = 0\), so \(\hat{\beta}^{FD1} \xrightarrow{p} \beta\). Its asymptotic variance is \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta x_i'\Delta x_i]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\Delta x_i'V_{4\times4}\Delta x_i]\mathbb{E}[\Delta x_i'\Delta x_i]^{-1}\) where:
\[
V_{4\times4} = \sigma_u^2\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 & 0\\-1 & 2 & -1 & 0\\0 & -1 & 2 & -1\\0 & 0 & -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}
\]
Step 2 — Feasible GLS: Estimate \(\hat{V}\) using residuals \(\hat{\Delta u}_{it} = \Delta y_{it} - \Delta x_{it}\hat{\beta}^{FD1}\):
\[
\hat{\sigma}_u^2 = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=2}^5\hat{\Delta u}_{it}^2, \qquad \hat{V} \xrightarrow{p} V
\]
The efficient estimator is:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{FD2} = \left(\sum_i \Delta x_i'\hat{V}^{-1}\Delta x_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i \Delta x_i'\hat{V}^{-1}\Delta y_i\right)
\]
with asymptotic variance:
\[
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}^{FD2}) = \mathbb{E}[\Delta x_i'V^{-1}\Delta x_i]^{-1}
\]

title: Problem Set 02
section: (b) FD vs. FE on the Full Sample
text:
(b) FD vs. FE on the Full Sample
With all time periods included, FE and FD produce different estimates. This is expected: FE subtracts each individual’s time mean (computed over all available \(T\)), while FD takes differences between adjacent periods. They are different transformations of the data and, for \(T > 2\), exploit different variation.
There is also a practical difference in handling unbalanced panels: FE can use individuals with gaps (e.g., observed at \(t = 1\) and \(t = 3\) but not \(t = 2\)) by averaging over all available periods, while FD requires consecutive observations and will drop or truncate such individuals.
Efficiency: FD is efficient when \(u_{it}\) follows a random walk (\(\Delta u_{it}\) is i.i.d.). FE is efficient when \(u_{it}\) is i.i.d. over time (no serial correlation). In practice, the truth typically lies somewhere between these extremes. We would generally expect FE to be more efficient when serial correlation in \(u_{it}\) is low, which is the more common assumption for short panels.
The FD estimator tends to have a higher standard error than FE when \(u_{it}\) is close to i.i.d., since differencing amplifies noise.
Making SEs robust: To allow for arbitrary heteroskedasticity and serial correlation in \(u_{it}\) within individuals, cluster standard errors at the individual level. This imposes no parametric assumption on \(\mathbb{E}[u_iu_i']\) and is valid as \(N \to \infty\).

title: Problem Set 02
section: (c) Dynamic FE with Lagged Life Satisfaction
text:
(c) Dynamic FE with Lagged Life Satisfaction
Including \(y_{i,t-1}\) as a regressor in the FE model:
\[
y_{it} = \alpha + y_{i,t-1}\gamma + \mathbf{x}_{it}'\beta + f_i + u_{it}
\]
the FE estimator is inconsistent due to the Nickell (1981) bias. The demeaned lagged variable \(\tilde{y}_{i,t-1} = y_{i,t-1} - \bar{y}_{i-}\) is correlated with the demeaned error \(\tilde{u}_{it} = u_{it} - \bar{u}_{i+}\) because \(\bar{u}_{i+}\) includes \(u_{i,t-1}\) while \(y_{i,t-1}\) depends on \(u_{i,t-1}\). This bias is of order \(O(1/T)\) and is substantial in short panels.

title: Problem Set 02
text:
(d) Arellano-Bond
To consistently estimate the dynamic model, we use the Arellano-Bond estimator. First differencing removes \(f_i\):
\[
\Delta y_{it} = \gamma\Delta y_{i,t-1} + \Delta\mathbf{x}_{it}'\beta + \Delta u_{it}
\]
Under serially uncorrelated \(u_{it}\), \(y_{i,t-2}\) and deeper lags are valid instruments for \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\). Arellano-Bond exploits all available moment conditions simultaneously in a GMM framework.
We implement the two-step estimator (xtabond with lags(1) maxldep(2) twostep). The two-step estimator is asymptotically efficient but standard errors in finite samples are typically downward biased; the Windmeijer (2005) correction addresses this.
We test for serial correlation in the differenced residuals via the Arellano-Bond \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) statistics:

\(m_1\): AR(1) in \(\widehat{\Delta u}_{it}\) — expected to be significant even under correct specification, since \(\Delta u_{it}\) and \(\Delta u_{i,t-1}\) share \(u_{i,t-1}\).
\(m_2\): AR(2) in \(\widehat{\Delta u}_{it}\) — under \(H_0\) (no serial correlation in \(u_{it}\)), this should be zero. A significant \(m_2\) indicates that \(y_{i,t-2}\) is not a valid instrument.

title: Synthetic Control Methods
text:
Synthetic control methods have become standard in empirical work since the early 2000s. The setting is one where treatment is implemented at an aggregate level; e.g., a policy applied to a country, state, or city; and data are available on only a small number of such units. Traditional regression requires large samples and is poorly suited to this setting. Comparative case studies have long been used to evaluate aggregate interventions, but the selection of comparison units is typically informal and hard to replicate. Synthetic control methods formalize this by constructing a weighted combination of untreated units that matches the treated unit’s pre-intervention characteristics as closely as possible.
Athey and Imbens (2017) describe synthetic controls as “arguably the most important innovation in the policy evaluation literature in the last 15 years.” The key idea is that a combination of unaffected units often provides a more appropriate comparison than any single unaffected unit alone. The overview below follows Abadie (2021, JEL) and the application of Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2015).



Suppose there are \(J + 1\) units indexed \(j = 1, \ldots, J + 1\). Unit \(j = 1\) is the treated unit and units \(j = 2, \ldots, J + 1\) form the donor pool – the set of untreated units not affected by the intervention. There are \(T\) time periods and the first \(T_0\) periods are before the intervention. For each unit \(j\) and period \(t\), the outcome \(Y_{jt}\) is observed. For each unit \(j\), a vector of \(k\) predictors \(X_{1j}, \ldots, X_{kj}\) is also observed. The predictors may include pre-intervention values of \(Y_{jt}\) and are themselves unaffected by the intervention.
Let \(Y^N_{jt}\) denote the potential outcome without intervention. Define \(Y^I_{1t}\) as the potential outcome for the treated unit under the intervention in post-intervention period \(t > T_0\). The treatment effect for the affected unit in period \(t\) is:
\[
\tau_{1t} = Y^I_{1t} - Y^N_{1t} \tag{1}
\]
While \(Y^I_{1t}\) is observed for \(t > T_0\), the counterfactual \(Y^N_{1t}\) is not. The goal is to estimate it. The treatment effect is allowed to vary over time.



Synthetic control methods approximate \(Y^N_{1t}\) using a weighted combination of donor pool outcomes. Given a weight vector \(\mathbf{W} = (w_2, \ldots, w_{J+1})'\), the synthetic control estimator of \(Y^N_{1t}\) and the corresponding treatment effect estimator are:
\[
\hat{Y}^N_{1t} = \sum_{j=2}^{J+1} w_j Y_{jt} \qquad \hat{\tau}_{1t} = Y^I_{1t} - \hat{Y}^N_{1t} \tag{2}
\]
To avoid extrapolation, weights are restricted to be non-negative and sum to one: \(w_j \geq 0\) and \(\sum_{j=2}^{J+1} w_j = 1\). Typically only a small number of donor units receive positive weights – the synthetic control is sparse.
Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003) propose choosing the synthetic control \(\mathbf{W}^* = (w_2^*, \ldots, w_{J+1}^*)'\) to minimize the distance between the treated unit’s predictor values and those of the weighted donor pool:
\[
\|\mathbf{X}_1 - \mathbf{X}_0 \mathbf{W}\| = \left(\sum_{h=1}^k v_h (X_{h1} - w_2 X_{h2} - \ldots - w_{J+1} X_{h,J+1})^2\right)^{1/2}
\]
subject to \(w_j \geq 0\) and \(w_2 + \ldots + w_{J+1} = 1\). Here \(\mathbf{X}_1\) is the \(k \times 1\) vector of predictor values for the treated unit and \(\mathbf{X}_0 = [\mathbf{X}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{X}_{J+1}]\) is the \(k \times J\) matrix of predictor values for the donor pool. The constants \(v_1, \ldots, v_k\) reflect the relative importance assigned to each predictor.
For a given diagonal matrix \(\mathbf{V}\) of importance weights, finding \(\mathbf{W}^*\) is a constrained quadratic optimization problem. Three approaches to choosing \(\mathbf{V}\) are common:

Use the inverse of the sample variance of each predictor \(X_{h1}, \ldots, X_{h,J+1}\).
Choose \(\mathbf{V}\) to minimize the mean squared prediction error of the synthetic control in the pre-intervention period.
Split the pre-intervention period into a training period and a validation period. Compute \(\mathbf{W}^*\) using training period data for a given \(\mathbf{V}\). Choose \(\mathbf{V}^*\) to minimize the MSPE in the validation period. The final weights are \(\mathbf{W}^* = \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{V}^*)\).




Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010) study the bias properties of the synthetic control estimator under a linear factor model:
\[
Y^N_{jt} = \delta_t + \boldsymbol{\theta}_t \mathbf{Z}_j + \boldsymbol{\lambda}_t \boldsymbol{\mu}_j + \varepsilon_{jt} \tag{3}
\]
where \(\delta_t\) is a common time trend, \(\mathbf{Z}_j\) is a vector of observed predictors with time-varying coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t\), \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_j\) is a vector of unobserved predictors with time-varying coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t\), and \(\varepsilon_{jt}\) are zero-mean transitory shocks. In the time-series literature, \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t\) and \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t\) are common factors and \(\mathbf{Z}_j\) and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_j\) are factor loadings.
This model nests the standard DiD and fixed effects panel models as a special case. Restricting \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t = \lambda\) to be time-invariant gives \(Y^N_{jt} = \delta_t + \boldsymbol{\theta}_t \mathbf{Z}_j + \lambda \boldsymbol{\mu}_j + \varepsilon_{jt}\), under which units with the same observed predictors follow parallel mean outcome trends. The linear factor model does not impose this restriction, allowing unobserved heterogeneity \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_j\) to have time-varying effects \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t\).
The bias of \(\hat{\tau}_{1t}\) depends positively on the scale of the transitory shocks \(\varepsilon_{jt}\) and negatively on the number of pre-intervention periods \(T_0\). A good pre-intervention fit – \(\mathbf{X}_1 \approx \mathbf{X}_0 \mathbf{W}^*\) – and the ability to reproduce the outcome trajectory over an extended pre-intervention period signal low bias.
Two practical implications follow. First, a large donor pool increases the risk of over-fitting, especially when \(T_0\) is small. Second, the donor pool should contain units that are similar to the treated unit in both observed attributes \(\mathbf{Z}_j\) and expected unobserved attributes \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_j\).



The credibility of the synthetic control estimator depends on its ability to track the pre-intervention trajectory of the outcome for the treated unit. The choice of predictors in \(\mathbf{X}_1\) and \(\mathbf{X}_0\) is a fundamental part of the estimation task.
Predictors should include summary measures of pre-intervention outcomes – for example, the average of \(Y_{jt}\) over a sub-period – along with other relevant covariates, rather than every annual pre-intervention outcome value. Using all annual outcomes as separate predictors increases over-fitting risk and tends to produce a dense synthetic control with poor bias properties. Summary measures lead to sparser weights and lower bias.
A data-driven approach to predictor selection:

Divide the pre-intervention period into a training period and a subsequent validation period.
Compute synthetic control weights using training period data for a candidate set of predictors.
Evaluate predictive fit using validation period data only.
Repeat for different predictor sets.
Choose the set with the best out-of-sample predictive power.




Abadie et al. (2010) propose a permutation inference procedure. The dynamic effect of the intervention is estimated separately for each unit in the donor pool, applying the same synthetic control method as if that unit had been treated. This produces a permutation distribution of “placebo effects.” The treatment is considered significant when the magnitude of the estimated effect for the treated unit is extreme relative to this distribution. The logic is similar to randomization inference in RCT settings.
One complication is that for some donor units, the synthetic control may not provide a good pre-intervention fit, so large post-intervention gaps may arise by construction rather than by treatment. The standard measure of pre-intervention fit is the root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE):
\[
R_j(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1 + 1} \sum_{t=t_1}^{t_2} (Y_{jt} - \hat{Y}^N_{jt})^2\right)^{1/2}
\]
Inference can be based on the permutation distribution after discarding placebo runs where \(R_j(1, T_0)\) is substantially larger than \(R_1(1, T_0)\), the pre-intervention RMSPE for the treated unit.



Compared to linear regression estimators, synthetic control methods have several advantages.


Synthetic control weights are non-negative and sum to one, so the estimated counterfactual always lies in the convex hull of the donor pool outcomes – no extrapolation occurs. A regression-based estimator of \(Y^N_{1t}\) uses weights \(\mathbf{W}^{reg} = \tilde{\mathbf{X}}_0'(\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_0 \tilde{\mathbf{X}}_0')^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{X}}_1\), where \(\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_0\) augments \(\mathbf{X}_0\) with a row of ones. While the regression weights sum to one, they may lie outside \([0, 1]\), meaning the fitted counterfactual may extrapolate outside the support of the data.



Regression uses extrapolation to guarantee a perfect fit of the treated unit’s characteristics by construction: \(\mathbf{X}_0 \mathbf{W}^{reg} = \mathbf{X}_1\) holds exactly even when the donor units are completely dissimilar to the treated unit. Synthetic controls, by contrast, make visible the actual discrepancy between the treated unit and the best convex combination of donor units. If the pre-intervention fit is poor, this is immediately apparent.



Because synthetic control coefficients are proper weights, the contribution of each comparison unit to the estimated counterfactual is explicit and interpretable. This allows the use of expert knowledge to evaluate whether the counterfactual is credible. In the German reunification application, the synthetic West Germany is a combination of Austria (0.42), Japan (0.16), Netherlands (0.09), Switzerland (0.11), and the United States (0.22).



Only a small number of donor units typically receive positive weight, making it straightforward to inspect and evaluate the estimated counterfactual. Sparsity can be further increased by imposing a bound on the number of non-zero weights in \(\mathbf{W}^*\). Regression estimators are typically not sparse.



Synthetic control methods do not require access to post-treatment outcomes in the design phase of the study. All design decisions – the donor pool, the predictors, the importance weights – can be made without knowing how they affect the conclusions. Weights can be computed and pre-registered before post-treatment outcomes are observed. This is a safeguard against specification searches and \(p\)-hacking, analogous to pre-analysis plans in RCTs.




There are some contextual conditions under which synthetic controls are appropriate tools for policy evaluation.
Effect size and volatility. The method estimates the effect of a single treatment on a single unit. Small effects will be hard to distinguish from the idiosyncratic transitory shocks \(\varepsilon_{jt}\). Note that volatility from the common factors \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t\) is differenced out by the construction of the synthetic control; the challenge comes specifically from unit-specific shocks.
Availability of a comparison group. The donor pool should exclude units affected by the same or similar interventions, units subject to large idiosyncratic shocks to \(Y_{jt}\), and units whose pre-intervention characteristics are too dissimilar from the treated unit. Including highly dissimilar units increases interpolation bias.
No anticipation. If forward-looking agents react in advance to the intervention, or if parts of the policy are put in place before the formal implementation date, the pre-intervention fit will be distorted and the estimator will be biased. If there are signs of anticipation, it is advisable to backdate the intervention start date.
No interference. The method relies on the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA): each unit’s outcome is unaffected by other units’ treatment status. This can be enforced by removing from the donor pool units whose outcomes are likely to be affected by the intervention on the treated unit. There is some tension here, since such units are often the most geographically proximate and thus the most similar. If spillover concerns remain, one can often deduce the direction of the resulting bias.
Convex hull condition. The treated unit’s pre-intervention characteristics must fall close to the convex hull of the donor units’ characteristics. If no combination of untreated units can credibly approximate the treated unit, the standard synthetic control estimator should not be used. Transforming the outcome variable may help in some cases.



Backdating. Pretend the intervention occurred earlier and check whether estimated effects appear before the true intervention date. Absent pre-“treatment” effects provide credibility; effects appearing only at the actual intervention date provide further support.
Leave-one-out. Re-estimate the synthetic control after dropping one donor unit at a time. If results change substantially when a particular unit is removed, the counterfactual is sensitive to that unit’s presence in the donor pool.
Predictor sensitivity. Vary the set of predictors and check whether the estimated effect is stable across specifications.



Arkhangelsky, Athey, Hirshberg, Imbens and Wagner (2021) propose the Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDID) estimator, which combines elements of DiD and synthetic control methods.
Traditional DiD and SCM target different settings. DiD is applied when many units are treated and relies on additive unit-specific and time-specific fixed effects to account for selection. SCM is applied when only one or a few units are treated and compensates for the absence of parallel trends by reweighting the donor pool to match pre-treatment outcome paths. SDID is designed to be competitive in both settings.


Consider a balanced sample with \(N\) units and \(T\) periods. Let \(Y_{it}\) be the outcome and \(D_{it} \in \{0, 1\}\) the binary treatment indicator. The first \(N_{co}\) units are controls (\(D_{it} = 0\)) and the last \(N_{tr} = N - N_{co}\) are treated. All treated units are exposed from period \(T_{pre} + 1\) onwards (non-staggered adoption).



The SDID estimator is based on a weighted two-way fixed effects regression:
\[
\left(\hat{\tau}^{sdid}, \hat{\mu}, \hat{\alpha}, \hat{\beta}\right) = \arg\min_{\tau, \mu, \alpha, \beta} \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^T (Y_{it} - \mu - \alpha_i - \beta_t - D_{it} \tau)^2 \hat{\omega}_i^{sdid} \hat{\lambda}_t^{sdid} \right\}
\]
where \(\hat{\omega}_i^{sdid}\) are unit weights that align pre-exposure trends between treated and control units, and \(\hat{\lambda}_t^{sdid}\) are time weights that balance pre-exposure time periods with post-exposure periods.
Unit weights are obtained by solving:
\[
(\hat{\omega}_0, \hat{\omega}^{sdid}) = \arg\min_{\omega_0 \in \mathbb{R},\, \omega \in \Omega} \ell_{unit}(\omega_0, \omega) \tag{4}
\]
where
\[
\ell_{unit}(\omega_0, \omega) = \sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}} \left(\omega_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}} \omega_i Y_{it} - \frac{1}{N_{tr}} \sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^N Y_{it}\right)^2 + \zeta^2 T_{pre} \|\omega\|_2^2
\]
and \(\Omega = \left\{\omega \in \mathbb{R}^N_+ : \sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}} \omega_i = 1,\; \omega_i = N_{tr}^{-1} \text{ for all } i = N_{co}+1, \ldots, N\right\}\).
Time weights are obtained by solving:
\[
(\hat{\lambda}_0, \hat{\lambda}^{sdid}) = \arg\min_{\lambda_0 \in \mathbb{R},\, \lambda \in \Lambda} \ell_{time}(\lambda_0, \lambda) \tag{5}
\]
where
\[
\ell_{time}(\lambda_0, \lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}} \left(\lambda_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}} \lambda_t Y_{it} - \frac{1}{T_{post}} \sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^T Y_{it}\right)^2
\]
and \(\Lambda = \left\{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^T_+ : \sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}} \lambda_t = 1,\; \lambda_t = T_{post}^{-1} \text{ for all } t = T_{pre}+1, \ldots, T\right\}\).
The unit weights are closely related to the standard SC weights, with two differences. First, the intercept \(\omega_0\) means the weights only need to make trends parallel rather than match pre-intervention levels exactly. Second, the regularization penalty \(\zeta^2 T_{pre} \|\omega\|^2_2\) increases the dispersion of the weights and ensures their uniqueness. Setting \(\omega_0 = 0\) and \(\zeta = 0\) in Equation (4) recovers the standard SC weighting problem.



Each of the three estimators can be written as a weighted average difference in adjusted outcomes \(\hat{\delta}_i\) with weights \(\hat{\omega}_i\):
\[
\hat{\tau} = \hat{\delta}_{tr} - \sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}} \hat{\omega}_i \hat{\delta}_i \qquad \text{where} \qquad \hat{\delta}_{tr} = \frac{1}{N_{tr}} \sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^N \hat{\delta}_i
\]
The adjusted outcomes differ across estimators:







Estimator
\(\hat{\delta}_i\)




SC
\(\frac{1}{T_{post}} \sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^T Y_{it}\)


DiD
\(\frac{1}{T_{post}} \sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^T Y_{it} - \frac{1}{T_{pre}} \sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}} Y_{it}\)


SDID
\(\frac{1}{T_{post}} \sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^T Y_{it} - \sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}} \hat{\lambda}_t^{sdid} Y_{it}\)



SC uses only post-treatment information. DiD subtracts a simple equal-weighted pre-treatment average. SDID subtracts a time-weighted pre-treatment average, where the weights \(\hat{\lambda}_t^{sdid}\) up-weight pre-treatment periods that are most predictive of post-treatment outcomes.



SDID combines the attractive features of both methods: like SC, it reweights to match pre-exposure trends; like DiD, it is invariant to additive unit-level shifts and allows for valid large-panel inference. The SDID weights are sparse but less so than pure SC weights, because the intercept \(\omega_0\) and regularization allow greater flexibility. No single unit receives outsized influence, which keeps the variance of the estimator low.
Simulations in Arkhangelsky et al. (2021) show that SDID performs well relative to DiD and SC benchmarks in both bias and RMSE, and is particularly successful when treatment assignment is not random.



Two inference procedures are available for SDID.
Clustered bootstrap. Construct a bootstrap sample \(\mathbf{Y}^{(b)}, \mathbf{D}^{(b)}\) by sampling \(N\) rows from \(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{D}\) with replacement (resample if the draw has no treated or control units). Compute the SDID estimator \(\hat{\tau}^{(b)}\) on each bootstrap sample and repeat \(B\) times. The variance estimator is:
\[
\hat{V}^b_\tau = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \left(\hat{\tau}^{(b)} - \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \hat{\tau}^{(b)}\right)^2
\]
Placebo variance estimation. Sample \(N_{tr}\) units from the \(N_{co}\) control units without replacement to “receive the placebo.” Construct a placebo treatment matrix \(\mathbf{D}^{(b)}_{co}\) for the controls and compute the SDID estimator \(\hat{\tau}^{(b)}\) on the control data. Repeat \(B\) times and estimate the variance as the sample variance of the placebo estimates. This procedure is valid even when \(N_{tr}\) is small, but relies on homoskedasticity.
SDID can be extended to staggered adoption by applying the estimator separately for each adoption date and taking a weighted average. It delivers a single ATT estimate rather than the full profile of dynamic treatment effects.

title: Synthetic Control Methods
text:
Synthetic control methods have become standard in empirical work since the early 2000s. The setting is one where treatment is implemented at an aggregate level; e.g., a policy applied to a country, state, or city; and data are available on only a small number of such units. Traditional regression requires large samples and is poorly suited to this setting. Comparative case studies have long been used to evaluate aggregate interventions, but the selection of comparison units is typically informal and hard to replicate. Synthetic control methods formalize this by constructing a weighted combination of untreated units that matches the treated unit’s pre-intervention characteristics as closely as possible.
Athey and Imbens (2017) describe synthetic controls as “arguably the most important innovation in the policy evaluation literature in the last 15 years.” The key idea is that a combination of unaffected units often provides a more appropriate comparison than any single unaffected unit alone. The overview below follows Abadie (2021, JEL) and the application of Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2015).

title: Synthetic Control Methods
text:
Suppose there are \(J + 1\) units indexed \(j = 1, \ldots, J + 1\). Unit \(j = 1\) is the treated unit and units \(j = 2, \ldots, J + 1\) form the donor pool – the set of untreated units not affected by the intervention. There are \(T\) time periods and the first \(T_0\) periods are before the intervention. For each unit \(j\) and period \(t\), the outcome \(Y_{jt}\) is observed. For each unit \(j\), a vector of \(k\) predictors \(X_{1j}, \ldots, X_{kj}\) is also observed. The predictors may include pre-intervention values of \(Y_{jt}\) and are themselves unaffected by the intervention.
Let \(Y^N_{jt}\) denote the potential outcome without intervention. Define \(Y^I_{1t}\) as the potential outcome for the treated unit under the intervention in post-intervention period \(t > T_0\). The treatment effect for the affected unit in period \(t\) is:
\[
\tau_{1t} = Y^I_{1t} - Y^N_{1t} \tag{1}
\]
While \(Y^I_{1t}\) is observed for \(t > T_0\), the counterfactual \(Y^N_{1t}\) is not. The goal is to estimate it. The treatment effect is allowed to vary over time.

\[

\]

Use the inverse of the sample variance of each predictor \(X_{h1}, \ldots, X_{h,J+1}\).
Choose \(\mathbf{V}\) to minimize the mean squared prediction error of the synthetic control in the pre-intervention period.
Split the pre-intervention period into a training period and a validation period. Compute \(\mathbf{W}^*\) using training period data for a given \(\mathbf{V}\). If no combination of untreated units can credibly approximate the treated unit, the standard synthetic control estimator should not be used. Transforming the outcome variable may help in some cases.

title: Synthetic Control Methods
text:
Backdating. Pretend the intervention occurred earlier and check whether estimated effects appear before the true intervention date. Absent pre-“treatment” effects provide credibility; effects appearing only at the actual intervention date provide further support.
Leave-one-out. Re-estimate the synthetic control after dropping one donor unit at a time. If results change substantially when a particular unit is removed, the counterfactual is sensitive to that unit’s presence in the donor pool.
Predictor sensitivity. Vary the set of predictors and check whether the estimated effect is stable across specifications.

title: Synthetic Control Methods
text:
Arkhangelsky, Athey, Hirshberg, Imbens and Wagner (2021) propose the Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDID) estimator, which combines elements of DiD and synthetic control methods.
Traditional DiD and SCM target different settings. DiD is applied when many units are treated and relies on additive unit-specific and time-specific fixed effects to account for selection. SCM is applied when only one or a few units are treated and compensates for the absence of parallel trends by reweighting the donor pool to match pre-treatment outcome paths. SDID is designed to be competitive in both settings.


Consider a balanced sample with \(N\) units and \(T\) periods. Let \(Y_{it}\) be the outcome and \(D_{it} \in \{0, 1\}\) the binary treatment indicator. The first \(N_{co}\) units are controls (\(D_{it} = 0\)) and the last \(N_{tr} = N - N_{co}\) are treated. All treated units are exposed from period \(T_{pre} + 1\) onwards (non-staggered adoption).



The SDID estimator is based on a weighted two-way fixed effects regression:
\[
\left(\hat{\tau}^{sdid}, \hat{\mu}, \hat{\alpha}, \hat{\beta}\right) = \arg\min_{\tau, \mu, \alpha, \beta} \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^T (Y_{it} - \mu - \alpha_i - \beta_t - D_{it} \tau)^2 \hat{\omega}_i^{sdid} \hat{\lambda}_t^{sdid} \right\}
\]
where \(\hat{\omega}_i^{sdid}\) are unit weights that align pre-exposure trends between treated and control units, and \(\hat{\lambda}_t^{sdid}\) are time weights that balance pre-exposure time periods with post-exposure periods.
Unit weights are obtained by solving:
\[
(\hat{\omega}_0, \hat{\omega}^{sdid}) = \arg\min_{\omega_0 \in \mathbb{R},\, \omega \in \Omega} \ell_{unit}(\omega_0, \omega) \tag{4}
\]
where
\[
\ell_{unit}(\omega_0, \omega) = \sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}} \left(\omega_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}} \omega_i Y_{it} - \frac{1}{N_{tr}} \sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^N Y_{it}\right)^2 + \zeta^2 T_{pre} \|\omega\|_2^2
\]
and \(\Omega = \left\{\omega \in \mathbb{R}^N_+ : \sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}} \omega_i = 1,\; \omega_i = N_{tr}^{-1} \text{ for all } i = N_{co}+1, \ldots, N\right\}\).
Time weights are obtained by solving:
\[
(\hat{\lambda}_0, \hat{\lambda}^{sdid}) = \arg\min_{\lambda_0 \in \mathbb{R},\, \lambda \in \Lambda} \ell_{time}(\lambda_0, \lambda) \tag{5}
\]
where
\[
\ell_{time}(\lambda_0, \lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}} \left(\lambda_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}} \lambda_t Y_{it} - \frac{1}{T_{post}} \sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^T Y_{it}\right)^2
\]
and \(\Lambda = \left\{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^T_+ : \sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}} \lambda_t = 1,\; \lambda_t = T_{post}^{-1} \text{ for all } t = T_{pre}+1, \ldots, T\right\}\).
The unit weights are closely related to the standard SC weights, with two differences. First, the intercept \(\omega_0\) means the weights only need to make trends parallel rather than match pre-intervention levels exactly. Second, the regularization penalty \(\zeta^2 T_{pre} \|\omega\|^2_2\) increases the dispersion of the weights and ensures their uniqueness. Setting \(\omega_0 = 0\) and \(\zeta = 0\) in Equation (4) recovers the standard SC weighting problem.



Each of the three estimators can be written as a weighted average difference in adjusted outcomes \(\hat{\delta}_i\) with weights \(\hat{\omega}_i\):
\[
\hat{\tau} = \hat{\delta}_{tr} - \sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}} \hat{\omega}_i \hat{\delta}_i \qquad \text{where} \qquad \hat{\delta}_{tr} = \frac{1}{N_{tr}} \sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^N \hat{\delta}_i
\]
The adjusted outcomes differ across estimators:







Estimator
\(\hat{\delta}_i\)




SC
\(\frac{1}{T_{post}} \sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^T Y_{it}\)


DiD
\(\frac{1}{T_{post}} \sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^T Y_{it} - \frac{1}{T_{pre}} \sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}} Y_{it}\)


SDID
\(\frac{1}{T_{post}} \sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^T Y_{it} - \sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}} \hat{\lambda}_t^{sdid} Y_{it}\)



SC uses only post-treatment information. DiD subtracts a simple equal-weighted pre-treatment average. SDID subtracts a time-weighted pre-treatment average, where the weights \(\hat{\lambda}_t^{sdid}\) up-weight pre-treatment periods that are most predictive of post-treatment outcomes.



SDID combines the attractive features of both methods: like SC, it reweights to match pre-exposure trends; like DiD, it is invariant to additive unit-level shifts and allows for valid large-panel inference. The SDID weights are sparse but less so than pure SC weights, because the intercept \(\omega_0\) and regularization allow greater flexibility. No single unit receives outsized influence, which keeps the variance of the estimator low.
Simulations in Arkhangelsky et al. (2021) show that SDID performs well relative to DiD and SC benchmarks in both bias and RMSE, and is particularly successful when treatment assignment is not random.



Two inference procedures are available for SDID.
Clustered bootstrap. Construct a bootstrap sample \(\mathbf{Y}^{(b)}, \mathbf{D}^{(b)}\) by sampling \(N\) rows from \(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{D}\) with replacement (resample if the draw has no treated or control units). Compute the SDID estimator \(\hat{\tau}^{(b)}\) on each bootstrap sample and repeat \(B\) times. The variance estimator is:
\[
\hat{V}^b_\tau = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \left(\hat{\tau}^{(b)} - \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \hat{\tau}^{(b)}\right)^2
\]
Placebo variance estimation. Sample \(N_{tr}\) units from the \(N_{co}\) control units without replacement to “receive the placebo.” Construct a placebo treatment matrix \(\mathbf{D}^{(b)}_{co}\) for the controls and compute the SDID estimator \(\hat{\tau}^{(b)}\) on the control data. Repeat \(B\) times and estimate the variance as the sample variance of the placebo estimates. This procedure is valid even when \(N_{tr}\) is small, but relies on homoskedasticity.
SDID can be extended to staggered adoption by applying the estimator separately for each adoption date and taking a weighted average. It delivers a single ATT estimate rather than the full profile of dynamic treatment effects.

title: Selection on Observables and Matching
text:
We want to estimate the causal effect of a treatment in situations where randomization is impossible and there are no convincing natural experiments. The methods introduced here rely on the identifying assumption of selection on observables, also referred to as unconfoundedness or conditional independence. The assumption says that conditional on observable variables that influence selection into treatment, treatment status is “as good as” randomized.



A common approach in empirical work is to control for confounders in an OLS regression:
\[
Y_i = \beta_D D_i + \beta_1 W_{1i} + \beta_2 W_{2i} + U_i \tag{1}
\]
The identifying assumption is that conditional on \(W_{1i}\) and \(W_{2i}\), \(U_i\) is mean-independent of \(D_i\):
\[
\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid D_i, W_{1i}, W_{2i}) = \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid W_{1i}, W_{2i}) = \gamma_1 W_{1i} + \gamma_2 W_{2i}
\]
Under this conditional independence assumption:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D = \beta_D \qquad \text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1 + \gamma_1 \qquad \text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_2 = \beta_2 + \gamma_2
\]


It is important to include as controls only variables that were not themselves affected by the treatment. A variable \(W_i\) that is a post-treatment outcome (or an outcome of the treatment) constitutes a bad control (Angrist and Pischke, 2009).
Including a bad control in the OLS regression leads to biased estimates. For a binary bad control \(W_i\), the OLS estimator for \(\beta_D\) converges to a weighted average of within-stratum treatment effects, but the comparison within each stratum is between treated units who obtained the outcome and untreated units who also obtained the outcome – a fundamentally different population. If individuals without treatment who end up with \(W_i = 1\) are more able or motivated than those with treatment who end up with \(W_i = 1\), this comparison is downward biased. The simple regression of \(Y_i\) on \(D_i\), or of \(W_i\) on \(D_i\), would be fine.




Unobserved confounders are a first-order concern in any observational study. Oster (2019) provides a method to estimate and adjust for bias from unobservables under additional assumptions about the relative degree of selection on observables vs. unobservables.
Consider the model:
\[
Y_i = \beta X_i + \gamma' w_i^o + W_{2i}
\]
where \(X_i\) denotes treatment status, \(w_i^o = (w_{1i}^o, \ldots, w_{Ji}^o)\) is a vector of observed control variables, and \(W_{2i}\) captures unobserved factors. Define \(W_{1i} = \gamma' w_i^o\) as an index of observed factors and note that \(W_{1i}\) and \(W_{2i}\) are independent by the CEF decomposition property.
Equal relative contributions assumption: The coefficient vector in a regression of \(X_i\) on \(w_i^o\) is proportional to the coefficient vector in a regression of \(Y_i\) on \(X_i\) and \(w_i^o\). Formally, \(\frac{\gamma_k}{\gamma_j} = \frac{\mu_k}{\mu_j}\) for all \(k, j\).
Define the proportional selection relationship:
\[
\delta \frac{\sigma_{1X}}{\sigma_1^2} = \frac{\sigma_{2X}}{\sigma_2^2}
\]
where \(\sigma_{kX} = \text{Cov}(W_k, X)\) and \(\sigma_k^2 = \text{Var}(W_k)\). The ratio \(\frac{\sigma_{1X}/\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_{2X}/\sigma_2^2}\) can be interpreted as the relative effects of observables vs. unobservables on treatment. The degree of relative selection \(\delta\) is unknown; the useful benchmark case is equal selection \(\delta = 1\).
Denote \(\hat{\beta}^S\) (short/simple regression R-squared: \(R^S\)), \(\hat{\beta}^L\) (long/multiple regression R-squared: \(R^L\)), and \(R_{max}\) as the R-squared from a hypothetical regression of \(Y_i\) on \(X_i\), \(W_{1i}\), and \(W_{2i}\). Oster shows that under \(\delta = 1\) and the equal relative contributions assumption:
\[
\hat{\beta}^L - (\hat{\beta}^S - \hat{\beta}^L)\frac{R_{max} - R^L}{R^L - R^S} \xrightarrow{p} \beta
\]
This provides a consistent estimate of the treatment effect by adjusting the controlled estimate \(\hat{\beta}^L\) by a factor that depends on coefficient and R-squared movements. If \(R^L\) is close to \(R_{max}\), the adjustment is small (controls account for almost all variation in \(Y\); little room for bias from unobservables). If \(R^L\) increases only modestly relative to \(R^S\) but \(\hat{\beta}^S - \hat{\beta}^L\) is non-negligible, the remaining bias from unobservables is large and the adjustment is consequential.
Under proportional selection (relaxing equal selection) the bias-adjusted estimator becomes:
\[
\hat{\beta}^L - \delta(\hat{\beta}^S - \hat{\beta}^L)\frac{R_{max} - R^L}{R^L - R^S} \xrightarrow{p} \beta
\]



A more flexible approach that drops the linearity assumption is exact matching. Using potential outcomes notation, the identifying assumption is:
\[
Y_{1i}, Y_{0i} \perp D_i \mid X_i
\]
where \(X_i\) denotes a cell with common pre-treatment characteristics. For example, \(X_i = 1\) could denote males (\(W_{1i} = 0\)) without college education (\(W_{2i} = 0\)), \(X_i = 2\) denotes males with college education, etc.
Under conditional independence:
\[
\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid D_i, X_i) = \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid X_i) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i, X_i) = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid X_i)
\]
The difference in average outcomes within cell \(x\) identifies the conditional average treatment effect (CATE):
\[
\beta_x \equiv \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid X_i = x) = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1, X_i = x] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0, X_i = x]
\]
The ATE and ATT are obtained as weighted averages of the CATE:
\[
\mathbb{E}(\beta_i) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid X_i)] = \sum_x \beta_x P(X_i = x)
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i = 1) = \sum_x \beta_x P(X_i = x \mid D_i = 1)
\]
The estimation strategy for exact matching is:

Stratify the data into cells defined by each particular value of \(X_i\).
Within each cell, compute the difference in average outcomes between treated and comparison units.
Average these differences with respect to the distribution of \(X_i\).




The only difference between a fully saturated-in-\(X\) regression and exact matching is the weighting scheme used to average treatment effects across cells. The matching estimand for the ATT weights by \(P(X_i = x \mid D_i = 1)\) (the distribution of \(X_i\) among the treated), while the regression estimand weights by \(P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x)(1 - P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x))P(X_i = x)\) – more weight to cells where the proportion of treated and untreated is similar.
Specifically, the ATT matching estimand is:
\[
\mathbb{E}(\beta_x \mid D_i = 1) = \sum_x \beta_x \frac{P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x)P(X_i = x)}{\sum_x P(D_i = 1, X_i = x)}
\]
The regression estimand (plim of the coefficient on \(D_i\) in a fully saturated-in-\(X\) regression) is:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{\tilde{D}} \xrightarrow{p} \frac{\text{Cov}(\tilde{D}_i, Y_i)}{\text{Var}(\tilde{D}_i)} = \frac{\sum_x \beta_x [P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x)(1 - P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x))]P(X_i = x)}{\sum_x [P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x)(1 - P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x))]P(X_i = x)}
\]
where \(\tilde{D}_i = D_i - \mathbb{E}(D_i \mid X_i)\). Key implications:

Both estimands equal \(\sum_x \beta_x P(X_i = x)\) when \(P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x) = p\) is constant, i.e. treatment is independent of \(X_i\), so plim \(\hat{\beta}_{\tilde{D}} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0]\).
Cells where \(P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x) = 0\) or \(P(D_i = 0 \mid X_i = x) = 0\) do not contribute to either estimand.
Regression gives more weight to cells where the proportion of treated and untreated is similar.
The matching estimand for the ATT gives more weight to cells where the proportion of treated is high.
With heterogeneous \(\beta_x\), the OLS estimand is a variance-weighted average of the \(\beta_x\).




Exact matching and fully saturated regression are infeasible when \(X_i\) is multivalued or continuous (the “curse of dimensionality”). Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983) propose an equivalent and feasible estimation strategy based on the propensity score:
\[
p(W_i) \equiv P(D_i = 1 \mid W_i) = \mathbb{E}(D_i \mid W_i)
\]
Propensity score theorem: If the CIA holds conditional on \(W_i\), i.e. \(\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid D_i, W_i) = \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid W_i)\), then treatment is also unconfounded given the propensity score: \(\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid D_i, p(W_i)) = \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid p(W_i))\).
Proof: We need to show \(P(D_i = 1 \mid U_i, p(W_i)) = p(W_i)\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(D_i = 1 \mid U_i, p(W_i)) &= \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid U_i, p(W_i)] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}(D_i \mid U_i, p(W_i), W_i) \mid U_i, p(W_i)] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}(D_i \mid W_i) \mid U_i, p(W_i)] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[p(W_i) \mid U_i, p(W_i)] = p(W_i)
\end{aligned}
\]
This reduces the dimensionality problem: instead of conditioning on the full vector \(W_i\), we only need to condition on the scalar \(p(W_i)\). The ATE and ATT can be obtained as \(p(W_i)\)-weighted averages of the conditional treatment effect \(\delta_{p(W)}\):
\[
\mathbb{E}(\beta_i) = \mathbb{E}[\delta_{p(W)}] = \sum_{p(W)} \delta_{p(W)} P(p(W_i) = p)
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i = 1) = \mathbb{E}[\delta_{p(W)} \mid D_i = 1] = \sum_{p(W)} \delta_{p(W)} P(p(W_i) = p \mid D_i = 1)
\]



In practice the recommended procedure follows these steps:


Using OLS to estimate \(p(W_i)\) typically yields predicted probabilities outside \([0,1]\). The standard approach is a logit model:
\[
p(W_i) = \frac{e^{h(W_i)}}{1 + e^{h(W_i)}} = \frac{1}{e^{-h(W_i)} + 1}
\]
where \(h(W_i) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 W_{1i} + \ldots + \alpha_k W_{ki}\) can include linear and higher order terms. The log-likelihood is:
\[
L(\alpha_0, \ldots, \alpha_k; D_1, \ldots, D_n, W_1, \ldots, W_n) = \sum_i D_i \ln p(W_i \mid \alpha) + \sum_i (1-D_i) \ln(1 - p(W_i \mid \alpha))
\]
Note that the MLE coefficients cannot be easily interpreted directly; the logit function has to be evaluated separately for different values of \(W_{1i}\), holding \(W_2\) through \(W_k\) constant at their mean values.



The ATT and ATE are only defined in the region of common support: the range of propensity scores where both treated and control units exist. This step involves checking the overlap of propensity score distributions between treatment and control groups. Units outside the common support must be excluded.



In practice it is rare to find two units with exactly the same propensity score. The three main algorithms are:
Nearest Neighbor Matching (with replacement):
For each treated unit \(i \in T\), find the nearest comparison unit \(j\):
\[
C(i) = \min_j \| \hat{p}_i - \hat{p}_j \|
\]
Use the nearest comparison unit again if it has already been matched (replacement). Drop unmatched comparison units. Delivers \(N^T\) pairs where comparison units may appear more than once.
Radius Matching:
For each treated unit, find all comparison units whose propensity score differs by less than a tolerance \(r\):
\[
C(i) = \{j \mid \| \hat{p}_i - \hat{p}_j \| < r\}
\]
Kernel Matching:
Every treated unit is matched with a weighted average of all comparison units \(N_i^C\) within a bandwidth \(h\), with weights inversely related to the distance between the scores:
\[
\hat{\tau}_K^{ATT} = \frac{1}{N^T} \sum_{i \in T} \left(Y_i^T - \frac{\sum_{j \in C(i)} Y_j^C \, G\!\left(\frac{\hat{p}_i - \hat{p}_j}{h_n}\right)}{\sum_{j \in C(i)} G\!\left(\frac{\hat{p}_i - \hat{p}_j}{h_n}\right)}\right)
\]
where \(G(\cdot)\) is a kernel function and \(h_n\) is a bandwidth parameter.



Observations with the same propensity score should have the same distribution of observable covariates independently of treatment status. To test for balance, stratify the sample over small propensity score intervals and test for each covariate whether the means for treated and controls are statistically different in each interval. If balance fails, improve the specification (more interactions or higher order terms) and restart.



The nearest neighbor and radius matching estimators for the ATT are:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{NN,R}^{ATT} = \frac{1}{N^T} \sum_{i \in T} \left[Y_i^T - \sum_{j \in C(i)} w_{ij} Y_j^C\right]
\]
where \(w_{ij} = 1/N_i^C\) if \(j \in C(i)\) and \(w_{ij} = 0\) otherwise. Standard errors of matching estimators are typically computed using the bootstrap (note: the standard bootstrap variance is not valid for nearest neighbor matching on a continuous covariate; see Abadie and Imbens (2008) for a valid alternative).



In support of the CIA assumption, perform the following diagnostics:

Estimate the effect of the treatment on unaffected outcomes, particularly the lagged outcome (placebo-type analysis).
Estimate the effect of a pseudo-treatment on an outcome.
Assess sensitivity of estimates to different choices of controls \(W_i\).





The propensity score can also be used directly as a weight to estimate causal parameters. The idea is to down-weight treated observations with high p-scores and up-weight those with low p-scores, making the weighted treated sample more similar to the comparison group.
For the ATE, the weights are:
\[
w_{1i} = \frac{p}{p(W_i)} \qquad w_{0i} = \frac{1-p}{1-p(W_i)}
\]
where \(p\) is the sample proportion treated. Under the CIA and plim \(\hat{p}(W_i) = p(W_i)\):
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y_i w_{1i} \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i w_{0i} \mid D_i = 0] = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i)
\]
For the ATT, the weights are:
\[
w_{1i} = 1 \qquad w_{0i} = \frac{\hat{p}(W_i)}{1 - \hat{p}(W_i)} \cdot \frac{1-p}{p}
\]
Under the CIA:
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y_i w_{1i} \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i w_{0i} \mid D_i = 0] = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i = 1)
\]



Compared to other policy evaluation methods, approaches relying on selection on observables are often viewed with great skepticism. The fundamental issue is that economic models are often all about self-selection, which is assumed away in these approaches. Before implementing a matching approach, the key question is:
“Why, if these units are so similar, did one get treated and another not?”
A good use of matching needs to make a rhetorical case for why it is plausible, not just a statistical case. It is more plausible that, conditional on observables, the reason one unit gets treated and another does not is random when:

A separate decision-maker with limited information decides on treatment (administrators make the relevant decisions).
Capacity limits and small frictions/noise affect who gets treated.
The decision-maker cares about a different outcome than the evaluator, or unobserved costs affect take-up but not outcomes.
Randomization substrata exist.

The validity of the conditional independence assumption needs to be carefully argued for on a case-by-case basis.
