Oster shows that under \(\delta = 1\) and the equal relative contributions assumption:
\[
\hat{\beta}^L - (\hat{\beta}^S - \hat{\beta}^L)\frac{R_{max} - R^L}{R^L - R^S} \xrightarrow{p} \beta
\]
This provides a consistent estimate of the treatment effect by adjusting the controlled estimate \(\hat{\beta}^L\) by a factor that depends on coefficient and R-squared movements. If \(R^L\) is close to \(R_{max}\), the adjustment is small (controls account for almost all variation in \(Y\); little room for bias from unobservables). If \(R^L\) increases only modestly relative to \(R^S\) but \(\hat{\beta}^S - \hat{\beta}^L\) is non-negligible, the remaining bias from unobservables is large and the adjustment is consequential.
Under proportional selection (relaxing equal selection) the bias-adjusted estimator becomes:
\[
\hat{\beta}^L - \delta(\hat{\beta}^S - \hat{\beta}^L)\frac{R_{max} - R^L}{R^L - R^S} \xrightarrow{p} \beta
\]

title: Selection on Observables and Matching
text:
A more flexible approach that drops the linearity assumption is exact matching. Using potential outcomes notation, the identifying assumption is:
\[
Y_{1i}, Y_{0i} \perp D_i \mid X_i
\]
where \(X_i\) denotes a cell with common pre-treatment characteristics. For example, \(X_i = 1\) could denote males (\(W_{1i} = 0\)) without college education (\(W_{2i} = 0\)), \(X_i = 2\) denotes males with college education, etc.
Under conditional independence:
\[
\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid D_i, X_i) = \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid X_i) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i, X_i) = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid X_i)
\]
The difference in average outcomes within cell \(x\) identifies the conditional average treatment effect (CATE):
\[
\beta_x \equiv \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid X_i = x) = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1, X_i = x] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0, X_i = x]
\]
The ATE and ATT are obtained as weighted averages of the CATE:
\[
\mathbb{E}(\beta_i) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid X_i)] = \sum_x \beta_x P(X_i = x)
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i = 1) = \sum_x \beta_x P(X_i = x \mid D_i = 1)
\]
The estimation strategy for exact matching is:

Stratify the data into cells defined by each particular value of \(X_i\).
Within each cell, compute the difference in average outcomes between treated and comparison units.
Average these differences with respect to the distribution of \(X_i\).

title: Selection on Observables and Matching
text:
The only difference between a fully saturated-in-\(X\) regression and exact matching is the weighting scheme used to average treatment effects across cells. The matching estimand for the ATT weights by \(P(X_i = x \mid D_i = 1)\) (the distribution of \(X_i\) among the treated), while the regression estimand weights by \(P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x)(1 - P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x))P(X_i = x)\) – more weight to cells where the proportion of treated and untreated is similar.
Specifically, the ATT matching estimand is:
\[
\mathbb{E}(\beta_x \mid D_i = 1) = \sum_x \beta_x \frac{P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x)P(X_i = x)}{\sum_x P(D_i = 1, X_i = x)}
\]
The regression estimand (plim of the coefficient on \(D_i\) in a fully saturated-in-\(X\) regression) is:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{\tilde{D}} \xrightarrow{p} \frac{\text{Cov}(\tilde{D}_i, Y_i)}{\text{Var}(\tilde{D}_i)} = \frac{\sum_x \beta_x [P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x)(1 - P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x))]P(X_i = x)}{\sum_x [P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x)(1 - P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x))]P(X_i = x)}
\]
where \(\tilde{D}_i = D_i - \mathbb{E}(D_i \mid X_i)\). Key implications:

Both estimands equal \(\sum_x \beta_x P(X_i = x)\) when \(P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x) = p\) is constant, i.e. treatment is independent of \(X_i\), so plim \(\hat{\beta}_{\tilde{D}} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0]\).
Cells where \(P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x) = 0\) or \(P(D_i = 0 \mid X_i = x) = 0\) do not contribute to either estimand.
Regression gives more weight to cells where the proportion of treated and untreated is similar.
The matching estimand for the ATT gives more weight to cells where the proportion of treated is high.
With heterogeneous \(\beta_x\), the OLS estimand is a variance-weighted average of the \(\beta_x\).

title: Selection on Observables and Matching
text:
Exact matching and fully saturated regression are infeasible when \(X_i\) is multivalued or continuous (the “curse of dimensionality”). Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983) propose an equivalent and feasible estimation strategy based on the propensity score:
\[
p(W_i) \equiv P(D_i = 1 \mid W_i) = \mathbb{E}(D_i \mid W_i)
\]
Propensity score theorem: If the CIA holds conditional on \(W_i\), i.e. \(\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid D_i, W_i) = \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid W_i)\), then treatment is also unconfounded given the propensity score: \(\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid D_i, p(W_i)) = \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid p(W_i))\).
Proof: We need to show \(P(D_i = 1 \mid U_i, p(W_i)) = p(W_i)\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(D_i = 1 \mid U_i, p(W_i)) &= \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid U_i, p(W_i)] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}(D_i \mid U_i, p(W_i), W_i) \mid U_i, p(W_i)] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}(D_i \mid W_i) \mid U_i, p(W_i)] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[p(W_i) \mid U_i, p(W_i)] = p(W_i)
\end{aligned}
\]
This reduces the dimensionality problem: instead of conditioning on the full vector \(W_i\), we only need to condition on the scalar \(p(W_i)\). The ATE and ATT can be obtained as \(p(W_i)\)-weighted averages of the conditional treatment effect \(\delta_{p(W)}\):
\[
\mathbb{E}(\beta_i) = \mathbb{E}[\delta_{p(W)}] = \sum_{p(W)} \delta_{p(W)} P(p(W_i) = p)
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i = 1) = \mathbb{E}[\delta_{p(W)} \mid D_i = 1] = \sum_{p(W)} \delta_{p(W)} P(p(W_i) = p \mid D_i = 1)
\]

title: Selection on Observables and Matching
text:
In practice the recommended procedure follows these steps:


Using OLS to estimate \(p(W_i)\) typically yields predicted probabilities outside \([0,1]\). The standard approach is a logit model:
\[
p(W_i) = \frac{e^{h(W_i)}}{1 + e^{h(W_i)}} = \frac{1}{e^{-h(W_i)} + 1}
\]
where \(h(W_i) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 W_{1i} + \ldots + \alpha_k W_{ki}\) can include linear and higher order terms. The log-likelihood is:
\[
L(\alpha_0, \ldots, \alpha_k; D_1, \ldots, D_n, W_1, \ldots, W_n) = \sum_i D_i \ln p(W_i \mid \alpha) + \sum_i (1-D_i) \ln(1 - p(W_i \mid \alpha))
\]
Note that the MLE coefficients cannot be easily interpreted directly; the logit function has to be evaluated separately for different values of \(W_{1i}\), holding \(W_2\) through \(W_k\) constant at their mean values.



The ATT and ATE are only defined in the region of common support: the range of propensity scores where both treated and control units exist. This step involves checking the overlap of propensity score distributions between treatment and control groups. Units outside the common support must be excluded.



In practice it is rare to find two units with exactly the same propensity score. The three main algorithms are:
Nearest Neighbor Matching (with replacement):
For each treated unit \(i \in T\), find the nearest comparison unit \(j\):
\[
C(i) = \min_j \| \hat{p}_i - \hat{p}_j \|
\]
Use the nearest comparison unit again if it has already been matched (replacement). Drop unmatched comparison units. Delivers \(N^T\) pairs where comparison units may appear more than once.
Radius Matching:
For each treated unit, find all comparison units whose propensity score differs by less than a tolerance \(r\):
\[
C(i) = \{j \mid \| \hat{p}_i - \hat{p}_j \| < r\}
\]
Kernel Matching:
Every treated unit is matched with a weighted average of all comparison units \(N_i^C\) within a bandwidth \(h\), with weights inversely related to the distance between the scores:
\[
\hat{\tau}_K^{ATT} = \frac{1}{N^T} \sum_{i \in T} \left(Y_i^T - \frac{\sum_{j \in C(i)} Y_j^C \, G\!\left(\frac{\hat{p}_i - \hat{p}_j}{h_n}\right)}{\sum_{j \in C(i)} G\!\left(\frac{\hat{p}_i - \hat{p}_j}{h_n}\right)}\right)
\]
where \(G(\cdot)\) is a kernel function and \(h_n\) is a bandwidth parameter.



Observations with the same propensity score should have the same distribution of observable covariates independently of treatment status. To test for balance, stratify the sample over small propensity score intervals and test for each covariate whether the means for treated and controls are statistically different in each interval. If balance fails, improve the specification (more interactions or higher order terms) and restart.



The nearest neighbor and radius matching estimators for the ATT are:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{NN,R}^{ATT} = \frac{1}{N^T} \sum_{i \in T} \left[Y_i^T - \sum_{j \in C(i)} w_{ij} Y_j^C\right]
\]
where \(w_{ij} = 1/N_i^C\) if \(j \in C(i)\) and \(w_{ij} = 0\) otherwise. Standard errors of matching estimators are typically computed using the bootstrap (note: the standard bootstrap variance is not valid for nearest neighbor matching on a continuous covariate; see Abadie and Imbens (2008) for a valid alternative).



In support of the CIA assumption, perform the following diagnostics:

Estimate the effect of the treatment on unaffected outcomes, particularly the lagged outcome (placebo-type analysis).
Estimate the effect of a pseudo-treatment on an outcome.
Assess sensitivity of estimates to different choices of controls \(W_i\).

title: Selection on Observables and Matching
text:
The propensity score can also be used directly as a weight to estimate causal parameters. The idea is to down-weight treated observations with high p-scores and up-weight those with low p-scores, making the weighted treated sample more similar to the comparison group.
For the ATE, the weights are:
\[
w_{1i} = \frac{p}{p(W_i)} \qquad w_{0i} = \frac{1-p}{1-p(W_i)}
\]
where \(p\) is the sample proportion treated. Under the CIA and plim \(\hat{p}(W_i) = p(W_i)\):
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y_i w_{1i} \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i w_{0i} \mid D_i = 0] = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i)
\]
For the ATT, the weights are:
\[
w_{1i} = 1 \qquad w_{0i} = \frac{\hat{p}(W_i)}{1 - \hat{p}(W_i)} \cdot \frac{1-p}{p}
\]
Under the CIA:
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y_i w_{1i} \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i w_{0i} \mid D_i = 0] = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i = 1)
\]

title: Selection on Observables and Matching
text:
Compared to other policy evaluation methods, approaches relying on selection on observables are often viewed with great skepticism. The fundamental issue is that economic models are often all about self-selection, which is assumed away in these approaches. Before implementing a matching approach, the key question is:
“Why, if these units are so similar, did one get treated and another not?”
A good use of matching needs to make a rhetorical case for why it is plausible, not just a statistical case. It is more plausible that, conditional on observables, the reason one unit gets treated and another does not is random when:

A separate decision-maker with limited information decides on treatment (administrators make the relevant decisions).
Capacity limits and small frictions/noise affect who gets treated.
The decision-maker cares about a different outcome than the evaluator, or unobserved costs affect take-up but not outcomes.
Randomization substrata exist.

The validity of the conditional independence assumption needs to be carefully argued for on a case-by-case basis.

title: Randomized Control Trials
text:
The use of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), also known as randomized controlled experiments, gives researchers “the ability to let questions determine the data to be obtained, instead of the data determining the questions that can be asked.” RCTs have become particularly common in labor, public, and development economics.
Suppose we want to estimate the causal effect of \(X_i\) on \(Y_i\). The answer is that there are good reasons to assign \(X_i\) to individuals at random, i.e. to give treatment to all sample members with equal probability. Random assignment circumvents the problems of identifying causal effects: by design, \(D_i\) will be independent of any other pre-treatment influences on \(Y_i\).
To see this formally, suppose \(X_i\) is a binary treatment indicator \(D_i\) and \(W_i\) is any discrete random variable. Under random assignment, \(P(D_i = d \mid W_i = w) = P(D_i = d)\) for all \(w\), so:
\[
\mathbb{E}[W_i \mid D_i = d] = \sum_w P(W_i = w \mid D_i = d) \cdot w = \sum_w P(W_i = w) \cdot w = \mathbb{E}[W_i]
\]
The key step is that \(P(D_i = d \mid W_i = w) = P(D_i = d)\): every individual has the same probability of being treated regardless of individual characteristics. This is not an assumption but follows directly from knowledge about the assignment process. Hence, the expected values of \(W_i\) (and \(U_i\)) are the same in treatment and control groups, and the only systematic reason for the outcome variable to differ is because of the treatment.



Under random assignment \((Y_{1i}, Y_{0i}) \perp D_i\), the selection bias in the naive difference:
\[
\beta \equiv \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0] = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y_{1i} - Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1]}_{\alpha_{ATT}} + \underbrace{(\mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 0])}_{\text{selection bias} = 0}
\]
vanishes since \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 0] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i}]\). It also implies \(\alpha_{ATE} = \alpha_{ATT} = \beta\). The average treatment effect can thus be estimated by a simple linear regression of \(Y_i\) on \(D_i\):
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_D D_i + U_i
\]
The OLS estimator is:
\[
\hat{\beta}_D^S = \frac{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i (D_i - \bar{D})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i (D_i - \bar{D})^2} \qquad \text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D^S = \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, Y_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)}
\]
Working through the covariance numerator using the law of iterated expectations and the fact that \(D_i^2 = D_i\):
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D^S = \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, Y_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0] = \beta_D
\]
so the OLS estimator is consistent. In the case of heterogeneous effects \(\beta_i \neq \beta_D\), one can show that under random assignment plim \(\hat{\beta}_D = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i) = ATE\).





Default OLS standard errors assume \(\text{Var}(Y_i \mid D_i = 1) = \text{Var}(Y_i \mid D_i = 0) = \text{Var}(U_i)\). Since the treatment may affect the variance of \(Y_i\) even if not its mean, this assumption is typically unjustified. The general formula for robust standard errors is:
\[
\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat{\beta}) = \frac{1}{N}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i x_i'\right]^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i x_i' \hat{u}_i^2\right]\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i x_i'\right]^{-1}
\]
An alternative is to compute the variance directly from the difference in means:
\[
\text{Var}(\bar{Y}_T - \bar{Y}_C) = \text{Var}(\bar{Y}_T) + \text{Var}(\bar{Y}_C) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_T^2}{N_1} + \frac{\hat{\sigma}_C^2}{N_0}
\]
where \(\hat{\sigma}_T^2\) and \(\hat{\sigma}_C^2\) are the sample variances within the treatment and control subsamples.



When observations are grouped into clusters (e.g. students within schools), within-cluster outcomes are likely correlated due to common factors. Robust standard errors are biased in this case. The clustered variance estimator is:
\[
\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat{\beta}) = \frac{1}{G}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_g X_g'X_g\right]^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_g X_g'\hat{u}_g\hat{u}_g'X_g\right]\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_g X_g'X_g\right]^{-1}
\]
where \(X_g\) is the \(N_g \times K\) matrix of stacked regressor vectors within cluster \(g\), and \(\hat{u}_g\) is the vector of stacked OLS residuals within cluster \(g\). This estimator is valid as long as the number of clusters \(G\) is large enough (typically above 30).



Conventional inference is based on large-sample approximations to the true asymptotic distribution of the estimator. Randomization inference produces an exact distribution irrespective of sample size. The idea is to repeatedly assign treatment at random and each time compute a corresponding estimate. The resulting distribution captures what estimates one could possibly get under the null hypothesis that the effect is zero for all units. If the original estimate falls sufficiently into the tails of this distribution, this is evidence against the null.






In an RCT, there is no assumption that omitted variables do not matter for the determination of \(Y_i\); the omission of variables that might influence \(Y_i\) does not prevent us from obtaining consistent estimates of the causal effect of \(D_i\) on \(Y_i\). Randomization ensures that \(D_i\) is independent of all other variables, so omitted variable bias does not arise.
Denote by \(\hat{\beta}_D^L\) the OLS estimator of \(\beta_D\) in the long regression \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_D D_i + \beta_W W_i + U_i\). If \(D_i\) is randomized:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D^L = \beta_D \qquad \text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_W = \beta_W + \frac{\text{Cov}(W_i, U_i)}{\text{Var}(W_i)}
\]
Including additional regressors does not affect the consistency of the treatment effect estimate. However, \(\hat{\beta}_W\) will not provide a consistent estimate of \(\beta_W\) unless \(\text{Cov}(W_i, U_i) = 0\).



An important advantage of including additional regressors is that it typically reduces the standard error of the estimated treatment effect. If \(D_i\) is randomized, the asymptotic variance of \(\hat{\beta}_D^L\) (with \(W_i\) included) is weakly lower than that of \(\hat{\beta}_D^S\) (without \(W_i\)). The variance will be strictly lower if \(W_i\) is a relevant predictor of \(Y_i\):









\(\beta_W = 0\)
\(\beta_W \neq 0\)




\(\sigma_{DW} = 0\)
\(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^S) = \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^L)\)
\(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^S) > \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^L)\)


\(\sigma_{DW} \neq 0\)
\(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^S) < \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^L)\)
\(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^S) \lessgtr \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^L)\)



If \(D_i\) is not randomized, then the net effect on precision is ambiguous.



In many real-world RCTs there are serious questions about how well the randomization was implemented in practice. One way to assess this is to check that the treatment variable is uncorrelated with the \(W_i\) variables. There are several ways to do this:

Compare the means of \(W_i\) in treatment and control groups.
Run a regression of \(D_i\) on the \(W_i\) variables and test whether the coefficients are jointly zero.
Compare the estimates of the treatment effect when including and excluding \(W_i\). By the OVB formula, plim \((\hat{\beta}_D^S - \hat{\beta}_D^L) = \beta_W \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, W_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)}\); randomization implies this should be zero.




Randomization ensures that \(D_i\) is independent of \(W_i\) in large samples, but in a small sample the correlation between \(D_i\) and \(W_i\) may not be exactly zero. We can guarantee balance by randomizing conditional on \(W_i\), i.e. \(P(D_i = 1 \mid W_i = w) = P(D_i = 1)\) for all \(w\). By equalizing treatment probabilities within each stratum defined by \(W_i\), we set the sample correlation between \(D_i\) and \(W_i\) to zero for any sample size.
When treatment probabilities are necessarily different for different subgroups (conditional randomization), \(D_i\) is no longer independent of \(X_i\) and the simple difference estimator may suffer from omitted variable bias. However, if we control for \(X_i\) in the regression, then \(D_i\) will be independent of all other omitted variables and we get a consistent estimate of the causal effect. One can show that conditional randomization implies \(\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid D_i, X_i) = \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid X_i)\), the conditional mean independence assumption.




So far we have assumed that the treatment effect is the same for everyone. Let \(\beta_i\) denote the individual-specific treatment effect, and decompose it as:
\[
\beta_i = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid W_i) + r_i = \beta_1 + \beta_2 W_i + r_i
\]
where \(\mathbb{E}(r_i \mid W_i) = 0\). The ATE for subgroup \(W_i = w\) is then \(\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid W_i = w) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 w\), and the unconditional ATE is \(\mathbb{E}(\beta_i) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \mathbb{E}(W_i)\).
To estimate treatment effects for different levels of \(W_i\), include \(W_i\) and its interaction with \(D_i\) in the regression:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 D_i W_i + \beta_3 W_i + U_i
\]
As long as \(D_i\) is randomized, the OLS estimators of \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) will be unbiased and consistent. Including \(W_i\) as a separate regressor is crucial to obtain consistent estimates of \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\).





In practice, individuals in the treatment group often cannot be forced to actually take the treatment they have been assigned. Similarly, individuals in the control group may manage to get the treatment. Let \(D_i\) be an indicator for actual receipt of the treatment and \(Z_i\) an indicator for being assigned to the treatment group.

No-shows: \(Z_i = 1\) but \(D_i = 0\) (assigned to treatment, did not receive it)
Cross-overs: \(Z_i = 0\) but \(D_i = 1\) (not assigned to treatment, received it anyway)

With imperfect compliance, \(D_i\) is likely correlated with \(U_i\), so OLS on the outcome equation is biased. Writing the first stage as \(D_i = \pi_0 + \pi_Z Z_i + V_i\), we have:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D^{OLS} = \beta_D + \frac{\text{Cov}(V_i, U_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)} \neq \beta_D
\]



Since \(Z_i\) is randomized, we can get an unbiased estimate of the intention-to-treat effect (ITT) as the difference in average outcomes between treatment and control groups:
\[
ITT = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0] = \beta_D \pi_Z + \beta_Z
\]
where \(\beta_Z\) is the effect of being assigned to the treatment group on outcome \(Y_i\) that is unrelated to \(Z_i\)’s impact on the probability of getting the treatment. The ITT is not the causal effect \(\beta_D\); it is attenuated compared to \(\beta_D\) since \(\pi_Z < 1\).
However, if being assigned to either group has no effect on the outcome in itself (exclusion restriction: \(\beta_Z = 0\)), we can use \(Z_i\) as an instrument for \(D_i\).



A common solution for imperfect compliance is to use assignment \(Z_i\) as an instrument for treatment receipt \(D_i\). In the exactly identified case, the IV estimator converges to the Wald estimand:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D^{IV} = \frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{\mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 0]}
\]
The denominator is the difference in the probability of receipt of treatment between treatment and control groups. With perfect compliance this is equal to 1 but with partial compliance it will be less than 1. Note that the Wald estimand can also be written as a ratio of the reduced form (ITT) to the first stage: \(ITT = ATT \times P(D_i = 1 \mid Z_i = 1)\).



The parameter identified by the Wald estimand depends on whether treatment effects are homogeneous and on the nature of deviations from randomization:
A1 Constant treatment effect and compliance: \(\beta_i = \beta_D\), \(\pi_i = \pi_Z\)
A2 Independence of \(Z_i\): \(Z_i \perp U_i, V_i\) (and \(Z_i \perp \beta_i, \pi_i\) if A1 fails)
A3 Exclusion restriction: \(\beta_Z = 0\)
A4 First stage: \(\mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 0] \neq 0\)
Under A1-A4 (homogeneous effects, full and two-sided non-compliance), the Wald estimand identifies \(\beta_D\).
Under A2-A4 with heterogeneous effects (dropping A1), the Wald estimand identifies a weighted average treatment effect (WATE):
\[
\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{\mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 0]} = \frac{\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \pi_i)}{\mathbb{E}(\pi_i)} = \mathbb{E}\left(\beta_i \frac{\pi_i}{\mathbb{E}(\pi_i)}\right)
\]
The WATE equals the ATE only if \(\pi_i = \pi_Z\) for all \(i\) or \(\text{Cov}(\beta_i, \pi_i) = 0\).
Under A2-A4 with one-sided non-compliance (no cross-overs, only no-shows) and effect heterogeneity, the Wald estimand identifies the ATT:
\[
\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{\mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 0]} = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i = 1)
\]



Under an additional monotonicity assumption (A5: \(P(\pi_i = -1) = 0\), ruling out defiers), the Wald estimand identifies the local average treatment effect (LATE) for compliers \(\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid \pi_i = 1)\):

Under A2-A5:

\]

\]

Despite providing convincing estimates of causal treatment effects, RCTs face several practical challenges:

Expense: RCTs are often expensive whereas non-experimental data is often available at little or no additional cost.
Ethical issues: Social experiments raise ethical concerns related to some people receiving treatment and others not.
Experimental effects: The Hawthorne and John Henry effects – the excitement of being “watched” – may bring forth greater effort that would not normally be present.
Non-representative sample: Experimental data can only provide estimates of average treatment effects for those in the experiment. One cannot necessarily generalize conclusions to other populations.
Non-representative program: A particular program will not necessarily have the same impact in other places or at other times when the context might be very different.
General equilibrium effects: If some intervention is found to be successful and is scaled up, the scale may have consequences for the effects of the intervention. For example, a program that helps individuals find work faster might have no aggregate effect on employment if the number of jobs is fixed.

title: Randomized Control Trials
text:
The use of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), also known as randomized controlled experiments, gives researchers “the ability to let questions determine the data to be obtained, instead of the data determining the questions that can be asked.” RCTs have become particularly common in labor, public, and development economics.
Suppose we want to estimate the causal effect of \(X_i\) on \(Y_i\). The answer is that there are good reasons to assign \(X_i\) to individuals at random, i.e. to give treatment to all sample members with equal probability. Random assignment circumvents the problems of identifying causal effects: by design, \(D_i\) will be independent of any other pre-treatment influences on \(Y_i\).
To see this formally, suppose \(X_i\) is a binary treatment indicator \(D_i\) and \(W_i\) is any discrete random variable. Under random assignment, \(P(D_i = d \mid W_i = w) = P(D_i = d)\) for all \(w\), so:
\[
\mathbb{E}[W_i \mid D_i = d] = \sum_w P(W_i = w \mid D_i = d) \cdot w = \sum_w P(W_i = w) \cdot w = \mathbb{E}[W_i]
\]
The key step is that \(P(D_i = d \mid W_i = w) = P(D_i = d)\): every individual has the same probability of being treated regardless of individual characteristics. This is not an assumption but follows directly from knowledge about the assignment process. Hence, the expected values of \(W_i\) (and \(U_i\)) are the same in treatment and control groups, and the only systematic reason for the outcome variable to differ is because of the treatment.

title: Randomized Control Trials
text:
Under random assignment \((Y_{1i}, Y_{0i}) \perp D_i\), the selection bias in the naive difference:
\[
\beta \equiv \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0] = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y_{1i} - Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1]}_{\alpha_{ATT}} + \underbrace{(\mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 0])}_{\text{selection bias} = 0}
\]
vanishes since \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 0] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i}]\). It also implies \(\alpha_{ATE} = \alpha_{ATT} = \beta\). The average treatment effect can thus be estimated by a simple linear regression of \(Y_i\) on \(D_i\):
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_D D_i + U_i
\]
The OLS estimator is:
\[
\hat{\beta}_D^S = \frac{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i (D_i - \bar{D})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i (D_i - \bar{D})^2} \qquad \text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D^S = \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, Y_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)}
\]
Working through the covariance numerator using the law of iterated expectations and the fact that \(D_i^2 = D_i\):
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D^S = \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, Y_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0] = \beta_D
\]
so the OLS estimator is consistent. In the case of heterogeneous effects \(\beta_i \neq \beta_D\), one can show that under random assignment plim \(\hat{\beta}_D = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i) = ATE\).

title: Randomized Control Trials
text:
Default OLS standard errors assume \(\text{Var}(Y_i \mid D_i = 1) = \text{Var}(Y_i \mid D_i = 0) = \text{Var}(U_i)\). Since the treatment may affect the variance of \(Y_i\) even if not its mean, this assumption is typically unjustified. The general formula for robust standard errors is:
\[
\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat{\beta}) = \frac{1}{N}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i x_i'\right]^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i x_i' \hat{u}_i^2\right]\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i x_i'\right]^{-1}
\]
An alternative is to compute the variance directly from the difference in means:
\[
\text{Var}(\bar{Y}_T - \bar{Y}_C) = \text{Var}(\bar{Y}_T) + \text{Var}(\bar{Y}_C) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_T^2}{N_1} + \frac{\hat{\sigma}_C^2}{N_0}
\]
where \(\hat{\sigma}_T^2\) and \(\hat{\sigma}_C^2\) are the sample variances within the treatment and control subsamples.



When observations are grouped into clusters (e.g. students within schools), within-cluster outcomes are likely correlated due to common factors. Robust standard errors are biased in this case. The clustered variance estimator is:
\[
\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat{\beta}) = \frac{1}{G}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_g X_g'X_g\right]^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_g X_g'\hat{u}_g\hat{u}_g'X_g\right]\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_g X_g'X_g\right]^{-1}
\]
where \(X_g\) is the \(N_g \times K\) matrix of stacked regressor vectors within cluster \(g\), and \(\hat{u}_g\) is the vector of stacked OLS residuals within cluster \(g\). This estimator is valid as long as the number of clusters \(G\) is large enough (typically above 30).



Conventional inference is based on large-sample approximations to the true asymptotic distribution of the estimator. Randomization inference produces an exact distribution irrespective of sample size. The idea is to repeatedly assign treatment at random and each time compute a corresponding estimate. The resulting distribution captures what estimates one could possibly get under the null hypothesis that the effect is zero for all units. If the original estimate falls sufficiently into the tails of this distribution, this is evidence against the null.

title: Randomized Control Trials
text:
In an RCT, there is no assumption that omitted variables do not matter for the determination of \(Y_i\); the omission of variables that might influence \(Y_i\) does not prevent us from obtaining consistent estimates of the causal effect of \(D_i\) on \(Y_i\). Randomization ensures that \(D_i\) is independent of all other variables, so omitted variable bias does not arise.
Denote by \(\hat{\beta}_D^L\) the OLS estimator of \(\beta_D\) in the long regression \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_D D_i + \beta_W W_i + U_i\). If \(D_i\) is randomized:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D^L = \beta_D \qquad \text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_W = \beta_W + \frac{\text{Cov}(W_i, U_i)}{\text{Var}(W_i)}
\]
Including additional regressors does not affect the consistency of the treatment effect estimate. However, \(\hat{\beta}_W\) will not provide a consistent estimate of \(\beta_W\) unless \(\text{Cov}(W_i, U_i) = 0\).



An important advantage of including additional regressors is that it typically reduces the standard error of the estimated treatment effect. If \(D_i\) is randomized, the asymptotic variance of \(\hat{\beta}_D^L\) (with \(W_i\) included) is weakly lower than that of \(\hat{\beta}_D^S\) (without \(W_i\)). The variance will be strictly lower if \(W_i\) is a relevant predictor of \(Y_i\):









\(\beta_W = 0\)
\(\beta_W \neq 0\)




\(\sigma_{DW} = 0\)
\(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^S) = \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^L)\)
\(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^S) > \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^L)\)


\(\sigma_{DW} \neq 0\)
\(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^S) < \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^L)\)
\(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^S) \lessgtr \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_D^L)\)



If \(D_i\) is not randomized, then the net effect on precision is ambiguous.



In many real-world RCTs there are serious questions about how well the randomization was implemented in practice. One way to assess this is to check that the treatment variable is uncorrelated with the \(W_i\) variables. There are several ways to do this:

Compare the means of \(W_i\) in treatment and control groups.
Run a regression of \(D_i\) on the \(W_i\) variables and test whether the coefficients are jointly zero.
Compare the estimates of the treatment effect when including and excluding \(W_i\). By the OVB formula, plim \((\hat{\beta}_D^S - \hat{\beta}_D^L) = \beta_W \frac{\text{Cov}(D_i, W_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)}\); randomization implies this should be zero.




Randomization ensures that \(D_i\) is independent of \(W_i\) in large samples, but in a small sample the correlation between \(D_i\) and \(W_i\) may not be exactly zero. We can guarantee balance by randomizing conditional on \(W_i\), i.e. \(P(D_i = 1 \mid W_i = w) = P(D_i = 1)\) for all \(w\). By equalizing treatment probabilities within each stratum defined by \(W_i\), we set the sample correlation between \(D_i\) and \(W_i\) to zero for any sample size.
When treatment probabilities are necessarily different for different subgroups (conditional randomization), \(D_i\) is no longer independent of \(X_i\) and the simple difference estimator may suffer from omitted variable bias. However, if we control for \(X_i\) in the regression, then \(D_i\) will be independent of all other omitted variables and we get a consistent estimate of the causal effect. One can show that conditional randomization implies \(\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid D_i, X_i) = \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid X_i)\), the conditional mean independence assumption.

title: Randomized Control Trials
text:
So far we have assumed that the treatment effect is the same for everyone. Let \(\beta_i\) denote the individual-specific treatment effect, and decompose it as:
\[
\beta_i = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid W_i) + r_i = \beta_1 + \beta_2 W_i + r_i
\]
where \(\mathbb{E}(r_i \mid W_i) = 0\). The ATE for subgroup \(W_i = w\) is then \(\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid W_i = w) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 w\), and the unconditional ATE is \(\mathbb{E}(\beta_i) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \mathbb{E}(W_i)\).
To estimate treatment effects for different levels of \(W_i\), include \(W_i\) and its interaction with \(D_i\) in the regression:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 D_i W_i + \beta_3 W_i + U_i
\]
As long as \(D_i\) is randomized, the OLS estimators of \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) will be unbiased and consistent. Including \(W_i\) as a separate regressor is crucial to obtain consistent estimates of \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\).

title: Randomized Control Trials
text:
In practice, individuals in the treatment group often cannot be forced to actually take the treatment they have been assigned. Similarly, individuals in the control group may manage to get the treatment. Let \(D_i\) be an indicator for actual receipt of the treatment and \(Z_i\) an indicator for being assigned to the treatment group.

No-shows: \(Z_i = 1\) but \(D_i = 0\) (assigned to treatment, did not receive it)
Cross-overs: \(Z_i = 0\) but \(D_i = 1\) (not assigned to treatment, received it anyway)

With imperfect compliance, \(D_i\) is likely correlated with \(U_i\), so OLS on the outcome equation is biased. Writing the first stage as \(D_i = \pi_0 + \pi_Z Z_i + V_i\), we have:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D^{OLS} = \beta_D + \frac{\text{Cov}(V_i, U_i)}{\text{Var}(D_i)} \neq \beta_D
\]



Since \(Z_i\) is randomized, we can get an unbiased estimate of the intention-to-treat effect (ITT) as the difference in average outcomes between treatment and control groups:
\[
ITT = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0] = \beta_D \pi_Z + \beta_Z
\]
where \(\beta_Z\) is the effect of being assigned to the treatment group on outcome \(Y_i\) that is unrelated to \(Z_i\)’s impact on the probability of getting the treatment. The ITT is not the causal effect \(\beta_D\); it is attenuated compared to \(\beta_D\) since \(\pi_Z < 1\).
However, if being assigned to either group has no effect on the outcome in itself (exclusion restriction: \(\beta_Z = 0\)), we can use \(Z_i\) as an instrument for \(D_i\).



A common solution for imperfect compliance is to use assignment \(Z_i\) as an instrument for treatment receipt \(D_i\). In the exactly identified case, the IV estimator converges to the Wald estimand:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D^{IV} = \frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{\mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 0]}
\]
The denominator is the difference in the probability of receipt of treatment between treatment and control groups. With perfect compliance this is equal to 1 but with partial compliance it will be less than 1. Note that the Wald estimand can also be written as a ratio of the reduced form (ITT) to the first stage: \(ITT = ATT \times P(D_i = 1 \mid Z_i = 1)\).



The parameter identified by the Wald estimand depends on whether treatment effects are homogeneous and on the nature of deviations from randomization:
A1 Constant treatment effect and compliance: \(\beta_i = \beta_D\), \(\pi_i = \pi_Z\)
A2 Independence of \(Z_i\): \(Z_i \perp U_i, V_i\) (and \(Z_i \perp \beta_i, \pi_i\) if A1 fails)
A3 Exclusion restriction: \(\beta_Z = 0\)
A4 First stage: \(\mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 0] \neq 0\)
Under A1-A4 (homogeneous effects, full and two-sided non-compliance), the Wald estimand identifies \(\beta_D\).
Under A2-A4 with heterogeneous effects (dropping A1), the Wald estimand identifies a weighted average treatment effect (WATE):
\[
\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{\mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 0]} = \frac{\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \pi_i)}{\mathbb{E}(\pi_i)} = \mathbb{E}\left(\beta_i \frac{\pi_i}{\mathbb{E}(\pi_i)}\right)
\]
The WATE equals the ATE only if \(\pi_i = \pi_Z\) for all \(i\) or \(\text{Cov}(\beta_i, \pi_i) = 0\).
Under A2-A4 with one-sided non-compliance (no cross-overs, only no-shows) and effect heterogeneity, the Wald estimand identifies the ATT:
\[
\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{\mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid Z_i = 0]} = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i = 1)
\]



Under an additional monotonicity assumption (A5: \(P(\pi_i = -1) = 0\), ruling out defiers), the Wald estimand identifies the local average treatment effect (LATE) for compliers \(\mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid \pi_i = 1)\):

title: Randomized Control Trials
text:
Despite providing convincing estimates of causal treatment effects, RCTs face several practical challenges:

Expense: RCTs are often expensive whereas non-experimental data is often available at little or no additional cost.
Ethical issues: Social experiments raise ethical concerns related to some people receiving treatment and others not.
Experimental effects: The Hawthorne and John Henry effects – the excitement of being “watched” – may bring forth greater effort that would not normally be present.
Non-representative sample: Experimental data can only provide estimates of average treatment effects for those in the experiment. One cannot necessarily generalize conclusions to other populations.
Non-representative program: A particular program will not necessarily have the same impact in other places or at other times when the context might be very different.

title: Heckit Estimator
text:
Standard OLS assumes a representative sample: all observations are drawn from the same population. Two closely related situations violate this, each requiring a different remedy.

The dependent variable is incompletely observed: some values of \(y\) are missing or replaced by a boundary value. This is censoring.
The dependent variable is only observed for a selected sample: entire observations are dropped based on the outcome. This is truncation.

OLS applied to censored or truncated data yields inconsistent estimates because the conditional mean is no longer linear in \(\mathbf{x}\).



Let \(y^*\) be the latent (true) value of the dependent variable. The observed \(y\) is a transformation \(y = g(y^*)\). The key distinction is:
Censoring (from below at \(L\)): We observe \(y^*\) when \(y^* > L\) but replace it with \(L\) when \(y^* \leq L\). The regressor data is kept for all observations.
\[
y = \begin{cases} y^* & \text{if } y^* > L \\ L & \text{if } y^* \leq L \end{cases}
\]
Example: earnings data where everyone below a threshold is reported as earning exactly the threshold amount (top-coding from above is the symmetric case).
Truncation (from below at \(L\)): We only observe the data when \(y^* > L\). Observations at or below the boundary are lost entirely.
\[
y = y^* \quad \text{if } y^* > L \quad \text{(only these are in the sample)}
\]
Example: sampling only employed workers. Truncation entails greater information loss than censoring since the regressors \(\mathbf{x}\) are also lost for out-of-sample observations.


Let \(f^*(y \mid \mathbf{x})\) and \(F^*(y \mid \mathbf{x})\) be the pdf and cdf of the latent \(y^*\). Define the censoring indicator \(d_i = \mathbf{1}[y_i > L]\). Then the conditional density of the observed \(y\) is:
\[
f(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = f^*(y \mid \mathbf{x})^d \cdot F^*(L \mid \mathbf{x})^{1-d}
\]
The censored MLE maximizes:
\[
\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[d_i \ln f^*(y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i, \theta) + (1-d_i) \ln F^*(L_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i, \theta)\right]
\]
where \(\theta\) collects the parameters of the distribution of \(y^*\). The censored MLE is consistent and asymptotically normal provided \(f^*(y^* \mid \mathbf{x})\) is correctly specified.



For truncation from below, the observed \(y\) has conditional density:
\[
f(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{f^*(y \mid \mathbf{x})}{\Pr[y > L \mid \mathbf{x}]} = \frac{f^*(y \mid \mathbf{x})}{1 - F^*(L \mid \mathbf{x})}
\]
The truncated MLE maximizes:
\[
\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[\ln f^*(y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i, \theta) - \ln\!\left(1 - F^*(L_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i, \theta)\right)\right]
\]




The Tobit model (Tobin, 1958) is the most common censored regression model. It assumes that the latent variable is linear in \(\mathbf{x}\) with normally distributed errors, and censoring occurs from below at zero:
\[
y_i^* = \mathbf{x}_i'\beta + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
\]
\[
y_i = \begin{cases} y_i^* & \text{if } y_i^* > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } y_i^* \leq 0 \end{cases}
\]
So \(y_i^* \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta, \sigma^2)\). Let \(w_i = \mathbf{x}_i'\beta/\sigma\) for shorthand. The Tobit MLE is inconsistent if \(\varepsilon_i\) is either heteroskedastic or non-normal.


Using the general censored MLE with \(f^* = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta, \sigma^2)\), the observed density indicator \(d_i = \mathbf{1}[y_i > 0]\), and \(F^*(0 \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = 1 - \Phi(w_i)\):
\[
\ell(\beta, \sigma^2) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{d_i\left[-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\pi - \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\sigma^2 - \frac{(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i'\beta)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right] + (1-d_i)\ln\!\left[1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)\right]\right\}
\]
The Tobit MLE \(\hat\theta = (\hat\beta', \hat\sigma^2)'\) maximizes this.



Differentiating with respect to \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\):
\[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta} = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\left(d_i(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i'\beta) - (1-d_i)\frac{\sigma\phi_i}{1-\Phi_i}\right)\mathbf{x}_i = 0
\]
\[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma^2} = \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{d_i\!\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i'\beta)^2}{2\sigma^4}\right) + (1-d_i)\frac{\phi_i\,\mathbf{x}_i'\beta}{(1-\Phi_i)\,2\sigma^3}\right\} = 0
\]
where \(\phi_i = \phi(w_i)\) and \(\Phi_i = \Phi(w_i)\).



The key insight is that the marginal effect of a regressor depends on which conditional mean we care about. Let \(w = \mathbf{x}'\beta/\sigma\) and define the inverse Mills ratio \(\lambda(z) = \phi(z)/\Phi(z)\) (derived below).








Quantity
Mean
\(\partial/\partial\mathbf{x}\)




Latent variable
\(E[y^* \mid \mathbf{x}] = \mathbf{x}'\beta\)
\(\beta\)


Truncated mean
\(E[y \mid y > 0, \mathbf{x}]\)
\(\left\{1 - w\lambda(w) - \lambda(w)^2\right\}\beta\)


Censored mean
\(E[y \mid \mathbf{x}]\)
\(\Phi(w)\,\beta\)



The factor \(\Phi(w)\) in the censored marginal effect is the probability that the observation is uncensored; at zero censoring (\(w \to \infty\)), \(\Phi(w) \to 1\) and the Tobit coefficient recovers the OLS coefficient. The censored marginal effect is the one reported in standard applied work.






The simple Tobit model assumes the selection mechanism (who is observed) and the outcome equation share the same latent variable. The bivariate sample selection model (also called the Type 2 or generalized Tobit) separates them into two distinct equations:
Participation equation (determines whether \(y_2\) is observed):
\[
y_1 = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y_1^* > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } y_1^* \leq 0 \end{cases}, \qquad y_1^* = \mathbf{x}_1'\beta_1 + \varepsilon_1
\]
Outcome equation (observed only when \(y_1 = 1\)):
\[
y_2 = \begin{cases} y_2^* & \text{if } y_1^* > 0 \\ - & \text{if } y_1^* \leq 0 \end{cases}, \qquad y_2^* = \mathbf{x}_2'\beta_2 + \varepsilon_2
\]
Example: \(y_1^*\) determines whether a person works at all (participation); \(y_2^*\) determines how many hours they work conditional on working. Different factors may drive each decision (e.g., fixed costs of commuting affect the participation margin but not hours conditional on working).



Estimation requires an assumption on the joint distribution of \((\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2)\). The standard assumption is joint normality with homoskedastic errors:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}\varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2\end{bmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix},\, \begin{bmatrix}1 & \sigma_{12} \\ \sigma_{12} & \sigma_2^2\end{bmatrix}\right)
\]
The normalization \(\sigma_1^2 = 1\) is imposed since only the sign of \(y_1^*\) is observed; rescaling \(y_1^*\) by any \(a > 0\) does not change the observed \(y_1\), so the variance is not identified.





Using the truncated normal distribution, for any \(\varepsilon_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\):
\[
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_1 \mid \varepsilon_1 > -c] = \frac{\phi(c)}{\Phi(c)} \equiv \lambda(c)
\]
The function \(\lambda(z) = \phi(z)/\Phi(z)\) is the inverse Mills ratio. It is always positive and decreasing in \(z\).



The mean of \(y_2\) for the observed (selected) subsample is:
\[
\mathbb{E}[y_2 \mid \mathbf{x}, y_1^* > 0] = \mathbf{x}_2'\beta_2 + \sigma_{12}\lambda(\mathbf{x}_1'\beta_1)
\]
This follows from writing \(\varepsilon_2 = \sigma_{12}\varepsilon_1 + \xi\) where \(\xi\) is independent of \(\varepsilon_1\), so \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_2 \mid \varepsilon_1 > -\mathbf{x}_1'\beta_1] = \sigma_{12}\lambda(\mathbf{x}_1'\beta_1)\).
The key implication: OLS on only the observed \(y_2\) is inconsistent unless \(\sigma_{12} = 0\) (the errors are uncorrelated), because the inverse Mills ratio acts as an omitted variable correlated with \(\mathbf{x}_2\).



If \(y_2 = 0\) when \(y_1^* \leq 0\), the unconditional mean is:
\[
\mathbb{E}[y_2 \mid \mathbf{x}] = \Phi(\mathbf{x}_1'\beta_1)\,\mathbf{x}_2'\beta_2 + \sigma_{12}\phi(\mathbf{x}_1'\beta_1)
\]





The full MLE for the bivariate sample selection model is efficient but computationally demanding. Heckman (1979) proposed a simpler two-step approach, known as the Heckit estimator.
Step 1: Estimate a Probit model for selection on the full sample (all \(N\) observations, including \(y_1 = 0\)). Since \(\Pr(y_1 = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_1) = \Phi(\mathbf{x}_1'\beta_1)\), this yields consistent estimates \(\hat\beta_1\). Compute the estimated inverse Mills ratio for each individual:
\[
\hat\lambda_i = \lambda(\mathbf{x}_{1i}'\hat\beta_1) = \frac{\phi(\mathbf{x}_{1i}'\hat\beta_1)}{\Phi(\mathbf{x}_{1i}'\hat\beta_1)}
\]
Step 2: Using only the selected subsample (\(y_{1i} = 1\)), run OLS of \(y_{2i}\) on \(\mathbf{x}_{2i}\) and \(\hat\lambda_i\):
\[
y_{2i} = \mathbf{x}_{2i}'\beta_2 + \sigma_{12}\hat\lambda_i + v_i
\]
The coefficient on \(\hat\lambda_i\) estimates \(\sigma_{12}\). A \(t\)-test of this coefficient is a test for sample selection (\(H_0: \sigma_{12} = 0\)).
Note: The standard errors from Step 2 OLS are incorrect. They must be adjusted to account for both heteroskedasticity and the fact that \(\hat\lambda_i\) was estimated in Step 1 (sampling variability of \(\hat\beta_1\) carries through). Stata’s heckman, twostep handles this automatically.
The Heckit estimator is less efficient than MLE under joint normality but is simpler to implement and more robust: it only requires \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_2 \mid \varepsilon_1] = \delta\varepsilon_1\) rather than full joint normality.



The bivariate sample selection model is in principle identified without any restrictions on the regressors, purely through the functional form of \(\lambda(\cdot)\). However, the inverse Mills ratio \(\lambda(\mathbf{x}_1'\beta_1)\) is approximately linear over a wide range of its argument. If \(\mathbf{x}_1 = \mathbf{x}_2\), this creates severe multicollinearity between \(\hat\lambda_i\) and \(\mathbf{x}_{2i}\) in Step 2.
In practice, reliable identification requires an exclusion restriction: at least one variable in \(\mathbf{x}_1\) (the participation equation) that is excluded from \(\mathbf{x}_2\) (the outcome equation). This instrument must affect selection but have no direct effect on \(y_2^*\) conditional on participation.

title: Heckit Estimator
text:
Standard OLS assumes a representative sample: all observations are drawn from the same population. Two closely related situations violate this, each requiring a different remedy.

The dependent variable is incompletely observed: some values of \(y\) are missing or replaced by a boundary value. This is censoring.
The dependent variable is only observed for a selected sample: entire observations are dropped based on the outcome. This is truncation.

OLS applied to censored or truncated data yields inconsistent estimates because the conditional mean is no longer linear in \(\mathbf{x}\).

title: Heckit Estimator
text:
Let \(y^*\) be the latent (true) value of the dependent variable. The observed \(y\) is a transformation \(y = g(y^*)\). The key distinction is:
Censoring (from below at \(L\)): We observe \(y^*\) when \(y^* > L\) but replace it with \(L\) when \(y^* \leq L\). The regressor data is kept for all observations.
\[
y = \begin{cases} y^* & \text{if } y^* > L \\ L & \text{if } y^* \leq L \end{cases}
\]
Example: earnings data where everyone below a threshold is reported as earning exactly the threshold amount (top-coding from above is the symmetric case).
Truncation (from below at \(L\)): We only observe the data when \(y^* > L\). Observations at or below the boundary are lost entirely.
\[
y = y^* \quad \text{if } y^* > L \quad \text{(only these are in the sample)}
\]
Example: sampling only employed workers. Truncation entails greater information loss than censoring since the regressors \(\mathbf{x}\) are also lost for out-of-sample observations.


Let \(f^*(y \mid \mathbf{x})\) and \(F^*(y \mid \mathbf{x})\) be the pdf and cdf of the latent \(y^*\). Define the censoring indicator \(d_i = \mathbf{1}[y_i > L]\). Then the conditional density of the observed \(y\) is:
\[
f(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = f^*(y \mid \mathbf{x})^d \cdot F^*(L \mid \mathbf{x})^{1-d}
\]
The censored MLE maximizes:
\[
\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[d_i \ln f^*(y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i, \theta) + (1-d_i) \ln F^*(L_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i, \theta)\right]
\]
where \(\theta\) collects the parameters of the distribution of \(y^*\). The censored MLE is consistent and asymptotically normal provided \(f^*(y^* \mid \mathbf{x})\) is correctly specified.



For truncation from below, the observed \(y\) has conditional density:
\[
f(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{f^*(y \mid \mathbf{x})}{\Pr[y > L \mid \mathbf{x}]} = \frac{f^*(y \mid \mathbf{x})}{1 - F^*(L \mid \mathbf{x})}
\]
The truncated MLE maximizes:
\[
\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[\ln f^*(y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i, \theta) - \ln\!\left(1 - F^*(L_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i, \theta)\right)\right]
\]

title: Heckit Estimator
text:
The Tobit model (Tobin, 1958) is the most common censored regression model. It assumes that the latent variable is linear in \(\mathbf{x}\) with normally distributed errors, and censoring occurs from below at zero:
\[
y_i^* = \mathbf{x}_i'\beta + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
\]
\[
y_i = \begin{cases} y_i^* & \text{if } y_i^* > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } y_i^* \leq 0 \end{cases}
\]
So \(y_i^* \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta, \sigma^2)\). Let \(w_i = \mathbf{x}_i'\beta/\sigma\) for shorthand. The Tobit MLE is inconsistent if \(\varepsilon_i\) is either heteroskedastic or non-normal.


Using the general censored MLE with \(f^* = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta, \sigma^2)\), the observed density indicator \(d_i = \mathbf{1}[y_i > 0]\), and \(F^*(0 \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = 1 - \Phi(w_i)\):
\[
\ell(\beta, \sigma^2) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{d_i\left[-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\pi - \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\sigma^2 - \frac{(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i'\beta)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right] + (1-d_i)\ln\!\left[1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)\right]\right\}
\]
The Tobit MLE \(\hat\theta = (\hat\beta', \hat\sigma^2)'\) maximizes this.



Differentiating with respect to \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\):
\[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta} = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\left(d_i(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i'\beta) - (1-d_i)\frac{\sigma\phi_i}{1-\Phi_i}\right)\mathbf{x}_i = 0
\]
\[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma^2} = \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{d_i\!\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i'\beta)^2}{2\sigma^4}\right) + (1-d_i)\frac{\phi_i\,\mathbf{x}_i'\beta}{(1-\Phi_i)\,2\sigma^3}\right\} = 0
\]
where \(\phi_i = \phi(w_i)\) and \(\Phi_i = \Phi(w_i)\).



The key insight is that the marginal effect of a regressor depends on which conditional mean we care about. Let \(w = \mathbf{x}'\beta/\sigma\) and define the inverse Mills ratio \(\lambda(z) = \phi(z)/\Phi(z)\) (derived below).








Quantity
Mean
\(\partial/\partial\mathbf{x}\)




Latent variable
\(E[y^* \mid \mathbf{x}] = \mathbf{x}'\beta\)
\(\beta\)


Truncated mean
\(E[y \mid y > 0, \mathbf{x}]\)
\(\left\{1 - w\lambda(w) - \lambda(w)^2\right\}\beta\)


Censored mean
\(E[y \mid \mathbf{x}]\)
\(\Phi(w)\,\beta\)



The factor \(\Phi(w)\) in the censored marginal effect is the probability that the observation is uncensored; at zero censoring (\(w \to \infty\)), \(\Phi(w) \to 1\) and the Tobit coefficient recovers the OLS coefficient. The censored marginal effect is the one reported in standard applied work.

title: Ordered Response Models
text:
So far, we have focused on unordered choice models, in which there was no natural ordering of alternatives or sequencing of decisions. We now look at the case where alternatives can be ordered, which then can be estimated with so-called Ordered Response Models.



To understand the ordered response model, we first need to define a Latent Variable Model:
We assume a latent (unobserved) outcome variable \(y_i^*\), which can be thought of as “Happiness” or “Utility”:
\[
y_i^* = x_i'\beta + u_i
\]

Note: No intercept is included in this specification. This is because if a constant exists when we try to calculate \(\mathbb{P}[\varepsilon_i \leq \alpha_m - x_i'\beta]\), we cannot separately identify the constant (intercept) from the thresholds.
Properties:

The observed values \(y_i \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots, 10\}\) are not cardinal.
Magnitude is meaningless (e.g., the difference between 1 and 2 is not necessarily the same as the difference between 3 and 4).
Linearity assumptions do not hold for the outcome categories.


This explains why OLS fails in this case; OLS implicitly assumes equidistant thresholds; i.e., the distance between \(y_i = 1\) & \(y_i = 2\) is the exact same as the distance between \(y_i = 2\) & \(y_i = 3\). Applied to our latent variable model, the ‘width’ of a category is determined by the distance between thresholds \((\text{e.g. } \alpha_2 - \alpha_1)\). Let’s say that \(y_i^*\) represents life satisfaction; the thresholds for life satisfaction \(\alpha_1\) \(\dots\) \(\alpha_m\) likely assume a non-equal form resembling the following structure:
\[ \mid \dots \dots \dots. \mid \dots \dots. \mid \dots .\mid ...\mid . \mid  .\mid ... \mid \dots. \mid \dots \dots.\mid \dots \dots \dots. \mid\]


The observed variable \(y_i\) is determined by where the latent variable \(y_i^*\) falls relative to thresholds (cut-points) \(\alpha_m\):
\[
y_i =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \alpha_0 < y_i^* \leq \alpha_1 \quad (\text{Assumed } \alpha_0 = -\infty) \\
2 & \text{if } \alpha_1 < y_i^* \leq \alpha_2 \\
\vdots & \vdots \\
m & \text{if } \alpha_{m-1} < y_i^* \leq \alpha_m \quad (\text{Assumed } \alpha_m = +\infty)
\end{cases}
\]



Deriving the probabilities for each outcome category conditional on \(x_i\):


\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[y_i = 1 \mid X_i] &= \mathbb{P}[y_i^* \leq \alpha_1 \mid X_i] \\
&= \mathbb{P}[x_i'\beta + u_i \leq \alpha_1 \mid X_i] \\
&= \mathbb{P}[u_i \leq \alpha_1 - x_i'\beta \mid X_i]
\end{aligned}
\]

Now depends on the distribution assumed on \(u_i\).
For example, if \(u_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) (Standard Normal):

\[
= F_x(\alpha_1 - x_i'\beta)= \Phi(\alpha_1 - x_i'\beta)
\]
Which gives us the Ordered Probit Model

Note: If \(u_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\), we divide by sigma to normalize:

\[
\Phi\left[ \frac{u_i}{\sigma} \leq \frac{\alpha_1}{\sigma} - x_i'\frac{\beta}{\sigma} \mid X_i \right]
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[y_i = 2 \mid x_i] &= \mathbb{P}[\alpha_1 < y_i^* \leq \alpha_2 \mid X_i] \\
&= \mathbb{P}[y_i^* \leq \alpha_2 \mid X_i] - \mathbb{P}[y_i^* \leq \alpha_1 \mid X_i] \\
&= \Phi(\alpha_2 - x_i'\beta) - \Phi(\alpha_1 - x_i'\beta)
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[y_i = m \mid X_i] &= \mathbb{P}[y_i^* > \alpha_{m-1} \mid X_i] \\
&= 1 - \Phi(\alpha_{m-1} - x_i'\beta)
\end{aligned}
\]






The log-likelihood for an individual \(i\), denoted \(\ell_i(\alpha, \beta)\), combines the probabilities using indicator functions \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_i(\alpha, \beta) &= \mathbf{1}[y_i=1] \log \Phi(\alpha_1 - x_i'\beta) \\
&+ \mathbf{1}[y_i=2] \log [\Phi(\alpha_2 - x_i'\beta) - \Phi(\alpha_1 - x_i'\beta)] \\
&   \dots \\
& + \mathbf{1}[y_i=m] \log \Phi(\alpha_{m-1} - x_i'\beta)
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\Rightarrow\) MLE yields estimates \(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\alpha}\).


An advantage of such models is that they are parsimonious: they only require \(K + (m-1)\) coefficient estimates \((\# \beta + \# \alpha)\). Compare this to multinomial logit, which requires: \((K+1) \cdot (m-1)\) coefficient estimates.
To see this, consider the following example:
Imagine predicting travel mode choice based on Income.

Ordered (Low, Med, High Quality): Higher income pushes you up the quality ladder uniformly. We need just one slope estimate for “Income” and cut-points for “Low/Med” and “Med/High”.
Multinomial (Bus, Bike, Car): Higher income might make you more likely to drive a Car but less likely to Bike. The effect of income is fundamentally different for each outcome, so we need to estimate separate slope parameters for each alternative.





We are interested in the impact of a change in regressor \(x_i\) on the probability of choosing alternative \(j\):
\[
\frac{\partial \mathbb{P}[y_i=j \mid x_i]}{\partial x_i}
\]
Using the Chain Rule on the probability definitions (where \(F' = f\), the PDF):
\[
= \left[ F'(\alpha_{j-1} - x_i'\beta) - F'(\alpha_j - x_i'\beta) \right] \beta
\]

Where \(F\) corresponds to the CDF (\(\Phi\) for Probit, \(\Lambda\) for Logit).
The term in brackets determines the sign of the effect (can be \(>0\) or \(<0\)).
However, the sign is ambiguous: we cannot use the sign of \(\beta\) to interpret the sign of the marginal effect.

The log-likelihood for an individual \(i\), denoted \(\ell_i(\alpha, \beta)\), combines the probabilities using indicator functions \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_i(\alpha, \beta) &= \mathbf{1}[y_i=1] \log \Phi(\alpha_1 - x_i'\beta) \\
&+ \mathbf{1}[y_i=2] \log [\Phi(\alpha_2 - x_i'\beta) - \Phi(\alpha_1 - x_i'\beta)] \\
&   \dots \\
& + \mathbf{1}[y_i=m] \log \Phi(\alpha_{m-1} - x_i'\beta)
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\Rightarrow\) MLE yields estimates \(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\alpha}\).


An advantage of such models is that they are parsimonious: they only require \(K + (m-1)\) coefficient estimates \((\# \beta + \# \alpha)\). Compare this to multinomial logit, which requires: \((K+1) \cdot (m-1)\) coefficient estimates.
To see this, consider the following example:
Imagine predicting travel mode choice based on Income.

Ordered (Low, Med, High Quality): Higher income pushes you up the quality ladder uniformly. We need just one slope estimate for “Income” and cut-points for “Low/Med” and “Med/High”.
Multinomial (Bus, Bike, Car): Higher income might make you more likely to drive a Car but less likely to Bike. The effect of income is fundamentally different for each outcome, so we need to estimate separate slope parameters for each alternative.





We are interested in the impact of a change in regressor \(x_i\) on the probability of choosing alternative \(j\):
\[
\frac{\partial \mathbb{P}[y_i=j \mid x_i]}{\partial x_i}
\]
Using the Chain Rule on the probability definitions (where \(F' = f\), the PDF):
\[
= \left[ F'(\alpha_{j-1} - x_i'\beta) - F'(\alpha_j - x_i'\beta) \right] \beta
\]

Where \(F\) corresponds to the CDF (\(\Phi\) for Probit, \(\Lambda\) for Logit).
The term in brackets determines the sign of the effect (can be \(>0\) or \(<0\)).
However, the sign is ambiguous: we cannot use the sign of \(\beta\) to interpret the sign of the marginal effect.

title: Multinomial Models
text:
A natural question that arises regarding our log-likelihood models for discrete outcomes is that of model specification. Specifically, how do we select a form for \(F_j (x_{i},\beta)\)?
Suppose we have \(j=1,2,...,m\) alternatives. We can then define the following:
\[U_j = V_j + \varepsilon_j \tag{1}\]
Where:

\(U_j\) : represents the utility of choosing alternative \(j\)
\(V_j\) : the deterministic component (comprised of all the possible regressors) for alternative \(j\)
\(\varepsilon_j\) : random error term – included since all individuals have the alternatives but possibly different utilities for a choice – allows for some randomness

When does an individual prefer alternative \(j\) to alternative \(k\)? Simply when they get more utility from \(j\) than they do \(k\). More formally:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[y_i = j \mid X_i] &= \mathbb{P}[U_j \ge U_k, \forall_{j \neq k}] \\
&= \mathbb{P}[U_k - U_j \leq 0, \forall_{j \neq k}] \\
&= \mathbb{P}[\varepsilon_k - \varepsilon_j \leq V_k - V_j, \forall_{j \neq k}] \\
&= \mathbb{P}[\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{kj} \leq -\widetilde{V}_{kj} , \forall_{j \neq k}]
\end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]
Note that in the last step we simply rewrite the difference between alternative \(k\) and alternative \(j\) as \(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{kj}\).
Lets explore this in a 3-choice model:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[y_i=1 \mid X_i] = \mathbb{P}[\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{31} \leq -\widetilde{V}_{31}, \widetilde{\varepsilon}_{21} \leq -\widetilde{V}_{21} \mid X_i]
\end{aligned} \tag{3}
\]
This is telling us the same thing as (2): the probability that individual \(i\) chooses alternative \(1\) (given a set of alternatives) is equal to the probability that individual \(i\) prefers alternative \(1\) to both alternative \(3\) as well as alternative \(2\).
We can write this as a joint probability density function of the error terms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
= \int_{-\infty}^{-\tilde{V}_{31}} \int_{-\infty}^{-\tilde{V}_{21}} f\left(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{31}, \tilde{\varepsilon}_{21} \right) d \tilde{\varepsilon}_{21} d \tilde{\varepsilon}_{31}
\end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]
Although this is the correct theoretical specification, an issue arises when we try to compute this for more alternatives. Imagine we have a set of 20 alternatives; we would have a 19-degree integration which would be computationally impossible to evaluate in any finite time period. Thus, we need to simplify this integration somehow.



To simplify the model, a key assumption we need to make is on the distribution of the error terms; specifically we need to assume that the errors follow a Type 1 Extreme Value Distribution (Gumbel Distribution):
\[f\left(\varepsilon_j \right) \sim Gumbel\left( \mu, \beta \right)\]
Which indirectly makes assumptions on the differenced errors (from our 3-alternative example above):
\[f\left(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{21} ,  \tilde{\varepsilon}_{31} \right) \sim Gumbel\left( \mu, \beta \right)\]
Where the Gumbel Distribution’s PDF has the following form:
\[ f(\varepsilon_j) = e^{-\varepsilon_j} \cdot e^{-e^{-\varepsilon_j}} \tag{5}\]



Figure 1: PDF of a Gumbel Distributed Random Variable


** Note: multinomial probit assumes a normal (Gaussian) distributional form of the error terms; we will not cover that case here.
Further, we also assume these errors are IID: importantly, this assumption is placed upon the alternatives, rather than the individuals (although that is always assumed in the background). This means that our error terms are uncorrelated across alternatives (\(j = 1, 2, ... , m\)); every alternative is drawn at random with equal probability.
Note:
This is a strong assumption that will be relaxed later on. For now, imagine the case where our set of alternatives consists of different cities an individual could to move to, say:
\[\{\text{Alternatives}\}_m = \{\text{Barcelona, Madrid, Beijing, Moscow}\}. \]
Intuitively, an individual’s utility for Barcelona and Madrid are likely highly correlated as they share similar characteristics (location, weather, language, etc), compared to other cities in our set, such as Beijing or Moscow. The IID assumption ignores this correlation, treating a preference for Barcelona as completely independent of a preference for Madrid.
The reason we choose the Gumbel distribution for our errors is that, after substituting the Gumbel PDF from (5) into our joint PDF function from (4), our conditional probability function simplifies to:
\[ \mathbb{P}[y_i = j \mid X_i] = \frac{e^{V_j}}{e^{V_1} + e^{V_2} + ... + e^{V_m}} \tag{6}\]
This result is much more computationally friendly, even when as th choice set increases to 20 or 30 alternatives, the Gumbel distribution allows for a closed-form solution (6).
Further, although the Gumbel distribution is asymmetrical, it is the standard choice here because it is an Extreme Value distribution. It is designed to model the maximum of a series of random variables, making it ideal for our utility framework where we assume the individual selects the alternative that yields the maximum utility.
In the real world, this distributional form is useful in predicting the chance that an extreme event will occur (earthquake prediction simulations, measuring financial losses, insurance risks, etc).



What remains is a specification of the deterministic component of the utility function. There exists two main specification methods (and a mixture between them):
\[
V_j = \begin{cases}
  X_{ij}'\beta &\text{"Conditional Logit"} \\
   \\
  X_i'\beta_j &\text{"Multinomial Logit"} \\
   \\
  X_{ij}'\beta + \omega_i'\alpha_j &\text{"Mixed Logit"}
\end{cases} \tag{7}
\]


We specify the deterministic component of utility of alternative \(j\) with alternative-varying regressors, i.e. 
\[V_j = X_{ij}'\beta \tag{8}\]
These regressors can vary across individuals and alternatives. Using our previous choice set of cities, we can think of these regressors as being characteristics of the cities themselves impacting the overall utility: weather, location, population, etc; varying across individuals.
These are the characteristics the regressors share but can vary in their utility for each individual. I.e. I might value the warm weather of Barcelona more than the cold of Moscow, but some other individual might value the inverse case.
Plugging in this specification for \(V_j\) into equation (1), we get the following form for the likelihood function:
\[P_{ij} = \mathbb{P}[y_i = j \mid X_i] = \frac{e^{x_{ij}'\beta}}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^me^{x_{ik}'\beta}} \tag{9}\]



In this case, the specified regressors contained in the deterministic component of utility are individual-specific, but not alternative-specific. We define these as alternative-invariant regressors:
\[V_j = X_i'\beta_j \tag{10}\]
Using our same cities choice set, we can think of this being individual-level characteristics affecting the utility assigned to a specific city; my current lifestyle/age will impact the utility I receive moving to a city like Barcelona versus a city like Moscow; however, characteristics of the city itself (its party scene, age of population, etc) has no effect on my utility assigned to moving to that city. (personal note: I find this hard to believe; I would expect that the utility you get from aspects like your age are tied in directly to the characteristics of the cities themselves. maybe another example would make this specifiation choice more clear, but it seems unrealistic for our correct model specification to be mlogit.)
Plugging in this specification for \(V_j\) into equation (1), we get the following form for the likelihood function:
\[P_{ij} = \mathbb{P}[y_i = j \mid X_i] = \frac{e^{x_i'\beta_j}}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^m e^{x_i'\beta_k}} \tag{11}\]




Let’s look at another example. Suppose that we are fishing in Barcelona, and we have the following set of alternatives for fishing locations:
\[\{\text{Fishing Choice Alternatives}\}_{m=4} = \{\text{Beach}_1, \text{Pier}_2, \text{Private Boat}_3, \text{Charter Boat}_4\}\]


\[U_{ij} = X_{ij}'\beta + \varepsilon_{ij} \tag{12}\]
Suppose we define the vector of regressors in \(X_{ij}\) as the following:
\[
X_{ij} = \begin{bmatrix}
  \text{Catch Rate} \\
  \text{Price}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Note that these regressors are alternative-variant:

Catch Rate depends on the choice of beach, boat, pier, etc;
same goes for the Price of fishing at a given location.



The marginal change in the probability of fishing at the beach is the marginal effect given by beta; in other words, how the probability of individual \(i\) choosing a specific location (e.g., \(\Delta P_{i,\text{beach}}\)) changes when a characteristic of that same location (e.g., \(\Delta \text{Catch Rate}_{i, \text{Beach}}\)) changes.
\[
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial P_{i1}}{\partial X_{i1}}
&= \frac{\partial \mathbb{P}[y_i = \text{Beach} \mid \{\text{Catch Rate, Price} \}_i]}{\partial X_{i, \text{Beach}}} \\
&= \left( \underbrace{\frac{e^{x_{i1}'\beta}}{\sum_{k=1}^m e^{x_{ik}'\beta}}}_{P_{i1}} - \underbrace{\left( \frac{e^{x_{i1}'\beta}}{\sum_{k=1}^m e^{x_{ik}'\beta}} \right)^2}_{(P_{i1})^2} \right) \beta \\
&= P_{i1}(1-P_{i1})\beta \tag{14}
\end{align}
\]
What does this tell us?

Beta tells us the sign of the marginal effect: since \(P_{ij} \in [0, 1]\), it must be that if beta is positive, so too is the marginal effect.
The marginal effect coffecient value is not directly interpretable – we cannot separate \(P_{ij}\) and \(1 - P_{ij}\) here.




What if we look across alternatives? I.e., how does a change in the characteristics of the Beach (\(\Delta X_{i,\text{Beach}}\)) affect the probability of individual \(i\) choosing to fish from the Pier (\(\Delta P_{i, \text{Pier}}\))?
Equivalently, this is expressed as:
\[
\begin{align}
\frac
{\partial \mathbb{P}[y_i = Pier \mid \{\text{Catch Rate, Price} \}_i]}
{\partial X_{i, Beach}}
&=
\frac
{\partial P_{i2}}
{\partial X_{i1}} \\
&=
\frac
{0 - e^{x_{i2}'\beta}e^{x_{i1}'\beta} \beta}
{\left(\sum_{k=1}^me^{x_{ik}'\beta}\right)^2} \\
&=
(-P_{i2})P_{i1}\beta \tag{15}
\end{align}
\]
Observations:

Beta and the Marginal Effect have opposing signs: if \(\beta \gt 0\), then \(ME(\beta) \lt 0\)
Again, cannot interpret the magnitude of beta.

In summary: we can write the two types of marginal effects as the following for a conditional logit model:
\[
\frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial X_{ik}} =
\begin{cases}
  P_{ij}(1-P_{ij}) & j = k \\
  P_{ij}(-P_{ik}) & j \neq k
\end{cases} \tag{16}
\]
Note that the direction is unambiguous for both cases.




What happens when applied to a multinomial logit model? Is the marginal effect the same?
The marginal effect is written as:
\[\frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial X_i} = P_{ij}(\beta_j - \bar{\beta}_i), \\ \text{where } \bar{\beta}_i \equiv \sum_{k=1}^m P_{ik}\beta_k \tag{17}\]
Where \(\bar{\beta}_i\) is a “weighted average” of \(\beta\)’s (coefficients), weighted by the probability of choosing a particular alternative \(k\).
The issue here is that finding the sign of \(\beta_j\) is not informative of the ME – it depends on the value of \(\bar{\beta}_i\); i.e., the direction is ambiguous.



Another way to interpret our coefficients is looking at the relative risk ratio (rrr), by taking the ratio of the probabilities of two distinct alternatives


\[
\begin{align}
\frac
{P_{ij}}
{P_{ik}} &=
\frac
{\mathbb{P}[y_i = j \mid X_i]}
{\mathbb{P}[y_i = k \mid X_i]} \\
&=
\frac
{e^{x_{ij}'\beta}}
{e^{x_{ik}'\beta}} && \text{by conditional logit def} \\
&=
e^{(x_{ij}-x_{ik})'\beta} && \text{property of exponents} \\
log
\frac
{P_{ij}}
{P_{ik}} &=
(X_{ij}-X_{ik})'\beta && \text{log both sides} \tag{18}
\end{align}
\]
Thus, we can interpret \(\beta\) as the change in the log-odds of choosing alternative \(j\) over alternative \(k\) for every one-unit increase in the difference between their characteristics (\(X_{ij}\)-\(X_{ik}\))
In our fishing example, suppose we get output of \(\beta_{price} = -0.05\) for (\(X_{i,Beach} - X_{i,Pier}\)) – we would interpret this as: for a $1 increase in the price of the Beach (relative to the Pier), the odds of choosing the Beach over the Pier drop by 5%.



For mlogit, its important to standardize a beta, essentially to set one alternative as our “base case” with which we can relatively compare the other alternatives. For example, suppose we set \(\beta_k = \beta_1 = 0\); then, our relative risk ratio (also know as odds-ratio) is derived as the following:
\[
\begin{align}
\frac
{P_{ij}}
{P_{ik}} &=
\frac
{\mathbb{P}[y_i = j \mid X_i]}
{\mathbb{P}[y_i = k \mid X_i]} \\
&=
\frac
{e^{x_i'\beta_j}}
{e^{x_i'\beta_k}} && \text{by conditional logit def} \\
&=
e^{x_i'(\beta_j-\beta_k)} && \text{property of exponents} \\
&=
\frac
{\mathbb{P}[y_i = j \mid X_i]}
{\mathbb{P}[y_i = 1 \mid X_i]} && \text{plug in } \beta_k  = \beta_1 \\
&=
e^{x_i'\beta_j}
&& \text{normalize: } \beta_1 = 0\\
log
\frac
{P_{ij}}
{P_{i1}} &=
(X_i)'\beta_j && \text{log both sides} \tag{19}
\end{align}
\]
Here we can interpret \(\beta\) as the change in the log-odds of choosing alternative \(j\) relative to the base case (alternative \(k\)) for a one-unit increase in individual-specific regressors (e.g., Income). Note that unlike the clogit model, where we look at the difference in characteristics between choices, here the characteristic is fixed for the individual, and the coefficient \(\beta_j\) represents how that trait shifts the individual’s preference toward alternative \(j\) specifically.





A seemingly powerful aspect of these models is the fact that the probabilities only depend the two specific alternatives we are comparing at a given time, stemming from out IID assumption early on. However, we can see an example as to why this might fail in reality.
Suppose we want to model traffic in a city, and there exists only two forms of transportation, a car and a red bus, s.t.:
\[\frac{\mathbb{P}[\text{car}]}{\mathbb{P}[\text{red bus}]} = \frac{0.5}{0.5}\]

Note that this is consistent since \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb{P}_i = 1\)

Now imagine we introduce a new form of transportation (i.e. a third alternative) in the city: a blue bus. Intuitively, we expect to see:
\[
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}[\text{blue bus}] = \mathbb{P}[\text{red bus}] = 25\% \\
\mathbb{P}[\text{car}] = 50\%
\end{align}
\]
Yet for our multinomal models, we instead derive from the IID (random sampling) assumption that our new choice distribution is:
\[\mathbb{P}[\text{blue bus}] = \mathbb{P}[\text{red bus}] = \mathbb{P}[\text{car}] = 33.33\%\] Another way to say the same thing is that an improved product gains share from all other products in proportion to their original shares; and when a product loses share, it loses to others in proportion to their shares.
As it stands, our current models cannot account for this phenomena; hence, we need to relax our IID assumption and try to construct a different variant of our models: Nested Logit.

\[
\frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial X_{ik}} =
\begin{cases}
  P_{ij}(1-P_{ij}) & j = k \\
  P_{ij}(-P_{ik}) & j \neq k
\end{cases} \tag{16}
\]
Note that the direction is unambiguous for both cases.




What happens when applied to a multinomial logit model? Is the marginal effect the same?
The marginal effect is written as:
\[\frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial X_i} = P_{ij}(\beta_j - \bar{\beta}_i), \\ \text{where } \bar{\beta}_i \equiv \sum_{k=1}^m P_{ik}\beta_k \tag{17}\]
Where \(\bar{\beta}_i\) is a “weighted average” of \(\beta\)’s (coefficients), weighted by the probability of choosing a particular alternative \(k\).
The issue here is that finding the sign of \(\beta_j\) is not informative of the ME – it depends on the value of \(\bar{\beta}_i\); i.e., the direction is ambiguous.



Another way to interpret our coefficients is looking at the relative risk ratio (rrr), by taking the ratio of the probabilities of two distinct alternatives


\[
\begin{align}
\frac
{P_{ij}}
{P_{ik}} &=
\frac
{\mathbb{P}[y_i = j \mid X_i]}
{\mathbb{P}[y_i = k \mid X_i]} \\
&=
\frac
{e^{x_{ij}'\beta}}
{e^{x_{ik}'\beta}} && \text{by conditional logit def} \\
&=
e^{(x_{ij}-x_{ik})'\beta} && \text{property of exponents} \\
log
\frac
{P_{ij}}
{P_{ik}} &=
(X_{ij}-X_{ik})'\beta && \text{log both sides} \tag{18}
\end{align}
\]
Thus, we can interpret \(\beta\) as the change in the log-odds of choosing alternative \(j\) over alternative \(k\) for every one-unit increase in the difference between their characteristics (\(X_{ij}\)-\(X_{ik}\))
In our fishing example, suppose we get output of \(\beta_{price} = -0.05\) for (\(X_{i,Beach} - X_{i,Pier}\)) – we would interpret this as: for a $1 increase in the price of the Beach (relative to the Pier), the odds of choosing the Beach over the Pier drop by 5%.



For mlogit, its important to standardize a beta, essentially to set one alternative as our “base case” with which we can relatively compare the other alternatives. {P_{ij}}

{e^{x_i'\beta_j}}

{\mathbb{P}[y_i = j \mid X_i]}

&& \text{normalize: } \beta_1 = 0\\
log

{P_{ij}}
{P_{i1}} &=

\end{align}
\]
Here we can interpret \(\beta\) as the change in the log-odds of choosing alternative \(j\) relative to the base case (alternative \(k\)) for a one-unit increase in individual-specific regressors (e.g., Income).
