title: Multinomial Models
text:
A seemingly powerful aspect of these models is the fact that the probabilities only depend the two specific alternatives we are comparing at a given time, stemming from out IID assumption early on. However, we can see an example as to why this might fail in reality.
Suppose we want to model traffic in a city, and there exists only two forms of transportation, a car and a red bus, s.t.:
\[\frac{\mathbb{P}[\text{car}]}{\mathbb{P}[\text{red bus}]} = \frac{0.5}{0.5}\]

Note that this is consistent since \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb{P}_i = 1\)

Now imagine we introduce a new form of transportation (i.e. a third alternative) in the city: a blue bus. Intuitively, we expect to see:
\[
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}[\text{blue bus}] = \mathbb{P}[\text{red bus}] = 25\% \\
\mathbb{P}[\text{car}] = 50\%
\end{align}
\]
Yet for our multinomal models, we instead derive from the IID (random sampling) assumption that our new choice distribution is:
\[\mathbb{P}[\text{blue bus}] = \mathbb{P}[\text{red bus}] = \mathbb{P}[\text{car}] = 33.33\%\] Another way to say the same thing is that an improved product gains share from all other products in proportion to their original shares; and when a product loses share, it loses to others in proportion to their shares.
As it stands, our current models cannot account for this phenomena; hence, we need to relax our IID assumption and try to construct a different variant of our models: Nested Logit.

title: Maximum Likelihood Estimators
text:
As discussed in the binary choice notes, OLS is a poor fit for binary outcomes: it produces unbounded predicted probabilities and heteroskedastic errors. Logit and Probit constrain \(F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta) \in [0,1]\) but are nonlinear in \(\beta\), so OLS cannot be applied. The solution is maximum likelihood estimation, which finds the parameter vector \(\beta\) that makes the observed data most probable under the assumed model.



Consider a sample of \(N\) independent observations \(\{y_i, \mathbf{x}_i\}\) where \(y_i \in \{0, 1\}\).
For \(y_i = 1\), the contribution to the likelihood is:
\[
L^i(\beta) = \Pr(y_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i;\beta) = F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)
\]
For \(y_i = 0\), the contribution is:
\[
L^i(\beta) = \Pr(y_i = 0 \mid \mathbf{x}_i;\beta) = 1 - F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)
\]
These two cases can be written compactly as:
\[
L^i(\beta) = F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)^{y_i}\left[1 - F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\right]^{1-y_i}
\]
Under random sampling, the joint likelihood for all \(N\) observations is:
\[
L(\beta) = \prod_{i=1}^N \Pr(y_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i;\beta)^{y_i} \Pr(y_i = 0 \mid \mathbf{x}_i;\beta)^{1-y_i}
\]
Taking logs yields the (conditional) log-likelihood function:
\[
\ell(\beta) = \ln L(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[y_i \ln F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta) + (1-y_i)\ln\left(1 - F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\right)\right]
\]
The MLE \(\hat{\beta}\) is the parameter vector that maximizes \(\ell(\beta)\).


For the Logit model, \(F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta) = \Lambda(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\), so:
\[
\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[y_i \ln \Lambda(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta) + (1-y_i)\ln\left(1 - \Lambda(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\right)\right]
\]



For the Probit model, \(F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta) = \Phi(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\), so:
\[
\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[y_i \ln \Phi(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta) + (1-y_i)\ln\left(1 - \Phi(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\right)\right]
\]






Differentiating the log-likelihood with respect to \(\beta\), where \(F'(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta) = \partial F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)/\partial(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\):
\[
\frac{\partial \ell(\beta)}{\partial \beta} = \ell_\beta(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[\frac{y_i}{F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)} - \frac{1-y_i}{1-F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)}\right] F'(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\mathbf{x}_i = 0
\]
Combining the fractions over a common denominator, the ML first-order conditions simplify to:
\[
\ell_\beta(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{y_i - F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)}{F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\left(1 - F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\right)} F'(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\mathbf{x}_i = 0
\]
There is no closed-form solution; \(\hat\beta\) is obtained numerically.



For the Logit MLE, since \(\Lambda'(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta) = \Lambda(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\left[1 - \Lambda(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\right]\), the factor \(F'/(F(1-F))\) cancels, and the FOCs simplify to:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N \left(y_i - \Lambda(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\right)\mathbf{x}_i = 0
\]
This is the same moment condition structure as OLS, but with \(\Lambda(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\) in place of \(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta\).



For the Probit model, \(\Lambda'\) does not cancel, so the FOCs involve observation-specific weights \(w_i\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N w_i \left(y_i - \Phi(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\right)\mathbf{x}_i = 0, \qquad w_i = \frac{\phi(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)}{\Phi(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\left[1 - \Phi(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\right]}
\]
Unlike the Logit case, \(w_i\) varies across observations.






Since \(\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i] = \Pr(y_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = F(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\), the marginal effect of \(x_{ij}\) on the probability is:
\[
\frac{\partial \mathbb{E}[y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i]}{\partial x_{ij}} = F'(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\,\beta_j
\]
This depends on the evaluation point \(\mathbf{x}_i\); unlike the LPM, marginal effects are not constant. Two standard choices:

Marginal effects at the mean (MEM): evaluate at \(F'(\bar{\mathbf{x}}'\hat\beta)\,\hat\beta_j\).
Average marginal effects (AME): compute \(F'(\mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)\,\hat\beta_j\) for each \(i\), then average: \(N^{-1}\sum_i F'(\mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)\,\hat\beta_j\).

The AME is generally preferred, as it does not require evaluating the nonlinear model at a possibly artificial or unrepresentative point.



Since \(\Lambda'(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta) = p_i(1-p_i)\) where \(p_i = \Lambda(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\):
\[
\frac{\partial \Pr(y_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i)}{\partial x_{ij}} = p_i(1-p_i)\,\beta_j
\]
The marginal effect is largest when \(p_i \approx 0.5\) and shrinks toward zero at the tails, consistent with the S-shaped logistic curve.
The Logit model also admits a convenient interpretation via the odds ratio. Note that:
\[
p = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{x}'\beta)}{1 + \exp(\mathbf{x}'\beta)} \implies \frac{p}{1-p} = \exp(\mathbf{x}'\beta) \implies \ln\!\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \mathbf{x}'\beta
\]
So \(\beta_j\) is the effect of \(x_j\) on the log-odds of \(y = 1\). A unit increase in \(x_j\) multiplies the odds by \(\exp(\beta_j)\).



Since \(F'(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta) = \phi(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\):
\[
\frac{\partial \Pr(y_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i)}{\partial x_{ij}} = \phi(\mathbf{x}_i'\beta)\,\beta_j
\]



The point estimates \(\hat\beta_{Logit}\) and \(\hat\beta_{Probit}\) differ by scale since the two distributions have different variances. The marginal effects should be similar across models given that the normal and logistic distributions have similar shapes (logit has fatter tails). Amemiya (1981) suggests the following rules of thumb:
\[
1.6\,\hat\beta_{Probit} \approx \hat\beta_{Logit} \qquad 4\,\hat\beta_{LPM} \approx \hat\beta_{Logit} \qquad 2.5\,\hat\beta_{LPM} \approx \hat\beta_{Probit}
\]
If the marginal effects from Logit and Probit differ substantially, this is a signal of model misspecification rather than a sampling artifact.




The general ML result gives us that \(\hat\beta\) is consistent and asymptotically normally distributed:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat\beta - \beta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0,\, A_0^{-1}B_0A_0^{-1'}\right)
\]
where \(\beta_0\) is the true parameter vector, and:
\[
A_0 = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta\,\partial\beta'}\Bigg|_{\beta_0}\right] \qquad B_0 = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta}\frac{\partial \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta'}\Bigg|_{\beta_0}\right]
\]
\(A_0\) is the expected Hessian (second derivative of the log-likelihood, always negative definite at the MLE) and \(B_0\) is the expected outer product of the score.


If the model is correctly specified, one can show that \(B_0 = -A_0\). This is the Information Matrix Equality (IME). As a result, the asymptotic variance simplifies to:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat\beta - \beta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\, (-A_0)^{-1}\right) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\, \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta}\frac{\partial \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta'}\right]^{-1}\right)
\]
The IME is a testable implication of correct specification: if the three variance estimators below disagree substantially, it suggests misspecification.




There are three alternative ways to estimate the asymptotic variance.


The OPG estimator uses only first derivatives of the log-likelihood:
\[
\hat{V}_0^{OPG} = \hat{B}_0^{-1} = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\partial \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta}\frac{\partial \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta'}\Bigg|_{\hat\beta}\right)^{-1}
\]
This only requires computing scores, so it is the cheapest to implement.



The Hessian estimator uses the observed second derivatives:
\[
\tilde{V}_0 = -\hat{A}_0^{-1} = \left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\partial^2 \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta\,\partial\beta'}\Bigg|_{\hat\beta}\right)^{-1}
\]
Most MLE routines in Stata report standard errors based on the Hessian by default.



The expected Hessian estimator takes the expectation of the second derivative conditional on \(\mathbf{x}_i\) before evaluating:
\[
\bar{V}_0 = -\bar{A}_0^{-1} = \left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta\,\partial\beta'}\Bigg|\mathbf{x}_i\right]\Bigg|_{\hat\beta}\right)^{-1}
\]
For binary choice models, differentiating the FOC in equation (1) and taking expectations gives the explicit form:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat\beta) = \frac{1}{N}\bar{V}_0 = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{F'(\mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)^2}{F(\mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)\left(1-F(\mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)\right)}\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i'\right)^{-1}
\]
Under the IME, all three estimators are consistent for the same quantity. They will agree in large samples but may differ in finite samples.



When the distributional assumption is misspecified (but \(\mathbb{E}[y \mid \mathbf{x}] = g(\mathbf{x}, \beta_0)\) is still correctly specified), the MLE remains consistent for the parameter of the conditional mean but the standard IME-based variance is incorrect. The sandwich estimator remains valid:
\[
\bar{V}_0^{SW} = \hat{A}_0^{-1}\hat{B}_0\hat{A}_0^{-1'}
\]
This is also the appropriate correction when observations are correlated across \(i\) (e.g., clustered data).




Any of the three classical tests (Wald, LM, LR) can be used for hypothesis testing. The Likelihood Ratio (LR) test is particularly convenient in the MLE context because the log-likelihood is already computed as part of estimation:
\[
LR = 2\left[\ell_U(\hat\beta) - \ell_R(\hat\beta)\right] \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_q \quad \text{under } H_0
\]
where \(\ell_U\) and \(\ell_R\) are the log-likelihoods of the unrestricted and restricted models, and \(q\) is the number of restrictions imposed. For example, testing \(H_0: \beta_2 = 0\) in \(\Pr(y_i = 1) = F(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_2 z_i)\) gives \(LR \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_1\).



Standard \(R^2\) from OLS does not apply to binary choice models. Two common alternatives:


Let \(\hat{p}_i = F(\mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)\) be the estimated probability. Predict \(\hat{y}_i = 1\) if \(\hat{p}_i > 0.5\) and \(\hat{y}_i = 0\) otherwise. The PCP is:
\[
\text{PCP} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{N}
\]
A naive model predicting the modal outcome for every observation sets a natural baseline; a meaningful model should beat this.



McFadden (1974) proposes:
\[
\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{\ell_U}{\ell_R}
\]
where \(\ell_U\) is the log-likelihood of the full model and \(\ell_R\) is the log-likelihood of a model with only an intercept. Since \(\ell_U \geq \ell_R\) (adding regressors weakly improves fit) and \(\ell_R \leq \ell_U \leq 0\), the pseudo \(R^2\) lies in \([0,1]\). In practice values between 0.2 and 0.4 are considered good fit for binary choice models. Goodness-of-fit is useful context but is generally secondary to statistical and economic significance.

\tilde{V}_0 = -\hat{A}_0^{-1} = \left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\partial^2 \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta\,\partial\beta'}\Bigg|_{\hat\beta}\right)^{-1}
\]
Most MLE routines in Stata report standard errors based on the Hessian by default.



The expected Hessian estimator takes the expectation of the second derivative conditional on \(\mathbf{x}_i\) before evaluating:
\[
\bar{V}_0 = -\bar{A}_0^{-1} = \left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ln L^i(\beta)}{\partial\beta\,\partial\beta'}\Bigg|\mathbf{x}_i\right]\Bigg|_{\hat\beta}\right)^{-1}
\]
For binary choice models, differentiating the FOC in equation (1) and taking expectations gives the explicit form:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat\beta) = \frac{1}{N}\bar{V}_0 = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{F'(\mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)^2}{F(\mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)\left(1-F(\mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)\right)}\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i'\right)^{-1}
\]
Under the IME, all three estimators are consistent for the same quantity. They will agree in large samples but may differ in finite samples.



When the distributional assumption is misspecified (but \(\mathbb{E}[y \mid \mathbf{x}] = g(\mathbf{x}, \beta_0)\) is still correctly specified), the MLE remains consistent for the parameter of the conditional mean but the standard IME-based variance is incorrect. The sandwich estimator remains valid:
\[
\bar{V}_0^{SW} = \hat{A}_0^{-1}\hat{B}_0\hat{A}_0^{-1'}
\]
This is also the appropriate correction when observations are correlated across \(i\) (e.g., clustered data).

title: Maximum Likelihood Estimators
text:
Any of the three classical tests (Wald, LM, LR) can be used for hypothesis testing. The Likelihood Ratio (LR) test is particularly convenient in the MLE context because the log-likelihood is already computed as part of estimation:
\[
LR = 2\left[\ell_U(\hat\beta) - \ell_R(\hat\beta)\right] \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_q \quad \text{under } H_0
\]
where \(\ell_U\) and \(\ell_R\) are the log-likelihoods of the unrestricted and restricted models, and \(q\) is the number of restrictions imposed. For example, testing \(H_0: \beta_2 = 0\) in \(\Pr(y_i = 1) = F(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_2 z_i)\) gives \(LR \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_1\).

title: Maximum Likelihood Estimators
text:
Standard \(R^2\) from OLS does not apply to binary choice models. Two common alternatives:


Let \(\hat{p}_i = F(\mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)\) be the estimated probability. Predict \(\hat{y}_i = 1\) if \(\hat{p}_i > 0.5\) and \(\hat{y}_i = 0\) otherwise. The PCP is:
\[
\text{PCP} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{N}
\]
A naive model predicting the modal outcome for every observation sets a natural baseline; a meaningful model should beat this.



McFadden (1974) proposes:
\[
\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{\ell_U}{\ell_R}
\]
where \(\ell_U\) is the log-likelihood of the full model and \(\ell_R\) is the log-likelihood of a model with only an intercept. Since \(\ell_U \geq \ell_R\) (adding regressors weakly improves fit) and \(\ell_R \leq \ell_U \leq 0\), the pseudo \(R^2\) lies in \([0,1]\). In practice values between 0.2 and 0.4 are considered good fit for binary choice models. Goodness-of-fit is useful context but is generally secondary to statistical and economic significance.

title: Anderson-Hsiao Estimator
text:
Consider a simple dynamic panel model with a lagged dependent variable:
\[
y_{it} = \alpha y_{i,t-1} + f_i + u_{it} \qquad i = 1, \ldots, N, \quad t = 1, \ldots, T
\]
where \(\alpha\) captures state dependence (habit formation, adjustment costs, etc.) and \(u_{it}\) is serially uncorrelated. Here \(x_{it} = y_{i,t-1}\), and it is immediately clear that strict exogeneity fails:
\[
E(u_{it} \mid x_{it+1}, f_i) = E(u_{it} \mid y_{it}, f_i) \neq 0
\]
since \(y_{it}\) is itself a function of \(u_{it}\). As a result, the regressors are only weakly exogenous (predetermined), not strictly exogenous, and both the FE and FD estimators are inconsistent.



Applying the within transformation to the dynamic model:
\[
y_{it} - \bar{y}_{i+} = \alpha(y_{i,t-1} - \bar{y}_{i-}) + (u_{it} - \bar{u}_{i+})
\]
where \(\bar{y}_{i+} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T y_{it}\), \(\bar{y}_{i-} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} y_{it}\), and \(\bar{u}_{i+} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T u_{it}\).
The demeaned regressor \(y_{i,t-1} - \bar{y}_{i-}\) is correlated with the demeaned error \(u_{it} - \bar{u}_{i+}\), since \(\bar{u}_{i+}\) includes \(u_{i,t-1}\) and \(y_{i,t-1}\) depends on \(u_{i,t-1}\). More formally, for \(j > t - 1\):
\[
E\left(u_{ij}\left(y_{i,t-1} - \bar{y}_{i-}\right)\right) = -\frac{1}{T}\sum_{s=j}^{T-1}\alpha^{s-j}\sigma_u^2 < 0
\]
implying that the FE estimator is downward biased. This is the Nickell (1981) bias, of order \(O(1/T)\); it vanishes as \(T \to \infty\) but is substantial in the short panels typical in microeconometrics.



Taking first differences to remove \(f_i\):
\[
\Delta y_{it} = \alpha \Delta y_{i,t-1} + \Delta u_{it}
\]
where \(\Delta y_{it} = y_{it} - y_{i,t-1}\), \(\Delta y_{i,t-1} = y_{i,t-1} - y_{i,t-2}\), and \(\Delta u_{it} = u_{it} - u_{i,t-1}\).
The regressor \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\) is endogenous: it contains \(u_{i,t-1}\) (through \(y_{i,t-1}\)), which also appears in \(\Delta u_{it} = u_{it} - u_{i,t-1}\). Since \(E(\Delta u_{it} \cdot \Delta y_{i,t-1}) \neq 0\), OLS on the differenced equation is inconsistent. We need an IV approach.



Anderson and Hsiao (1982) observe that \(y_{i,t-2}\) (or equivalently \(\Delta y_{i,t-2}\)) is a valid instrument for \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\) in the first-differenced equation. This instrument is built into the panel and requires no external data.


Relevance: \(\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(y_{i,t-2}, \Delta y_{i,t-1}) \neq 0\) since \(\Delta y_{i,t-1} = y_{i,t-1} - y_{i,t-2}\) contains \(y_{i,t-2}\) directly.
Exogeneity: Under serially uncorrelated \(u_{it}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(y_{i,t-2}\Delta u_{it}) &= E\left[y_{i,t-2}(u_{it} - u_{i,t-1})\right] \\
&= E(y_{i,t-2}u_{it}) - E(y_{i,t-2}u_{i,t-1}) = 0
\end{aligned}
\]
since \(y_{i,t-2}\) is determined by \(u_{i,t-2}\) and earlier shocks, which are uncorrelated with both \(u_{it}\) and \(u_{i,t-1}\) under serial independence.
\(\star\) Caution on the rank condition. The exclusion restriction holds, but the rank condition can fail. Suppose \(\alpha = 1\) (random walk), so \(\Delta y_{i,t-1} = u_{i,t-1}\). Then:
\[
E(y_{i,t-2}\Delta y_{i,t-1}) = E(y_{i,t-2}u_{i,t-1}) = 0
\]
and \(y_{i,t-2}\) is irrelevant as an instrument. More generally, when \(\alpha\) is close to 1, the instrument is weak, leading to severely biased IV estimates in finite samples.




For the first-differenced dynamic panel model estimated over \(t = 3, \ldots, T\), the instrument matrix for individual \(i\) is a column vector using \(y_{i,t-2}\) for each period. For \(T = 5\):
\[
Z_i = \begin{bmatrix} y_{i1} \\ y_{i2} \\ y_{i3} \end{bmatrix}
\]
This is the just-identified choice (one instrument per period). The AH estimator is then the standard IV formula applied to the first-differenced data:
\[
\hat{\alpha}^{AH} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]
where \(\Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}\) is the vector of \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\) for \(t = 3, \ldots, T\). Alternatively, \(\Delta y_{i,t-2}\) can be used in place of \(y_{i,t-2}\); both satisfy relevance and exogeneity under the same conditions.




Consistent: \(\hat{\alpha}^{AH} \xrightarrow{p} \alpha\) under the moment conditions \(E[Z_i'\Delta u_i] = 0\) and the rank condition.
Asymptotically normal: \(\sqrt{N}(\hat{\alpha}^{AH} - \alpha) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar})\).
Not efficient: AH uses at most one valid instrument per period. For \(T > 3\), the levels \(y_{i1}, \ldots, y_{i,t-2}\) are all valid instruments for period \(t\), providing additional identifying information that the AH estimator ignores. The Arellano-Bond estimator exploits all of these simultaneously.




When both \(y_{i,t-2}\) and \(\Delta y_{i,t-2}\) are used simultaneously as instruments (giving \(L > K\)), the overidentifying restrictions can be tested via the Sargan-Hansen J statistic:
\[
J = N \cdot \bar{g}'\hat{S}^{-1}\bar{g} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{L-K} \quad \text{under } H_0: E[Z_i'\Delta u_i] = 0
\]
where \(\bar{g} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'\widehat{\Delta u}_i\) and \(\hat{S} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'\widehat{\Delta u}_i\widehat{\Delta u}_i'Z_i\). Rejection indicates at least one instrument is not exogenous.

title: Anderson-Hsiao Estimator
text:
Consistent: \(\hat{\alpha}^{AH} \xrightarrow{p} \alpha\) under the moment conditions \(E[Z_i'\Delta u_i] = 0\) and the rank condition.
Asymptotically normal: \(\sqrt{N}(\hat{\alpha}^{AH} - \alpha) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar})\).

For \(T > 3\), the levels \(y_{i1}, \ldots, y_{i,t-2}\) are all valid instruments for period \(t\), providing additional identifying information that the AH estimator ignores. text:

\[

where \(\bar{g} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'\widehat{\Delta u}_i\) and \(\hat{S} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'\widehat{\Delta u}_i\widehat{\Delta u}_i'Z_i\). Rejection indicates at least one instrument is not exogenous.

title: First Differences
text:
The FE estimator eliminates \(f_i\) by subtracting individual-specific time means. First differencing is an alternative: subtract consecutive observations rather than group means. Both transformations remove \(f_i\) and yield consistent estimators under the same exogeneity assumption, but they impose different homoskedasticity conditions and differ in efficiency depending on the structure of \(\mu_{it}\).
Under the FE homoskedasticity assumption (\(\mu_{it}\) i.i.d. over \(t\)), first differencing introduces MA(1) serial correlation into \(\Delta\mu_{it}\) and FE is more efficient. Under the FD homoskedasticity assumption (\(\Delta\mu_{it}\) i.i.d., i.e., \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk), FD is the more efficient estimator. When \(T = 2\), the two estimators are numerically identical.





Same as before:
\[
y_{it} = \mathbf{x}_{it}'\beta + \mathbf{z}_{i}'\gamma + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



Same as FE:
\[
E(f_i \mid X_i) \neq 0
\]
\(f_i\) can be correlated with the regressors and is eliminated by first differencing.



Same as before:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid \mathbf{x}_{i1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]



NEW. The homoskedasticity condition is imposed on the first-differenced error \(\Delta\mu_{it} = \mu_{it} - \mu_{i,t-1}\):
\[
\begin{cases}
1. \ \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{e}^2 & \text{Constant Variance After Differencing} \\
2. \ \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\Delta\mu_{it}, \Delta\mu_{is} \mid X_i, f_i) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation After Differencing}
\end{cases}
\]
\(\star\) This implies \(\mu_{it} = \mu_{i,t-1} + e_{it}\) where \(e_{it}\) is i.i.d. with variance \(\sigma_e^2\); in other words, \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk. This is qualitatively different from the FE homoskedasticity assumption and is not nested in it (for \(T > 2\)).



NEW. The rank condition is imposed on the first-differenced regressors \(\Delta X_i\):
\[
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(\Delta X_i'\Delta X_i)}_{M_{\Delta X \Delta X}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank } K^*
\]
Where \(K^*\) represents the number of time-varying regressors. Time-constant regressors satisfy \(\Delta z_i = 0\) and cannot enter the first-differenced model; like FE, FD cannot identify the coefficients on time-invariant covariates.



Taking first differences of the model for \(t = 2, \ldots, T\):
\[
\underbrace{y_{it} - y_{i,t-1}}_{\Delta y_{it}} = \underbrace{(\mathbf{x}_{it} - \mathbf{x}_{i,t-1})'}_{\Delta\mathbf{x}_{it}'}\beta + \underbrace{(\mathbf{z}_{i} - \mathbf{z}_{i})}_{=0}'\gamma + \underbrace{(f_i - f_i)}_{=0} +  \underbrace{(\mu_{it} - \mu_{i,t-1})}_{\Delta\mu_{it}}
\]
since \(\Delta f_i = f_i - f_i = 0\) and \(\Delta \mathbf{z}_{i} = \mathbf{z}_{i} - \mathbf{z}_{i} =0\). In matrix notation, the \((T-1) \times T\) first-difference matrix is:
\[
D_T = \begin{bmatrix}
-1 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & -1 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & -1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
so that \(\Delta\mathbf{y}_i = D_T\mathbf{y}_i\), \(\Delta X_i = D_T X_i\), and \(\Delta\mu_i = D_T\mu_i\). We lose one time period per individual, giving \(N(T-1)\) total observations.
The FD estimator is OLS applied to the first-differenced model:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{FD} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]






The sampling error is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta &= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i - \beta \\
&= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'(\Delta X_i\beta + \Delta\mu_i) - \beta \\
&= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking conditional expectations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta \mid X, f] &= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i' \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i \mid X_i, f_i]}_{\text{=0 via A3}} = 0 \\
\Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FD}] &= \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i] = 0 \text{ via LLN and strict exogeneity (A3)} \\
\hat{\beta}_{FD} &\xrightarrow{p} \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta) &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i)\right) \text{ via CLT}
\end{aligned}
\]
Under assumption 4, \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i\Delta\mu_i' \mid X_i, f_i] = \sigma_e^2 I_{T-1}\), so \(\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i) = \sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}\). Thus:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1}\right) \qquad \blacksquare
\]


The A\(\mathbb{V}\)AR under assumption 4 is \(\sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1}\). To estimate \(\sigma_e^2\), compute FD residuals \(\hat{e}_{it} = \Delta y_{it} - \Delta\mathbf{x}_{it}'\hat{\beta}_{FD}\) and use:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_e^2 = \frac{1}{N(T-1) - K}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=2}^T \hat{e}_{it}^2
\]
Using the analogy principle:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_e^2\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \sigma_e^2\,\mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta X_i]^{-1}
\]
If assumption 4 fails, we instead use the cluster-robust ‘sandwich’ estimator:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{FD}) = \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\hat{e}_i\hat{e}_i'\Delta X_i\right)\left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}
\]
\(\star\) In practice, standard errors should always be clustered at the individual level in a first-difference model, since the true structure of \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i\Delta\mu_i']\) is generally unknown.






When \(T = 2\): FE and FD produce numerically identical estimates and inference. (to see this, check out Q3 of PS1)
When \(T > 2\) and \(\mu_{it}\) is i.i.d. over \(t\): FE is more efficient. Differencing introduces MA(1) serial correlation into \(\Delta\mu_{it}\), which loses information relative to the within transformation.
When \(T > 2\) and \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk: FD is more efficient, since \(\Delta\mu_{it} = e_{it}\) is then i.i.d. and assumption 4 holds exactly.
If FE and FD estimates differ in ways that cannot be attributed to sampling error, this signals a violation of strict exogeneity: if \(\mu_{it}\) is correlated with \(\mathbf{x}_{is}\) for any \(t\) and \(s\), both estimators are inconsistent but will generally have different probability limits.

To see the difference in FE and FD being blue under different assumptions of serial correlation of the error terms, suppose that \(\mu_{it}\)is serially uncorrelated such that \(\text{cov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is}) = 0, \quad \forall_{t \neq s}\).
In this case, estimating the variance-covariance matrix on the first-differenced idiosyncratic errors takes the following form:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_i ' \Delta \mu_i \mid X_i] = \sigma_{\mu}^2
\begin{bmatrix}
  2 & -1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
  -1 & 2 & -1 & \cdots & 0 \\
  0 & -1 & 2 & \ddots & \vdots \\
  \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & -1 \\
  0 & 0 & \cdots & -1 & 2
\end{bmatrix}
\]
To derive this matrix, we simply calculate the variance-covariance between first-differenced errors at different \(t\):
\[
\begin{align}
\text{1. Diagonal } (t=2):
  & \quad \mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_{i2} \Delta \mu_{i2} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) (\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}\mu_{i2} - 2\mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} + \mu_{i1}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}^2 \mid X_i]  - 2\mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i1}^2 \mid X_i] \\
  &= \sigma_{\mu}^2 - 0 + \sigma_{\mu}^2 = 2\sigma_{\mu}^2
  \\ \\
  \text{2. Off-Diagonal }(t=3):
  & \quad \mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_{i3} \Delta \mu_{i2} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(\mu_{i3} - \mu_{i2}) (\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} - \mu_{i2}\mu_{i2} +  \mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} \mid X_i]  - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}^2 \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= 0 - 0 - \sigma_{\mu}^2 + 0 = -\sigma_{\mu}^2
  \\ \\
  \text{3. Off-Diagonal }(t \geq 4):
  & \quad \mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_{i4} \Delta \mu_{i2} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(\mu_{i4} - \mu_{i3}) (\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i4}\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i4}\mu_{i1} - \mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} +  \mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i4}\mu_{i2} \mid X_i]  - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i4}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= 0 - 0 - 0 + 0 = 0
\end{align}
\]
Thus, if \(\mu_{it}\) are i.i.d. (no serial correlation) rather than a random walk, applying FD now introduces serial correlation! Hence, FE would be BLUE.


There exists a third case wherein the idiosyncratic errors are serially correlated, but do NOT follow a random walk.






Warning



In reality, it is very hard for the random walk assumption to hold in this setting; it would imply that a shock from 10-20 years ago is still perfectly persistent today, with no decay whatsoever.


More formally, \(\mu_{it} = \rho \mu_{it-1} + e_{it}\) where \(0 < \rho < 1\); this means our errors follow an AR(1) error structure (see ARMA notes for an extensive overview of AR(p) and MA(q) models). \(\rho\) is a measure of “persistence,” telling us how much a shock from last period (\(t-1\)) is carried over to today, \(t\). When \(\rho\) is between zero and one, the shock decays over time, eventually converging to zero, determined by how close the value is to zero.
In such a case, neither FD nor FE are BLUE! As a result, if we run either estimator without corrections, our standard errors will be incorrectly estimated (typically underestimated). This leads to inflated t-statistics, artificially tight confidence intervals, and a high risk of Type I errors (finding statistical significance where there is none).
While neither estimator is BLUE, their relative efficiency depends entirely on the value of \(\rho\):

As \(\rho \rightarrow 0\), FE becomes closer to being efficient.
As \(\rho \rightarrow 1\), FD becomes closer to being efficient.
If \(\rho \approx 0.5\), both estimators suffer from significant inefficiency.

There are two different approaches to take when dealing with such a situation:





In modern empirical practice, researchers generally care more about consistency than absolute efficiency, provided they can get inference right.
The idea here is to stick with the Fixed Effects (FE) estimator (or FD, if \(\rho\) is empirically very high), but now estimate the model using clustered (robust) standard errors.
Clustering here allows the variance-covariance matrix to be completely agnostic about the exact nature of the serial correlation within an pre-defined cluster. It corrects the standard errors for any pattern of autocorrelation (and heteroskedasticity) over time.



To strictly achieve BLUE (or asymptotically efficient estimates), you must explicitly model the AR(1) process using Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS). The process is multi-step:

Estimate the model using FE to get consistent residuals.
Use those residuals to get \(\hat{\rho}\).
Apply a quasi-differencing transforatmion to the panel data. Instead of subtracting 100% of the previous period (like FD) or the total average (like FE), you subtract \(\hat{\rho}\) of the previous period:

\[
y_{it}− \hat{\rho} y_{it-1} = (x_{it}−\hat{\rho}x_{it−1})'\beta + f_i(1−\hat{\rho})+e_{it}
\]
Note: FGLS requires strict assumptions about the exact structure of the error variance. If your estimate of \(\rho\) is wrong, or if the true process is actually AR(2) or MA(1), FGLS can perform worse than FE.

title: First Differences
text:
The FE estimator eliminates \(f_i\) by subtracting individual-specific time means. First differencing is an alternative: subtract consecutive observations rather than group means. Both transformations remove \(f_i\) and yield consistent estimators under the same exogeneity assumption, but they impose different homoskedasticity conditions and differ in efficiency depending on the structure of \(\mu_{it}\).
Under the FE homoskedasticity assumption (\(\mu_{it}\) i.i.d. over \(t\)), first differencing introduces MA(1) serial correlation into \(\Delta\mu_{it}\) and FE is more efficient. Under the FD homoskedasticity assumption (\(\Delta\mu_{it}\) i.i.d., i.e., \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk), FD is the more efficient estimator. When \(T = 2\), the two estimators are numerically identical.

title: First Differences
text:
Same as before:
\[
y_{it} = \mathbf{x}_{it}'\beta + \mathbf{z}_{i}'\gamma + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



Same as FE:
\[
E(f_i \mid X_i) \neq 0
\]
\(f_i\) can be correlated with the regressors and is eliminated by first differencing.



Same as before:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid \mathbf{x}_{i1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]



NEW. The homoskedasticity condition is imposed on the first-differenced error \(\Delta\mu_{it} = \mu_{it} - \mu_{i,t-1}\):
\[
\begin{cases}
1. \ \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{e}^2 & \text{Constant Variance After Differencing} \\
2. \ \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\Delta\mu_{it}, \Delta\mu_{is} \mid X_i, f_i) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation After Differencing}
\end{cases}
\]
\(\star\) This implies \(\mu_{it} = \mu_{i,t-1} + e_{it}\) where \(e_{it}\) is i.i.d. with variance \(\sigma_e^2\); in other words, \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk. This is qualitatively different from the FE homoskedasticity assumption and is not nested in it (for \(T > 2\)).



NEW. The rank condition is imposed on the first-differenced regressors \(\Delta X_i\):
\[
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(\Delta X_i'\Delta X_i)}_{M_{\Delta X \Delta X}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank } K^*
\]
Where \(K^*\) represents the number of time-varying regressors. Time-constant regressors satisfy \(\Delta z_i = 0\) and cannot enter the first-differenced model; like FE, FD cannot identify the coefficients on time-invariant covariates.



Taking first differences of the model for \(t = 2, \ldots, T\):
\[
\underbrace{y_{it} - y_{i,t-1}}_{\Delta y_{it}} = \underbrace{(\mathbf{x}_{it} - \mathbf{x}_{i,t-1})'}_{\Delta\mathbf{x}_{it}'}\beta + \underbrace{(\mathbf{z}_{i} - \mathbf{z}_{i})}_{=0}'\gamma + \underbrace{(f_i - f_i)}_{=0} +  \underbrace{(\mu_{it} - \mu_{i,t-1})}_{\Delta\mu_{it}}
\]
since \(\Delta f_i = f_i - f_i = 0\) and \(\Delta \mathbf{z}_{i} = \mathbf{z}_{i} - \mathbf{z}_{i} =0\). In matrix notation, the \((T-1) \times T\) first-difference matrix is:
\[
D_T = \begin{bmatrix}
-1 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & -1 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & -1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
so that \(\Delta\mathbf{y}_i = D_T\mathbf{y}_i\), \(\Delta X_i = D_T X_i\), and \(\Delta\mu_i = D_T\mu_i\). We lose one time period per individual, giving \(N(T-1)\) total observations.
The FD estimator is OLS applied to the first-differenced model:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{FD} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]

title: First Differences
text:
The sampling error is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta &= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i - \beta \\
&= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'(\Delta X_i\beta + \Delta\mu_i) - \beta \\
&= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking conditional expectations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta \mid X, f] &= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i' \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i \mid X_i, f_i]}_{\text{=0 via A3}} = 0 \\
\Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FD}] &= \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i] = 0 \text{ via LLN and strict exogeneity (A3)} \\
\hat{\beta}_{FD} &\xrightarrow{p} \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta) &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i)\right) \text{ via CLT}
\end{aligned}
\]
Under assumption 4, \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i\Delta\mu_i' \mid X_i, f_i] = \sigma_e^2 I_{T-1}\), so \(\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i) = \sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}\). Thus:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1}\right) \qquad \blacksquare
\]


The A\(\mathbb{V}\)AR under assumption 4 is \(\sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1}\). To estimate \(\sigma_e^2\), compute FD residuals \(\hat{e}_{it} = \Delta y_{it} - \Delta\mathbf{x}_{it}'\hat{\beta}_{FD}\) and use:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_e^2 = \frac{1}{N(T-1) - K}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=2}^T \hat{e}_{it}^2
\]
Using the analogy principle:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_e^2\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \sigma_e^2\,\mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta X_i]^{-1}
\]
If assumption 4 fails, we instead use the cluster-robust ‘sandwich’ estimator:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{FD}) = \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\hat{e}_i\hat{e}_i'\Delta X_i\right)\left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}
\]
\(\star\) In practice, standard errors should always be clustered at the individual level in a first-difference model, since the true structure of \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i\Delta\mu_i']\) is generally unknown.

title: First Differences
text:
When \(T = 2\): FE and FD produce numerically identical estimates and inference. (to see this, check out Q3 of PS1)
When \(T > 2\) and \(\mu_{it}\) is i.i.d. over \(t\): FE is more efficient. Differencing introduces MA(1) serial correlation into \(\Delta\mu_{it}\), which loses information relative to the within transformation.
When \(T > 2\) and \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk: FD is more efficient, since \(\Delta\mu_{it} = e_{it}\) is then i.i.d. and assumption 4 holds exactly.
If FE and FD estimates differ in ways that cannot be attributed to sampling error, this signals a violation of strict exogeneity: if \(\mu_{it}\) is correlated with \(\mathbf{x}_{is}\) for any \(t\) and \(s\), both estimators are inconsistent but will generally have different probability limits.

To see the difference in FE and FD being blue under different assumptions of serial correlation of the error terms, suppose that \(\mu_{it}\)is serially uncorrelated such that \(\text{cov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is}) = 0, \quad \forall_{t \neq s}\).
In this case, estimating the variance-covariance matrix on the first-differenced idiosyncratic errors takes the following form:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_i ' \Delta \mu_i \mid X_i] = \sigma_{\mu}^2
\begin{bmatrix}
  2 & -1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
  -1 & 2 & -1 & \cdots & 0 \\
  0 & -1 & 2 & \ddots & \vdots \\
  \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & -1 \\
  0 & 0 & \cdots & -1 & 2
\end{bmatrix}
\]
To derive this matrix, we simply calculate the variance-covariance between first-differenced errors at different \(t\):
\[
\begin{align}
\text{1. Diagonal } (t=2):
  & \quad \mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_{i2} \Delta \mu_{i2} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) (\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}\mu_{i2} - 2\mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} + \mu_{i1}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}^2 \mid X_i]  - 2\mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i1}^2 \mid X_i] \\
  &= \sigma_{\mu}^2 - 0 + \sigma_{\mu}^2 = 2\sigma_{\mu}^2
  \\ \\
  \text{2. Off-Diagonal }(t=3):
  & \quad \mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_{i3} \Delta \mu_{i2} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(\mu_{i3} - \mu_{i2}) (\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} - \mu_{i2}\mu_{i2} +  \mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} \mid X_i]  - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}^2 \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= 0 - 0 - \sigma_{\mu}^2 + 0 = -\sigma_{\mu}^2
  \\ \\
  \text{3. Off-Diagonal }(t \geq 4):
  & \quad \mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_{i4} \Delta \mu_{i2} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(\mu_{i4} - \mu_{i3}) (\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i4}\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i4}\mu_{i1} - \mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} +  \mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i4}\mu_{i2} \mid X_i]  - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i4}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= 0 - 0 - 0 + 0 = 0
\end{align}
\]
Thus, if \(\mu_{it}\) are i.i.d. (no serial correlation) rather than a random walk, applying FD now introduces serial correlation! Hence, FE would be BLUE.


There exists a third case wherein the idiosyncratic errors are serially correlated, but do NOT follow a random walk.






Warning



In reality, it is very hard for the random walk assumption to hold in this setting; it would imply that a shock from 10-20 years ago is still perfectly persistent today, with no decay whatsoever.


More formally, \(\mu_{it} = \rho \mu_{it-1} + e_{it}\) where \(0 < \rho < 1\); this means our errors follow an AR(1) error structure (see ARMA notes for an extensive overview of AR(p) and MA(q) models). \(\rho\) is a measure of “persistence,” telling us how much a shock from last period (\(t-1\)) is carried over to today, \(t\). When \(\rho\) is between zero and one, the shock decays over time, eventually converging to zero, determined by how close the value is to zero.
In such a case, neither FD nor FE are BLUE! As a result, if we run either estimator without corrections, our standard errors will be incorrectly estimated (typically underestimated). This leads to inflated t-statistics, artificially tight confidence intervals, and a high risk of Type I errors (finding statistical significance where there is none).
While neither estimator is BLUE, their relative efficiency depends entirely on the value of \(\rho\):

As \(\rho \rightarrow 0\), FE becomes closer to being efficient.
As \(\rho \rightarrow 1\), FD becomes closer to being efficient.
If \(\rho \approx 0.5\), both estimators suffer from significant inefficiency.

There are two different approaches to take when dealing with such a situation:

The idea here is to stick with the Fixed Effects (FE) estimator (or FD, if \(\rho\) is empirically very high), but now estimate the model using clustered (robust) standard errors.
Clustering here allows the variance-covariance matrix to be completely agnostic about the exact nature of the serial correlation within an pre-defined cluster. It corrects the standard errors for any pattern of autocorrelation (and heteroskedasticity) over time.

text:
To strictly achieve BLUE (or asymptotically efficient estimates), you must explicitly model the AR(1) process using Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS). The process is multi-step:

Estimate the model using FE to get consistent residuals.
Use those residuals to get \(\hat{\rho}\).
Apply a quasi-differencing transforatmion to the panel data. Instead of subtracting 100% of the previous period (like FD) or the total average (like FE), you subtract \(\hat{\rho}\) of the previous period:

\[
y_{it}− \hat{\rho} y_{it-1} = (x_{it}−\hat{\rho}x_{it−1})'\beta + f_i(1−\hat{\rho})+e_{it}
\]
Note: FGLS requires strict assumptions about the exact structure of the error variance. If your estimate of \(\rho\) is wrong, or if the true process is actually AR(2) or MA(1), FGLS can perform worse than FE.

title: Random Effects
text:
As we saw with the pooled OLS estimator, it yields a consistent and unbiased estimator but is not efficient, due to the serial correlation in the composite error induced by the unobserved effect. Thus, there exists an estimator that is efficient under similar conditions, known as the Random Effects estimator; this is the equivalent to the generalized least squares (GLS) estimator from finite sample OLS.



Our assumptions here follow almost exactly the same from pooled OLS, with one slight change in assumption 5.


Same as before
\[
y_{it} = x_{it}'\beta + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



Same as before
\[
\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}] \equiv \mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i] = 0
\]



Same as before
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]



Same as before
\[
\begin{cases}
  1. \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(f_i \mid X_i) = \sigma_{f}^2 &\text{Constant Variance in the Unobserved Error} \\
  2. \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{\mu}^2 & \text{Constant Variance in the Idiosyncratic Error} \\
  3. \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is}) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation}
\end{cases}
\]



SLIGHT MODIFICATION
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} X_i  \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(X_i'V^{-1}X_i)}_{M_{XVX}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank K}
\]



Under the same assumptions as pooled OLS, the only difference in how we derive the estimator. To find the efficient estimator under these conditions, suppose that \(B'B = V^{-1}\), where \(B\) is some matrix. We can then define our model as:
\[
By_i = BX_i'\beta + Bv_{i}
\]
This model satisfies all of our assumptions: to see this, check Appendix (1) for a thorough handling.




Similar to pooled OLS, when applying the OLS estimator to our regressor we find it has the form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  & \hat{\beta}_{RE} = \left( X'V^{-1}X \right)^{-1}X'V^{-1}y  &&\text{RE estimator}\\
  & \hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta = \left( X'V^{-1}X \right)^{-1}X'V^{-1}v && \text{sampling error}
\end{aligned}
\]
To see the full derivation of the RE estimator and the sampling error, see Appendix (2)


To see that the RE estimator is an unbiased estimator, we want to show that \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE}] = \beta \Leftrightarrow \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta] = 0\)
Thus, we simply need to take expectations of the sampling error:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}v] \\
&=  \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X \mid X]\right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}v \mid X]] && \text{via LIE}\\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\mathbb{E}[v\mid X]] && \text{via LCE} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[v \mid X] = \mathbb{E}[f + u \mid X] && \text{via def} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[f \mid X] + \mathbb{E}[u \mid X] = 0 && \text{via assumption} \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\cdot 0] = 0 \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \\
&= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)}_{(1)}^{-1} \underbrace{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i}_{(2)} \\
(1):&  \text{ via the WLLN, this converges in probability:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right] \\
& \text{via the CMT, this convergence implies that:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right]^{-1} \\
(2):& \text{ via the WLLN, this converges in probability:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right] \\
&\text{ which we know equals zero due to unbiasedness:} \\
& \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right] = 0 \\
& \text{therefore, via Slutsky's Theorem,} \\
& \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right]^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0 \\
& \hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta \xrightarrow{p} 0 && \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



To derive the asymptotic normality of the RE estimator, we simply rescale the sampling error by \(\sqrt{N}\), s.t.:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE} - \beta \right)& = \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} X_i \right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} v_i}_{(2)} \\
  & (1) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X' V^{-1} X]^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
  & (2) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(X' V^{-1}v) \right) \text{ via CLT} \\
  & \text{thus, via Slutsky's theorem, } \\
  \sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE} - \beta \right)& \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}(X'V^{-1}vv'V^{-1}X)\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \right)
\end{aligned}
\]




Note that \(\mathbb{E}[vv' \mid X] = V\); thus, using the Linearity of Iterated Expectations, we can rewrite \(\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})\) as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE}) &= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\mathbb{E}[vv' \mid X]V^{-1}X]\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1} V V^{-1}X] \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X] \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, the RE estimator is the best linear and unbiased estimator (BLUE) under our given model and assumptions. For a formal proof, see Appendix (3)
Importantly: \(V^{-1}\) is unknown in reality; we need to compute an estimate of the matrix \(\hat{V}\) in order to construct \(\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE})\). In other words, we need to find:
\[
\hat{V_i} = \mathbb{E}[ \hat{v}_i \hat{v}_i' \mid X ]
\]
In order to get an estimate of the variance, we thereby need to get estimates of the residuals from our model using an unbiased and consistent estimator. Fortunately, we already found that \(\hat{\beta}_{POLS}\) has these properties and thereby is a valid choice of an estimator! Hence, we can find \(v_iv_i' = (y_i - X_i' \beta)(y_i - X_i' \beta)'\).
However, we need to compute two separate estimates for the \(\hat{V}_i\) matrix:

\(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{v}_{it}^2 \mid X] = \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\): diagonal elements (variance)
\(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{v_{it}v_{is}} \mid X] = \widehat{\sigma}_f^2, \forall_{ t \neq s}\): off-diagonal elements (co-variance)

To compute these estimates, we need to use our estimated residuals to construct the variance & co-variance elements composing each matrix, \(\forall_{i \in N}\):
\(\widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} = \frac{1}{NT-K} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^T \widehat{v}_{it}^2\)
\(\widehat{\sigma}_f^2 = \frac{1}{\frac{NT(T-1)}{2}-K} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \sum_{s=t+1}^T \widehat{v_{it}v_{is}}\)






Note



Note the denominator term for our covariance terms; this simply comes from the fact that for each individual variance-covariance matrix, we are computing \(\frac{T^2 -T}{2}\) elements, since our matrix has dimensions \((T \times T)\). To compute the off-diagonal elements of a symmetric matrix, we need to calculate \(T^2\) elements, subtracted by the \(T\) diagonal elements, and then divide by 2 as we only need to estimate \(U \equiv L\). We then iterate through this process for all \(N\) individuals, and subtract by the number of \(K\) regressors in our model.


Note that the estimated \(\hat{V}_i\) variance-covariance matrix is for an individual \(i\) for all panels \(t= 1, 2, \dots , T\) and is thereby \((T \times T)\); the entire \(\hat{V}\) matrix consists of all \(\hat{V}_i\) matrices across all \(i= 1, 2, \dots, N\) individuals, giving it dimensions \((NT \times NT)\). It is given by the form:
\[
\underset{(NT \times NT)}{\hat{V}} =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots &  \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}
  \end{bmatrix}_{i=1} & 0 & \\
  0 & \begin{bmatrix}
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots &  \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}
  \end{bmatrix}_{i=2} \\  &  & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Thus, to find \(\hat{\sigma}_{\mu}\), we simply take the difference between the diagonal (variance) elements \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\) and the off-diagonal (covariance) elements \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2}\):
\[
\widehat{\sigma}_{\mu}^2 = \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} - \widehat{\sigma}_f^2
\]
In other words, we can simply retrieve the idiosyncratic variance terms by off-diagonal from the diagonal. Since the matrix is symmetric across all \(\hat{V}_i\) matrices, we simply only need to calculate \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\) and \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2}\) to fully determine the entire \((NT \times NT)\) matrix \(\hat{V}\). Furthermore, this equicorrelation structure implies that \(V^{-1}\) has a known closed-form, allowing us to replace full GLS inversion with the computationally equivalent quasi-demeaning transformation (see here: Appendix (4))
Finally, we plug in these \(\hat{V}\) estimates back into the RE estimator:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{RE} = \left(\sum X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i \right)^{-1} \left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1} y_i  \right)
\]
We simply use the analogy principle to get the asymptotic variance matrix:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{RE}) =
\frac{1}{N} \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N  X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i \right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i]^{-1}
= \text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})
\]






Note



Following Woolridge’s notation, this equivalently can be expressed as:
\(\hat{\beta}_{RE} \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta, \frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}[X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i]^{-1} )\)





If we relax the assumption of homoskedasticity of the idiosyncratic error terms, we cannot reduce down the variance any further and thereby estimate the following “sandwich” form of the variance:
\[
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE}) =
\mathbb{E}\left[X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right]^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[ X_i'V^{-1}v_iv_i'V^{-1}X_i\right] \mathbb{E}\left[ X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right]^{-1}
\]
To get estimates of the asymptotic variance, we follow a 2-stage process:

Apply Pooled OLS and collect \(\widehat{v_{it}}\), then use \(\widehat{v_{it}}\) to construct \(\widehat{\sigma_{f}^2}\) and \(\widehat{\sigma_{f}^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\), giving us the invertible matrix \(\hat{V}\).
Apply RE estimator and collect \(\widehat{\widehat{v_{it}}}\); plug in \(\widehat{\widehat{v_{it}}}\) and \(\hat{V}{}^{-1}\) into the asymptotic variance formula \(\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})\).

More formally:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  & 1. \quad \widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS})^\text{CLUSTER(id)} =    \left(\sum X_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum X_i'\hat{v}_i\hat{v}_i'X_i\right) \left(\sum X_i'X_i\right)^{-1} \\
  & 2. \quad  \widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE})^\text{CLUSTER(id)} =    \left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}\hat{\hat{v}}_i\hat{\hat{v}}_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_i\right) \left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]






Warning



Note the notation for our two stage-estimation process: CLUSTER(id)
This stands for ‘clustering on the individual level,’ allowing for arbitrary serial correlation within a given \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{i}\), whilst maintaining independence across \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N\). In other words, we can treat a single individual’s timeline as a single “mega-observation,” allowing an individual \(i\) to be correlated with itself across periods in the panel.




What if we cluster on a higher level? Rather than the individual level, say we cluster on households, cities, countries, etc. Our asymptotic variance can simply be expressed as:
\[\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{\text{RE}})^\text{CLUSTER(c)} =\left(\sum_c X_c'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_c \right)^{-1} \left(\sum_c X_c'\hat{V}{}^{-1} \hat{\hat{v}}_c \hat{\hat{v}}_c' \hat{V}{}^{-1}X_c \right) \left(\sum_c X_c'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_c \right)^{-1}\]
To better understand, imagine simply grouping together multiple different \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{i}\) into a single ‘cluster’ based on some shared factor. For example, we would likely expect individuals within the same household to be correlated with one another; thus, we say that individuals \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{1}\) and \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{2}\) are both in \(c_1\), such that this matrix \(c_1\) “supersedes” the original \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{1, } \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{2}\) matrices. This allows for arbitrary serial correlation between individuals in the cluster.
\[
V =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{1} \\
  & \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{2} \end{bmatrix}_{c_1} & & \\
  & & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{3} \end{bmatrix}_{c_2} & & \\
  & & & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{4} \\
  & & & & \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{5} \end{bmatrix}_{c_3} \\
  & & & & & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
\]






Warning



Note that we still need a sufficient number of clusters for asymptotic properties to hold. At least \(\geq\) 30, however, usually it is expected/found that ~50 is the standard. Any lower and we will need clustering bootstrap methods to construct robust standard errors.
Furthermore, we can do ‘multi-dimensional’ clustering; e.g., on industry, then households, etc. Of course we need even more data points for such a case.
Clustering is standard practice. Stata does it automatically for us.






In practice, nobody uses the random effects estimator; the assumption of random individual effects is too strong of an assumption. Typically, we expect for there to exist some correlation between the exogenous regressors and the unobserved effect(s). In other words, random effects treats the unobserved effect as a random variable.
This motivates the introduction of a new estimator, namely the Fixed Effects estimator that relaxes this assumption, by allowing for non-zero correlation between \(f_i\) and \(X_i\).

title: Random Effects
text: As we saw with the pooled OLS estimator, it yields a consistent and unbiased estimator but is not efficient, due to the serial correlation in the composite error induced by the unobserved effect. Thus, there exists an estimator that is efficient under similar conditions, known as the Random Effects estimator; this is the equivalent to the generalized least squares (GLS) estimator from finite sample OLS.

title: Random Effects
text:
Our assumptions here follow almost exactly the same from pooled OLS, with one slight change in assumption 5.


Same as before
\[
y_{it} = x_{it}'\beta + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



Same as before
\[
\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}] \equiv \mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i] = 0
\]



Same as before
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]



Same as before
\[
\begin{cases}
  1. \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(f_i \mid X_i) = \sigma_{f}^2 &\text{Constant Variance in the Unobserved Error} \\
  2. \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{\mu}^2 & \text{Constant Variance in the Idiosyncratic Error} \\
  3. \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is}) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation}
\end{cases}
\]



SLIGHT MODIFICATION
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} X_i  \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(X_i'V^{-1}X_i)}_{M_{XVX}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank K}
\]



Under the same assumptions as pooled OLS, the only difference in how we derive the estimator. To find the efficient estimator under these conditions, suppose that \(B'B = V^{-1}\), where \(B\) is some matrix. We can then define our model as:
\[
By_i = BX_i'\beta + Bv_{i}
\]
This model satisfies all of our assumptions: to see this, check Appendix (1) for a thorough handling.

title: Random Effects
text:
Similar to pooled OLS, when applying the OLS estimator to our regressor we find it has the form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  & \hat{\beta}_{RE} = \left( X'V^{-1}X \right)^{-1}X'V^{-1}y  &&\text{RE estimator}\\
  & \hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta = \left( X'V^{-1}X \right)^{-1}X'V^{-1}v && \text{sampling error}
\end{aligned}
\]
To see the full derivation of the RE estimator and the sampling error, see Appendix (2)


To see that the RE estimator is an unbiased estimator, we want to show that \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE}] = \beta \Leftrightarrow \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta] = 0\)
Thus, we simply need to take expectations of the sampling error:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}v] \\
&=  \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X \mid X]\right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}v \mid X]] && \text{via LIE}\\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\mathbb{E}[v\mid X]] && \text{via LCE} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[v \mid X] = \mathbb{E}[f + u \mid X] && \text{via def} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[f \mid X] + \mathbb{E}[u \mid X] = 0 && \text{via assumption} \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\cdot 0] = 0 \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \\
&= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)}_{(1)}^{-1} \underbrace{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i}_{(2)} \\
(1):&  \text{ via the WLLN, this converges in probability:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right] \\
& \text{via the CMT, this convergence implies that:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right]^{-1} \\
(2):& \text{ via the WLLN, this converges in probability:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right] \\
&\text{ which we know equals zero due to unbiasedness:} \\
& \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right] = 0 \\
& \text{therefore, via Slutsky's Theorem,} \\
& \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right]^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0 \\
& \hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta \xrightarrow{p} 0 && \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



To derive the asymptotic normality of the RE estimator, we simply rescale the sampling error by \(\sqrt{N}\), s.t.:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE} - \beta \right)& = \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} X_i \right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} v_i}_{(2)} \\
  & (1) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X' V^{-1} X]^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
  & (2) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(X' V^{-1}v) \right) \text{ via CLT} \\
  & \text{thus, via Slutsky's theorem, } \\
  \sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE} - \beta \right)& \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}(X'V^{-1}vv'V^{-1}X)\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \right)
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Random Effects
text:
Note that \(\mathbb{E}[vv' \mid X] = V\); thus, using the Linearity of Iterated Expectations, we can rewrite \(\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})\) as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE}) &= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\mathbb{E}[vv' \mid X]V^{-1}X]\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1} V V^{-1}X] \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X] \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, the RE estimator is the best linear and unbiased estimator (BLUE) under our given model and assumptions. For a formal proof, see Appendix (3)

\[
\hat{V_i} = \mathbb{E}[ \hat{v}_i \hat{v}_i' \mid X ]
\]
In order to get an estimate of the variance, we thereby need to get estimates of the residuals from our model using an unbiased and consistent estimator. Fortunately, we already found that \(\hat{\beta}_{POLS}\) has these properties and thereby is a valid choice of an estimator! Hence, we can find \(v_iv_i' = (y_i - X_i' \beta)(y_i - X_i' \beta)'\).
