\]
\[
\underset{(NT \times K)}{X} = \begin{bmatrix} X_1 \\ X_2 \\ \vdots \\ X_N \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} X_{111} & X_{112} & \dots & X_{11K} \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ X_{1T1} & X_{1T2} & \dots & X_{1TK} \\ \hdashline X_{211} & X_{212} & \dots & X_{21K} \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ X_{2T1} & X_{2T2} & \dots & X_{2TK} \\ \hdashline \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ \hdashline X_{NT1} & X_{NT2} & \dots & X_{NTK} \end{bmatrix} \begin{matrix} \leftarrow t=1 \\ \dots \\ \leftarrow t=T \\ \leftarrow t=1 \\ \dots \\ \leftarrow t=T \\ \dots \\ \end{matrix}
\]
(Columns: Predictor 1, Predictor 2 … Predictor K. Rows grouped by Individual 1, Individual 2, … N) \(\quad X_i : (T \times K)\)
Note that \(X'X = (K \times NT)(NT \times K) = (K \times K)\)
\[
\underset{(K \times 1)}{\vec{\beta}} = \begin{bmatrix} \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_K \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\underset{(NT \times 1)}{\vec{v}} = \begin{bmatrix} \vec{v}_1 \\ \vec{v}_2 \\ \vdots \\ \vec{v}_N \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} v_{11} \\ \vdots \\ v_{1T} \\ \hdashline v_{21} \\ \vdots \\ v_{2T} \\ \hdashline \vdots \\ \hdashline v_{NT} \end{bmatrix} \quad \vec{v}_i : (T \times 1)
\]
Further:

\(v'v = (1 \times NT)(NT \times 1) = (1 \times 1)\): Sum of Squared Residuals

(inner product, total magnitude of errors squared; what OLS is minimizing)

\(vv' = (NT \times 1)(1 \times NT) = (NT \times NT)\): Variance-Covariance Matrix

(outer product, shows how errors relate to one other across obs)







These datasets track the exact same people and families over years or decades, making them the gold standard for microeconometrics (labor, health, education).

Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID): The longest-running household panel in the world (USA). Tracks families and their descendants since 1968.
National Longitudinal Surveys (NLSY): US Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Massive for labor econ, tracking specific cohorts (like the 1979 or 1997 cohorts) over their lifespans.
Understanding Society (UKHLS): The UK’s massive household panel study (formerly the British Household Panel Survey or BHPS).
Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP): The German equivalent to the PSID, running since 1984.
Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE): Cross-national panel database covering health, socio-economic status, and social networks of individuals aged 50+ in Europe.




These track corporate financials, productivity, and behavior. Note that many of the best firm-level panels require institutional access.

Compustat / CRSP (via WRDS): The holy grail for finance and firm-level econ. Tracks massive amounts of data on publicly traded companies over time. (Usually requires university access).
World Bank Enterprise Surveys: Firm-level survey data tracking businesses in emerging markets and developing economies.
Longitudinal Business Database (LBD): US Census data tracking establishment openings, closings, and employment. (Note: Highly restricted access, but famous in literature).




Used for cross-country growth regressions, trade, and macroeconomics.

Penn World Table (PWT): The standard dataset for comparing real GDP, employment, and capital across countries over time.
World Bank Open Data / WDI: The World Development Indicators provide a massive unbalanced panel of hundreds of metrics for almost every country.
IMF Data: Great for international financial statistics, government debt, and exchange rate panels.




Used to study structural change, automation, and industry-level productivity.

EU KLEMS: Industry-level data on capital, labor, energy, materials, and service inputs for EU countries (and the US).
NBER-CES Manufacturing Industry Database: Annual data on output, employment, payroll, and investment for US manufacturing industries from 1958 onward.
UNIDO INDSTAT: Industrial statistics database maintained by the UN, offering time-series data on manufacturing sectors globally.






Endogeneity: May solve problem of dealing w/ unobserved heterogeneity across \(N\)

Omitted variable bias: OLS becomes biased & inconsistent in its variance
\(\rightarrow\) OLS can consistently estimate \(\beta\) for panel under \(E[\Delta x_{it}' \Delta u_{it}] = 0\)

Dynamics: Required in estimating dynamic econ models in presence of individual lvl heterogeneity

\(\rightarrow\) e.g. Behaviors: smoking (habit formation), immigration to a city (motivation to earn \(\uparrow\) wage)
\(\Rightarrow\) Past levels affect future levels
\(\rightarrow\) i.e. Can remove unobservable / endogenous effects using p.d.





Consistent for:

\(\star\) 1. Fixed \(T\), \(N \rightarrow \infty\) : Focus for this class

\(T \rightarrow \infty\), fixed \(N\) : Time-series techniques


\(T \rightarrow \infty\) & \(N \rightarrow \infty\)


\(\star\) We will assume random sampling of observations: IID observations

\((y_{it}, \vec{x}_{it}) \perp (y_{jt}, \vec{x}_{jt}) \quad \forall i \neq j\) (Independent)
\((y_{it}, \vec{x}_{it}) \sim F, \ (y_{jt}, \vec{x}_{jt}) \sim F \quad \forall i \neq j\) (Same dist)




\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{it} &= \vec{x}_{it}'\beta + v_{it} \\
&= \vec{x}_{it}'\beta + f_i + u_{it}
\end{aligned}
\]

\(\vec{x}_{it} : (K \times 1)\)
\(\beta : (K \times 1)\) \(\Rightarrow \vec{x}_{it}'\beta : (1 \times 1)\)

Error Term Breakdown:

\(\star \ V_{it} = f_i + u_{it}\) (“Composite error term”)
\(\star \ f_i\): “Unobserved effect” \(\rightarrow\) time-constant individual heterogeneity

Country’s culture, city proximity to coast, innate ability, etc.

\(\star \ u_{it}\): “Idiosyncratic error” \(\rightarrow\) true random noise

\(\rightarrow\) Vary over \(t\)


\(\star\) Note alt assumptions on the errors:

Str. exogeneity: \(E[u_{it} | x_{i1}, \dots, x_{iT}, f_i] = E[u_{it} | X_i, f_i] = 0\)

\(\overset{\text{L.I.E.}}{\Rightarrow} E[u_{it}] = 0\)

Weak exogeneity: \(E[u_{it} | \{x_{is}\}_{s \leq t}, f_i] = 0\)

(Predetermined regs)
\(\Rightarrow\) Allows \(u_{it}\) to be correlated w/ future \(X\) values but not w/ past ones
\(\Rightarrow\) i.e. Past shocks (\(u_{i, t-1}\)) can influence future values (\(x_{i, t+1}\))
Reasonable assumption

title: Pooled OLS
text: What if try running a Pooled OLS estimator on our data, given the aforementioned model form? First, we need to state our model assumptions to then derive properites of the estimator.

title: Pooled OLS
text:
Here our assumption that the relationship between the regressors \(X_i\) and the outcome variable \(y_{i}\) is linear.
\[
y_{it} = x_{it}'\beta + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



We assume that the unobserved effects, \(f_i\), are strictly exogenous; in other words, conditional on the regressors \(X_i\), the expected value of \(f_i\) is zero. More formally:
\[
\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}] \equiv \mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i] = 0
\]



We assume that the expected value of the idiosyncratic error terms is equal to zero, conditional on the regressors and the unobservable effect(s). More formally,
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]
In other words, the error terms are uncorrelated with the regressors in this model; to see this, we can use a simple proof:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  &\text{Note that } \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\vec x_{it}, \mu_{it}) = \mathbb{E}[\vec x_{it} \cdot \mu_{it}] + \mathbb{E}[\vec x_{it}] \cdot  \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it}] \\
  & \text{Via the Law of Iterated Expectation, note that: } \\
  & \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it}] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i]] \\
  & \text{via assumption 3, } \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0; \text{ thus,} \\
  & \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it}] = 0. \\
  & \text{Plugging into our equation, we get: } \\
  &\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\mu_{it}, \vec x_{it}) = \mathbb{E}[\vec x_{it} \cdot \mu_{it}] + 0 \\
  & \text{Finally, via LIE, we can show that: } \\
  & \mathbb{E}[\vec x_{it} \cdot \mu_{it}] = \mathbb{E}[  \mathbb{E}[\vec x_{it} \cdot \mu_{it} \mid \vec x_{it}, f_i]] \\
  & \text{via the Linearity of Conditional Expectations, } \\
  & \mathbb{E}[  \mathbb{E}[\vec x_{it} \cdot \mu_{it} \mid \vec x_{it}, f_i]] =
    \mathbb{E}[ \vec x_{it} \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid \vec x_{it}, f_i]] \\
  & \text{via assumption 3, we get that } \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid \vec x_{it}, f_i] = 0; \text{thus,} \\
  & \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\vec x_{it}, \mu_{it}) = 0. \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



For homoskedasticity, we make a total of three assumptions:
\[
\begin{cases}
  1. \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(f_i \mid X_i) = \sigma_{f}^2 &\text{Constant Variance in the Unobserved Error} \\
  2. \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{\mu}^2 & \text{Constant Variance in the Idiosyncratic Error} \\
  3. \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is}) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation}
\end{cases}
\]



\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'X_i  \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(X_i'X_i)}_{M_{XX}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank K}
\]
In other words, our matrix of regressors \(X_i\) has full column rank, thus, the symmetric matrix \(X_i'X_i\) will have full rank, meaning it is invertible.



Note that assumptions 2-4 imply the following properties:

\(\mathbb{E}[v_{it} \mid X_i] = 0\)

Proof:
\(\mathbb{E}[v_{it} \mid X_i] = \mathbb{E}[f_i + \mu_{it} \mid X_i] = \mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i] =\)
\(\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[ \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] ] = 0\) via assumption.

\(\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(v_{it}, v_{is} \mid X_i) = \sigma_f^2 + \delta_{ts} \sigma_{\mu}^2\)

Proof:
\(\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(v_{it}, v_{is} \mid X_i) = \mathbb{E}[v_{it} v_{is} \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[v_{it} \mid X_i] \mathbb{E}[v_{is} \mid X_i] =\)
\(\mathbb{E}[v_{it} v_{is} \mid X_i] + 0 \cdot 0\) via proof above
\(\mathbb{E}[v_{it} v_{is} \mid X_i] = \mathbb{E}[ \left( f_i + \mu_{it} \right) \left( f_i + \mu_{is} \right) \mid X_i] =\)
\(\mathbb{E}[f_i^2 \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[f_i \mu_{it} \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[f_i \mu_{is} \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mu_{is} \mid X_i] =\)
\(\sigma_f^2 + \mathbb{E} [f_i \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] ] + \mathbb{E} [f_i \mathbb{E}[\mu_{is} \mid X_i, f_i] ] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mu_{is} \mid X_i] =\)
\(\sigma_f^2 + 0 + 0 + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mu_{is} \mid X_i]\)
Note that if \(s=t\), then \(\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it}^2 \mid X_i] = \sigma_{\mu}^2\);
However, if \(s \neq t\), then \(\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mu_{is} \mid X_i] = 0\) (since it must hold under our assumption that \(\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is}) = 0\)).
Thus, \(\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(v_{it}, v_{is} \mid X_i) = \sigma_f^2 + \delta_{ts} \sigma_{\mu}^2\), where \(\delta = 1\) if \(s=t\), and \(\delta = 0\) otherwise.

title: Pooled OLS
text:
To show that the POLS estimator is an unbiased regressor, we want to show that \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS}] = \beta\). Note that the OLS regressor is derived from minimizing SSR, which is found as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  & \min_{\tilde{\beta}} \sum v_i^2 \equiv \min_{\tilde{\beta}} \quad (y-X{\tilde{\beta}})(y-X{\tilde{\beta}})' \\
  = & \min_{\tilde{\beta}} \quad y'y - 2{\tilde{\beta}}'X'y + {\tilde{\beta}}'X'X{\tilde{\beta}} \\
  \text{FOC: } & \frac{\partial y'y}{\partial {\tilde{\beta}} } - \frac{\partial 2{\tilde{\beta}}'X'y}{\partial {\tilde{\beta}}} + \frac{\partial{\tilde{\beta}}'X'X{\tilde{\beta}}}{\partial {\tilde{\beta}}} = 0 \\
  & 2X'y = 2X'X{\tilde{\beta}} \Rightarrow {\tilde{\beta}} = (X'X)^{-1}X'y
\end{aligned}
\]
To show unbiasedness, note that showing \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}] = \beta\) is equivalent to showing \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta} - \beta] = 0\), via the linearity of expectations. Furthermore, note that:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \hat{\beta}_\text{POLS} - \beta &= (X'X)^{-1}X'y - \beta \\
  &= (X'X)^{-1}X'(X\beta + v) - \beta \\
  &= (X'X)^{-1}X'X\beta + (X'X)^{-1}X'v - \beta \\
  &= \beta + (X'X)^{-1}X'v - \beta \\
  &= (X'X)^{-1}X'v
\end{aligned}
\]
Which is known as the sampling error of our estimator.
Using this definition, we can finally prove the unbiasedness of our estimator by taking expectations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS} - \beta] &= \mathbb{E}[(X'X)^{-1}X'v] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(X'X)^{-1}X' \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[v \mid X]}_\text{=0}] \\
  \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS} - \beta] &= 0 \\
  \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS}] &= \beta   \qquad \qquad    \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



To show that \(\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS}\) is a consistent estimator, we want to show that the estimator converges in probability to \(\beta\); more formally, that:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \hat{\beta}_\text{POLS} &\xrightarrow{p} \beta \\
  &\Leftrightarrow \\
  \hat{\beta}_\text{POLS} - &\beta \xrightarrow{p} 0
\end{aligned}
\]
To do so, we will use a trick of adding in \(n\) and \(\frac{1}{n}\) which cancel out \(\frac{n}{n} = 1\) to impose asymptotic properties such as LLN and CMT.
\[
\begin{aligned}
  &\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS} - \beta = \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum X_i'X_i \right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{n} \sum X_i'v_i}_{(2)} \\
  & (1) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X'X]^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
  & (2) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X'v] \text{ via LLN} \\
  & \text{note that } \mathbb{E}[X'(f + \mu)] = \mathbb{E}[X'f] + \mathbb{E}[X'\mu] \\
  & = \mathbb{E}[X' \mathbb{E}[f \mid X]] + \mathbb{E}[X'\mathbb{E}[\mu \mid X]] = 0 \\
  & \text{thus, via Slutsky's Theorem, } \mathbb{E}[X'X]^{-1} \cdot 0 \\
  &\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS} - \beta \xrightarrow{p} 0 \Leftrightarrow \hat{\beta}_\text{POLS} \xrightarrow{p} \beta \qquad \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



To understand the distributional form of our estimator, we will invoke the following form of the LHS, in order to use to impose the Lindeberg-Levy CLT:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{n}\left(\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS} - \beta \right)& = \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum X_i'X_i \right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum X_i'v_i}_{(2)} \\
  & (1) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X'X]^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
  & (2) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(X'v) \right) \text{ via CLT} \\
  & \text{thus, via Slutsky's theorem, } \\
  \sqrt{n}\left(\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS} - \beta \right)& \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{E}[X'X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}(X'vv'X)\mathbb{E}[X'X]^{-1} \right) \quad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]


Although the Pooled OLS estimator has very nice properties for our model, the issue lies in estimating its asymptotic variance. To see this, note that from the last section we found
\[
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS}) = \mathbb{E}[X'X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}(X'vv'X)\mathbb{E}[X'X]^{-1}
\]
The issue is that we cannot simply assume that \(\mathbb{E}[v_iv_i' \mid X_i] = \sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}\) as we could for a regular OLS model; to see the issue, recall that \(\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(v_{it}, v_{is}) = \sigma_f^2 + \delta_{ts} \sigma_{\mu}^2\). Thus, our variance-covariance matrix takes the form:
\[
\mathbb{E}[v_iv_i' \mid X_i] \equiv V_i = \begin{bmatrix}
\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2 & \sigma_f^2 & \cdots & \sigma_f^2\\
\sigma_f^2 & \ddots & \sigma_f^2 & \vdots \\
\vdots &  \sigma_f^2 & \ddots & \vdots\\
\sigma_f^2 & \cdots &  & \sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2
\end{bmatrix}
\]
This comes from the fact that the asymptotic variance of the OLS estimator is given by the sandwich formula:
\[
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS}) = M_{xx}^{-1} \mathbb{E}[X'vv'X] M_{xx}^{-1}
\]
(Note: \(vv'\) is unknown. To estimate, we use the analogy principle).
We substitute the composite error term \(v_i = f_i + \mu_{it}\) and expand out the inner term \(\mathbb{E}[X'vv'X]\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X'vv'X] &= \mathbb{E}[X'(f+\mu)(f+\mu)'X] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'(f+\mu)(f'+\mu')X] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'ff'X] + \mathbb{E}[X'f\mu'X] + \mathbb{E}[X'\mu f'X] + \mathbb{E}[X'\mu\mu'X] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'ff'X] + 2\mathbb{E}[X'f\mu'X] + \mathbb{E}[X'\mu\mu'X]
\end{aligned}
\]
Note that \(2\mathbb{E}[X'f\mu'X] = 0\) via strict exogeneity assumption; \(\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0\) implies the unobserved effect and idiosyncratic error are uncorrelated.
Using the Law of Iterated Expectations, we can isolate out \(\sigma_{\mu}^2\) via homoskedasticity and no serial correlation assumption for \(\mu\):
\[
\mathbb{E}[X'\mu\mu'X] = \mathbb{E}[X' \mathbb{E}[\mu\mu' \mid X] X] = \sigma_\mu^2 \cdot \mathbb{E}[X'X]
\]
Finally, for the unobserved effect, we can use LIE to get the following:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X'ff'X] = \mathbb{E}[X' \mathbb{E}[ff' \mid X] X]
\]
However, note that \(f_i\) is constant over time; thus, \(\mathbb{E}[ff' \mid X]\) is not an identity matrix \(\sigma_f^2 I\). Rather, it is a full \(T \times T\) matrix of \(\sigma_f^2\); therefore, the matrices cannot cancel out, leaving Pooled OLS standard errors heavily biased due to serial correlation.
This motivates the transformation of our model to properly deal with the estimates of the asymptotic variance, named the Random Effects estimator.

title: Fixed Effects
text:
The RE estimator is BLUE under its assumptions, but it requires \(\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i] = 0\); the unobserved individual effect must be uncorrelated with the regressors. In many settings this fails. For example, consider a wage regression where \(f_i\) captures innate ability: individuals with higher ability self-select into more schooling, so \(f_i\) and \(x_{it}\) are correlated and RE is inconsistent.
We now consider the case where
\[
E(f_i \mid X_i) \equiv g(X_i) \neq 0
\]
for some non-constant function \(g\). This is the fixed effects assumption: \(f_i\) may be an arbitrary function of \(X_i\), so \(\text{corr}(\mathbf{x}_{it}, f_i) \neq 0\) in general. The FE estimator handles this by eliminating \(f_i\) entirely through a within-group transformation, making the correlation structure between \(f_i\) and \(X_i\) irrelevant.
Note that this comes at a cost: any regressor that is time-invariant (e.g., gender, country of birth) is absorbed by the transformation and cannot be identified under FE.





Same as before, however in our model we now include \(\mathbf{z}_i\) to consider what happens to time-invariant regressors.
\[
y_{it} = \mathbf{x}_{it}'\beta + \mathbf{z}_i'\gamma + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



NEW. We relax the RE assumption and allow the unobserved effect to be a non-constant function of the regressors:
\[
E(f_i \mid X_i) = g(X_i) \neq 0
\]
The implication is that \(\text{corr}(\mathbf{x}_{it}, f_i) \neq 0\) in general. Unlike random effects, \(f_i\) is treated as a fixed parameter that need not be modelled.



Same as before:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid \mathbf{x}_{i1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]



We retain homoskedasticity for the idiosyncratic error only, since \(f_i\) is no longer modelled as a random variable:
\[
\begin{cases}
1. \ \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{\mu}^2 & \text{Constant Variance} \\
2. \ \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is} \mid X_i, f_i) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation}
\end{cases}
\]



NEW. The rank condition is imposed on the demeaned (within-transformed) regressors \(\tilde{X}_i = M_0 X_i\), rather than on the raw regressors:
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i)}_{M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank K}
\]
Since the demeaning annihilates any time-constant column, only time-varying regressors can appear in \(X_i\); any time-invariant covariates must be dropped from the model.



Since \(f_i\) is time-invariant, subtracting individual-specific means from both sides of the model eliminates it. Define:
\[
\bar{y}_{i} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T y_{it}, \qquad \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T \mathbf{x}_{it}, \qquad \bar{\mu}_{i} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T \mu_{it}
\]
The within (demeaned) model is:
\[
\underbrace{y_{it} - \bar{y}_{i}}_{\tilde{y}_{it}} = \underbrace{(\mathbf{x}_{it} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i})'}_{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{it}'}\beta + \underbrace{(\mu_{it} - \bar{\mu}_{i})}_{\tilde{\mu}_{it}}
\]
since \(f_i - f_i = 0\). The fixed effect drops out entirely, since it is time-invariant: \(\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T f_i = f_i\); the same holds for \(\mathbf{z}_i\).


In matrix notation, define the \((T \times T)\) projection (averaging) matrix, where \(\ell_T = (1, 1, \ldots, 1)' \in \mathbb{R}^T\):
\[
P_0 = \frac{1}{T}\ell_T\ell_T' \equiv 1_T(1_T'1_T)^{-1}1_T'
\]
\[
P_0 =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \frac{1}{T} & \frac{1}{T} & \cdots \\
  \frac{1}{T} & \ddots & \vdots \\
  \vdots & \cdots & \frac{1}{T}
\end{bmatrix}
\]






Note



The projection matrix has a nice property such that \(P_Ty_t = \bar{y}_t\). For a comprehensive list of the projection matrix & annihilator matrix’s properties with subsequent proofs, see Appendix(1)


and the \((T \times T)\) annihilator (demeaning) matrix:
\[
M_0 = (I_T - P_0)
\]
These satisfy \(M_0 + P_0 = I_T\), and both are symmetric and idempotent. The key property is \(M_0\ell_T = 0\): the annihilator kills any time-constant vector. The explicit form of \(M_0\) is:
\[
M_0 = \begin{bmatrix}
1 - \frac{1}{T} & -\frac{1}{T} & \cdots & -\frac{1}{T} \\
-\frac{1}{T} & 1 - \frac{1}{T} & \cdots & -\frac{1}{T} \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\
-\frac{1}{T} & \cdots & & 1 - \frac{1}{T}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
For the full panel, define the \((NT \times NT)\) within-group and between-group matrices:
\[
Q = I_N \otimes M_0 \qquad F = I_N \otimes P_0
\]
satisfying \(Q + F = I_{NT}\). Since \(M_0 \ell_T = 0\), applying \(Q\) to the stacked model \(\mathbf{y}_i = X_i\beta + f_i\ell_T + \mu_i\) gives:
\[
Q\mathbf{y} = QX\beta + Q\mu
\]
with \(f_i\) eliminated. The FE estimator is then OLS applied to this within-transformed system:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{FE} = (X'QX)^{-1}X'Q\mathbf{y} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_i\right)
\]
where the last equality follows from \(Q\) being symmetric and idempotent (\(Q^2 = Q\)), so \(X'QX = \tilde{X}'\tilde{X}\) and \(X'Q\mathbf{y} = \tilde{X}'\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\).







The sampling error of \(\hat{\beta}_{FE}\) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FE} - \beta &= (X'QX)^{-1}X'Q\mathbf{y} - \beta \\
&= (X'QX)^{-1}X'Q(X\beta + \mu) - \beta \\
&= (X'QX)^{-1}X'Q\mu
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking conditional expectations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FE} - \beta \mid X, f] &= (X'QX)^{-1}X'Q \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\mu \mid X, f]}_{\text{=0 via A3}} = 0 \\
\Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FE}] &= \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FE} - \beta &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i] = \mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{X}_i' \mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mu}_i \mid X_i, f_i]\right] = 0 \text{ via LLN and A3} \\
\hat{\beta}_{FE} &\xrightarrow{p} \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FE} - \beta) &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i)\right) \text{ via CLT}
\end{aligned}
\]
Under assumption 4, \(\mathbb{E}[\mu_i\mu_i' \mid X_i, f_i] = \sigma_\mu^2 I_T\), so:
\[
\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i) = \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i\tilde{\mu}_i'\tilde{X}_i] = \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}_i'(\sigma_\mu^2 I_T)\tilde{X}_i] = \sigma_\mu^2 \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i] = \sigma_\mu^2 M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}
\]
Thus, via Slutsky’s theorem:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FE} - \beta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \sigma_\mu^2 M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}^{-1}\right) \qquad \blacksquare
\]



The asymptotic variance under assumption 4 is \(\sigma_\mu^2 M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}^{-1}\). To estimate \(\sigma_\mu^2\), use the within residuals \(\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_{it} = \tilde{y}_{it} - \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{it}'\hat{\beta}_{FE}\) (since we showed already that \(\hat{\beta}_{FE}\) is consistent, unbiased, and asymp. normal).
Note that demeaning costs \(N\) degrees of freedom (one per individual mean subtracted), and estimating \(\beta\) costs \(K\) more; the consistent estimator of \(\sigma_\mu^2\) is:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_\mu^2 = \frac{1}{N(T-1) - K}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^T \hat{\tilde{\mu}}_{it}^2
\]
Using the analogy principle:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_\mu^2 \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \sigma_\mu^2 \mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right]^{-1}
\]






Note



For a more rigorous proof demonstrating the loss of one time period per individual and how this affects our variance estimation, see Question 2 from Problem Set 1 here






If assumption 4 fails (heteroskedasticity or serial correlation in \(\mu_{it}\)), the homoskedastic AVAR formula is incorrect. We instead use the cluster-robust sandwich estimator, clustering at the individual level:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{FE}) = \left(\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_i\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)\left(\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}
\]
This allows for arbitrary heteroskedasticity and serial correlation in \(\mu_{it}\) within each individual \(i\), placing no additional restrictions beyond assumptions 1 to 3.

title: Fixed Effects
text:
The RE estimator is BLUE under its assumptions, but it requires \(\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i] = 0\); the unobserved individual effect must be uncorrelated with the regressors. In many settings this fails. For example, consider a wage regression where \(f_i\) captures innate ability: individuals with higher ability self-select into more schooling, so \(f_i\) and \(x_{it}\) are correlated and RE is inconsistent.
We now consider the case where
\[
E(f_i \mid X_i) \equiv g(X_i) \neq 0
\]
for some non-constant function \(g\). This is the fixed effects assumption: \(f_i\) may be an arbitrary function of \(X_i\), so \(\text{corr}(\mathbf{x}_{it}, f_i) \neq 0\) in general. The FE estimator handles this by eliminating \(f_i\) entirely through a within-group transformation, making the correlation structure between \(f_i\) and \(X_i\) irrelevant.
Note that this comes at a cost: any regressor that is time-invariant (e.g., gender, country of birth) is absorbed by the transformation and cannot be identified under FE.

title: Fixed Effects
text:
Same as before, however in our model we now include \(\mathbf{z}_i\) to consider what happens to time-invariant regressors.
\[
y_{it} = \mathbf{x}_{it}'\beta + \mathbf{z}_i'\gamma + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



NEW. We relax the RE assumption and allow the unobserved effect to be a non-constant function of the regressors:
\[
E(f_i \mid X_i) = g(X_i) \neq 0
\]
The implication is that \(\text{corr}(\mathbf{x}_{it}, f_i) \neq 0\) in general. Unlike random effects, \(f_i\) is treated as a fixed parameter that need not be modelled.



Same as before:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid \mathbf{x}_{i1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]



We retain homoskedasticity for the idiosyncratic error only, since \(f_i\) is no longer modelled as a random variable:
\[
\begin{cases}
1. \ \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{\mu}^2 & \text{Constant Variance} \\
2. \ \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is} \mid X_i, f_i) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation}
\end{cases}
\]



NEW. The rank condition is imposed on the demeaned (within-transformed) regressors \(\tilde{X}_i = M_0 X_i\), rather than on the raw regressors:
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i)}_{M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank K}
\]
Since the demeaning annihilates any time-constant column, only time-varying regressors can appear in \(X_i\); any time-invariant covariates must be dropped from the model.



Since \(f_i\) is time-invariant, subtracting individual-specific means from both sides of the model eliminates it. Define:
\[
\bar{y}_{i} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T y_{it}, \qquad \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T \mathbf{x}_{it}, \qquad \bar{\mu}_{i} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T \mu_{it}
\]
The within (demeaned) model is:
\[
\underbrace{y_{it} - \bar{y}_{i}}_{\tilde{y}_{it}} = \underbrace{(\mathbf{x}_{it} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i})'}_{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{it}'}\beta + \underbrace{(\mu_{it} - \bar{\mu}_{i})}_{\tilde{\mu}_{it}}
\]
since \(f_i - f_i = 0\). The fixed effect drops out entirely, since it is time-invariant: \(\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T f_i = f_i\); the same holds for \(\mathbf{z}_i\).


In matrix notation, define the \((T \times T)\) projection (averaging) matrix, where \(\ell_T = (1, 1, \ldots, 1)' \in \mathbb{R}^T\):
\[
P_0 = \frac{1}{T}\ell_T\ell_T' \equiv 1_T(1_T'1_T)^{-1}1_T'
\]
\[
P_0 =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \frac{1}{T} & \frac{1}{T} & \cdots \\
  \frac{1}{T} & \ddots & \vdots \\
  \vdots & \cdots & \frac{1}{T}
\end{bmatrix}
\]






Note



The projection matrix has a nice property such that \(P_Ty_t = \bar{y}_t\). For a comprehensive list of the projection matrix & annihilator matrix’s properties with subsequent proofs, see Appendix(1)


and the \((T \times T)\) annihilator (demeaning) matrix:
\[
M_0 = (I_T - P_0)
\]
These satisfy \(M_0 + P_0 = I_T\), and both are symmetric and idempotent. The key property is \(M_0\ell_T = 0\): the annihilator kills any time-constant vector. The explicit form of \(M_0\) is:
\[
M_0 = \begin{bmatrix}
1 - \frac{1}{T} & -\frac{1}{T} & \cdots & -\frac{1}{T} \\
-\frac{1}{T} & 1 - \frac{1}{T} & \cdots & -\frac{1}{T} \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\
-\frac{1}{T} & \cdots & & 1 - \frac{1}{T}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
For the full panel, define the \((NT \times NT)\) within-group and between-group matrices:
\[
Q = I_N \otimes M_0 \qquad F = I_N \otimes P_0
\]
satisfying \(Q + F = I_{NT}\). Since \(M_0 \ell_T = 0\), applying \(Q\) to the stacked model \(\mathbf{y}_i = X_i\beta + f_i\ell_T + \mu_i\) gives:
\[
Q\mathbf{y} = QX\beta + Q\mu
\]
with \(f_i\) eliminated. The FE estimator is then OLS applied to this within-transformed system:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{FE} = (X'QX)^{-1}X'Q\mathbf{y} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_i\right)
\]
where the last equality follows from \(Q\) being symmetric and idempotent (\(Q^2 = Q\)), so \(X'QX = \tilde{X}'\tilde{X}\) and \(X'Q\mathbf{y} = \tilde{X}'\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\).

title: Fixed Effects
text:
The sampling error of \(\hat{\beta}_{FE}\) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FE} - \beta &= (X'QX)^{-1}X'Q\mathbf{y} - \beta \\
&= (X'QX)^{-1}X'Q(X\beta + \mu) - \beta \\
&= (X'QX)^{-1}X'Q\mu
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking conditional expectations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FE} - \beta \mid X, f] &= (X'QX)^{-1}X'Q \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\mu \mid X, f]}_{\text{=0 via A3}} = 0 \\
\Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FE}] &= \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FE} - \beta &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i] = \mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{X}_i' \mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mu}_i \mid X_i, f_i]\right] = 0 \text{ via LLN and A3} \\
\hat{\beta}_{FE} &\xrightarrow{p} \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FE} - \beta) &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i)\right) \text{ via CLT}
\end{aligned}
\]
Under assumption 4, \(\mathbb{E}[\mu_i\mu_i' \mid X_i, f_i] = \sigma_\mu^2 I_T\), so:
\[
\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i) = \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{\mu}_i\tilde{\mu}_i'\tilde{X}_i] = \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}_i'(\sigma_\mu^2 I_T)\tilde{X}_i] = \sigma_\mu^2 \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i] = \sigma_\mu^2 M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}
\]
Thus, via Slutsky’s theorem:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FE} - \beta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \sigma_\mu^2 M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}^{-1}\right) \qquad \blacksquare
\]



The asymptotic variance under assumption 4 is \(\sigma_\mu^2 M_{\tilde{X}\tilde{X}}^{-1}\). To estimate \(\sigma_\mu^2\), use the within residuals \(\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_{it} = \tilde{y}_{it} - \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{it}'\hat{\beta}_{FE}\) (since we showed already that \(\hat{\beta}_{FE}\) is consistent, unbiased, and asymp. normal).
Note that demeaning costs \(N\) degrees of freedom (one per individual mean subtracted), and estimating \(\beta\) costs \(K\) more; the consistent estimator of \(\sigma_\mu^2\) is:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_\mu^2 = \frac{1}{N(T-1) - K}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^T \hat{\tilde{\mu}}_{it}^2
\]
Using the analogy principle:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_\mu^2 \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \sigma_\mu^2 \mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right]^{-1}
\]






Note



For a more rigorous proof demonstrating the loss of one time period per individual and how this affects our variance estimation, see Question 2 from Problem Set 1 here

title: Fixed Effects
text:
If assumption 4 fails (heteroskedasticity or serial correlation in \(\mu_{it}\)), the homoskedastic AVAR formula is incorrect. We instead use the cluster-robust sandwich estimator, clustering at the individual level:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{FE}) = \left(\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_i\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)\left(\sum_i \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}
\]
This allows for arbitrary heteroskedasticity and serial correlation in \(\mu_{it}\) within each individual \(i\), placing no additional restrictions beyond assumptions 1 to 3.

title: Fixed Effects
text:
1 Projection & Annihilator Matrix Properties
Note that the general projection matrix is \(P_X = X(X'X)^{-1}X'\), projecting onto the column space of whatever \(X\) you pass in. Here, we are projecting specifically onto the space spanned by a constant, so \(X = \ell_T\) (the \(T \times 1\) vector of ones). The properties thereby slightly shift their interpretation as a result.

1.1 Projection Matrix

1.1.1 Symmetric & Idempotent
Symmetric (\(P_0' = P_0\)):
\[
P_0' = \left(\frac{1}{T}\ell_T\ell_T'\right)' = \frac{1}{T}(\ell_T')'\ell_T' = \frac{1}{T}\ell_T\ell_T' = P_0 \qquad \blacksquare
\]
Idempotent (\(P_0^2 = P_0\)):
\[
P_0^2 = \left(\frac{1}{T}\ell_T\ell_T'\right)\left(\frac{1}{T}\ell_T\ell_T'\right) = \frac{1}{T^2}\ell_T\underbrace{(\ell_T'\ell_T)}_{=T}\ell_T' = \frac{1}{T}\ell_T\ell_T' = P_0 \qquad \blacksquare
\]


1.1.2 \(P_0\ell_T = \ell_T\)
\[
P_0\ell_T = \frac{1}{T}\ell_T\ell_T'\ell_T = \frac{1}{T}\ell_T \cdot T = \ell_T \qquad \blacksquare
\]
More generally, \(P_0 y_i = \bar{y}_i \ell_T\). Applying the projection yields a \(T \times 1\) vector filled with the individual time mean:
\[
P_0 y_i = \frac{1}{T}\ell_T\ell_T'y_i = \frac{1}{T}\ell_T\sum_{t=1}^T y_{it} = \bar{y}_i\ell_T \qquad \blacksquare
\]



1.2 Annihilator Matrix

1.2.1 Symmetric & Idempotent
Symmetric (\(M_0' = M_0\)):
\[
M_0' = (I_T - P_0)' = I_T' - P_0' = I_T - P_0 = M_0 \qquad \blacksquare
\]
Idempotent (\(M_0^2 = M_0\)):
\[
M_0^2 = (I_T - P_0)^2 = I_T - 2P_0 + P_0^2 = I_T - 2P_0 + P_0 = I_T - P_0 = M_0 \qquad \blacksquare
\]


1.2.2 \(M_0\ell_T = 0\)
\[
M_0\ell_T = (I_T - P_0)\ell_T = \ell_T - P_0\ell_T = \ell_T - \ell_T = 0 \qquad \blacksquare
\]
More generally, \(M_0 y_i = \tilde{y}_i\). Applying the annihilator yields the demeaned vector:
\[
M_0 y_i = (I_T - P_0)y_i = y_i - \bar{y}_i\ell_T = \tilde{y}_i \qquad \blacksquare
\]
And since \(\mu_i\) is just another \(T \times 1\) vector, the same argument gives \(\tilde{\mu}_i = M_0\mu_i\); that is, the demeaned error is exactly the annihilator applied to the true idiosyncratic error.


1.2.3 \(M_0 P_0 = 0\) (Orthogonality)
\(P_0\) and \(M_0\) are orthogonal complements: the “mean part” and the “demeaned part” of any vector are orthogonal.
\[
M_0 P_0 = (I_T - P_0)P_0 = P_0 - P_0^2 = P_0 - P_0 = 0 \qquad \blacksquare
\]

title: Generalized Method of Moments Estimators
text:
OLS, GLS, RE, FE, and FD can all be interpreted as method-of-moments estimators: they set sample analogs of population moment conditions to zero and solve for \(\beta\). GMM generalizes this to allow more moment conditions than parameters. When we have \(L > K\) moment conditions, we cannot set all of them to zero simultaneously, so we instead minimize a weighted quadratic form in the sample moments.
In the panel data context, GMM arises naturally when the strict exogeneity assumption fails and we must use instrumental variables. This is the central motivation for the Anderson-Hsiao and Arellano-Bond estimators discussed next.



Consider the system with \(N\) i.i.d. observations:
\[
y_{it} = \mathbf{x}_{it}'\beta + u_{it} \qquad t = 1, \ldots, T
\]
where \(\mathbf{x}_{it}\) may be correlated with \(u_{it}\). In vector form: \(\mathbf{y}_i = X_i\beta + \mathbf{u}_i\).
Suppose we have a \((T \times L)\) instrument matrix \(Z_i\) satisfying two conditions:

Exclusion restriction: \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'\mathbf{u}_i] = 0\)
Rank condition: \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'X_i]\) has rank \(K\)



When the number of instruments equals the number of regressors, the \(L\) moment conditions \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'(\mathbf{y}_i - X_i\hat{\beta}) = 0\) have a unique solution:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{IV} = (Z'X)^{-1}Z'Y = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]



When \(L > K\), the system is over-determined. The 2SLS estimator projects \(X\) onto the column space of \(Z\):
\[
\hat{X} = Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'X
\]
and uses \(\hat{X}\) as the instrument in a second-stage regression:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{2SLS} = (\hat{X}'X)^{-1}\hat{X}'Y = \left(\sum_i \hat{X}_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i \hat{X}_i'\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]
The 2SLS estimator corresponds to a specific choice of GMM weighting matrix \(\hat{W} = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'Z_i\right)^{-1}\).




GMM1. Valid set of instrumental variables: \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'\mathbf{u}_i] = 0\), where \(Z_i\) is a \(T \times L\) matrix.
GMM2. Rank condition: \(\text{rank}\;\mathbb{E}[Z_i'X_i] = K\).
GMM3. Positive definite weighting matrix: \(\hat{W} \xrightarrow{p} W\), where \(W\) is a nonrandom, symmetric, \((L \times L)\) positive definite matrix.



For a given weighting matrix \(\hat{W}\), the GMM estimator minimizes the weighted quadratic form in the sample moments:
\[
\min_\beta \left[\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'(\mathbf{y}_i - X_i\beta)\right]'\hat{W}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'(\mathbf{y}_i - X_i\beta)\right]
\]
The unique solution is:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{GMM} = \left(X'Z\hat{W}Z'X\right)^{-1}X'Z\hat{W}Z'Y
\]
Under GMM1 to GMM3, this estimator is consistent for any positive definite \(W\). Letting \(C = \mathbb{E}[Z_i'X_i] = M_{ZX}\) and \(\Lambda = \mathbb{E}[Z_i'u_iu_i'Z_i]\), its asymptotic distribution is:
\[
\sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}_{GMM} - \beta\right) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, (C'WC)^{-1}C'W\Lambda WC(C'WC)^{-1}\right)
\]



The asymptotic variance above is minimized (in the positive semi-definite sense) when \(W = \Lambda^{-1}\). This gives the optimal GMM estimator:
\[
\sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}^{GMM*} - \beta\right) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, (C'\Lambda^{-1}C)^{-1}\right) = \mathcal{N}\left(0, \left(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'X_i]'\,\mathbb{E}[Z_i'u_iu_i'Z_i]^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}[Z_i'X_i]\right)^{-1}\right)
\]
To see that \(W = \Lambda^{-1}\) is optimal, note that for any positive definite \(W\):
\[
(C'WC)^{-1}C'W\Lambda WC(C'WC)^{-1} - (C'\Lambda^{-1}C)^{-1} \geq 0
\]
in the positive semi-definite sense, so \(\Lambda^{-1}\) yields the smallest asymptotic variance.



Since \(\Lambda = \mathbb{E}[Z_i'u_iu_i'Z_i]\) is unknown, the optimal estimator is implemented in two steps:

Step 1. Use \(\hat{W}_1 = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'Z_i\right)^{-1}\) to compute the first-stage 2SLS estimator \(\hat{\beta}^{2SLS}\), and form residuals \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i = \mathbf{y}_i - X_i\hat{\beta}^{2SLS}\).
Step 2. Estimate \(\Lambda^{-1}\) using: \[
\hat{\Lambda}^{-1} = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i'Z_i\right)^{-1}
\] and compute the Feasible GMM (FGMM) estimator: \[
\hat{\beta}^{FGMM} = \left[\left(\sum_i X_i'Z_i\right)\hat{\Lambda}^{-1}\left(\sum_i Z_i'X_i\right)\right]^{-1}\left(\sum_i X_i'Z_i\right)\hat{\Lambda}^{-1}\left(\sum_i Z_i'\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]

This estimator is consistent and asymptotically equivalent to the infeasible optimal GMM. Its asymptotic variance is estimated by:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}^{FGMM}) = N\left[\left(\sum_i X_i'Z_i\right)\hat{\Lambda}^{-1}\left(\sum_i Z_i'X_i\right)\right]^{-1}
\]



When \(L > K\), we can test whether the additional \(r = L - K\) moment conditions (the overidentifying restrictions) are valid. The hypotheses are:
\[
H_0: \mathbb{E}[Z_i'\mathbf{u}_i] = 0 \quad \text{(all } L \text{ instruments valid)}
\] \[
H_1: \mathbb{E}[Z_i'\mathbf{u}_i] \neq 0 \quad \text{(some instruments invalid)}
\]
Under \(H_0\), the CLT gives \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_i Z_i'u_i \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbb{E}[Z_i'u_iu_i'Z_i])\). Using consistent estimates, the Sargan-Hansen test statistic is:
\[
S\left(\hat{\beta}_{GMM}\right) = \hat{\mathbf{u}}'Z\left(Z'\hat{\mathbf{u}}\hat{\mathbf{u}}'Z\right)^{-1}Z'\hat{\mathbf{u}} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{L-K} \quad \text{under } H_0
\]
where \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i = \mathbf{y}_i - X_i\hat{\beta}_{GMM}\) and \(L - K\) is the number of overidentifying restrictions.

Under homoskedasticity and no serial correlation, this is the Sargan statistic.
Under heteroskedastic or serially correlated errors, this is Hansen’s J statistic.

Rejection of \(H_0\) indicates at least one instrument fails the exclusion restriction. Note that in first-differences models, we replace \(\mathbf{u}\), \(y\), and \(X\) with \(\Delta\mathbf{u}\), \(\Delta y\), and \(\Delta X\) throughout.


When we wish to test whether a subset of instruments is valid, conditional on a baseline set of valid instruments being maintained, we use the C-statistic (difference-in-Sargan):

Let \(S_1\) be the Sargan-Hansen statistic using all \(r_1\) instruments.
Let \(S_0\) be the Sargan-Hansen statistic using only the restricted subset of \(r_0 < r_1\) instruments.

Then:
\[
C = S_1 - S_0 \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{r_1 - r_0} \quad \text{under } H_0
\]
The degrees of freedom equal the number of instruments being tested. A rejection implies that the additional instruments are not exogenous.

title: Generalized Method of Moments Estimators
text:
OLS, GLS, RE, FE, and FD can all be interpreted as method-of-moments estimators: they set sample analogs of population moment conditions to zero and solve for \(\beta\). GMM generalizes this to allow more moment conditions than parameters. When we have \(L > K\) moment conditions, we cannot set all of them to zero simultaneously, so we instead minimize a weighted quadratic form in the sample moments.
In the panel data context, GMM arises naturally when the strict exogeneity assumption fails and we must use instrumental variables. This is the central motivation for the Anderson-Hsiao and Arellano-Bond estimators discussed next.

title: Generalized Method of Moments Estimators
text:
Consider the system with \(N\) i.i.d. observations:
\[
y_{it} = \mathbf{x}_{it}'\beta + u_{it} \qquad t = 1, \ldots, T
\]
where \(\mathbf{x}_{it}\) may be correlated with \(u_{it}\). In vector form: \(\mathbf{y}_i = X_i\beta + \mathbf{u}_i\).
Suppose we have a \((T \times L)\) instrument matrix \(Z_i\) satisfying two conditions:

Exclusion restriction: \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'\mathbf{u}_i] = 0\)
Rank condition: \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'X_i]\) has rank \(K\)



When the number of instruments equals the number of regressors, the \(L\) moment conditions \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'(\mathbf{y}_i - X_i\hat{\beta}) = 0\) have a unique solution:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{IV} = (Z'X)^{-1}Z'Y = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]



When \(L > K\), the system is over-determined. The 2SLS estimator projects \(X\) onto the column space of \(Z\):
\[
\hat{X} = Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'X
\]
and uses \(\hat{X}\) as the instrument in a second-stage regression:
\[
\hat{\beta}^{2SLS} = (\hat{X}'X)^{-1}\hat{X}'Y = \left(\sum_i \hat{X}_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i \hat{X}_i'\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]
The 2SLS estimator corresponds to a specific choice of GMM weighting matrix \(\hat{W} = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'Z_i\right)^{-1}\).

title: Generalized Method of Moments Estimators
text:
GMM1. Valid set of instrumental variables: \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'\mathbf{u}_i] = 0\), where \(Z_i\) is a \(T \times L\) matrix.
GMM2. Rank condition: \(\text{rank}\;\mathbb{E}[Z_i'X_i] = K\).
GMM3. Positive definite weighting matrix: \(\hat{W} \xrightarrow{p} W\), where \(W\) is a nonrandom, symmetric, \((L \times L)\) positive definite matrix.

title: Generalized Method of Moments Estimators
text:
For a given weighting matrix \(\hat{W}\), the GMM estimator minimizes the weighted quadratic form in the sample moments:
\[
\min_\beta \left[\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'(\mathbf{y}_i - X_i\beta)\right]'\hat{W}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'(\mathbf{y}_i - X_i\beta)\right]
\]
The unique solution is:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{GMM} = \left(X'Z\hat{W}Z'X\right)^{-1}X'Z\hat{W}Z'Y
\]
Under GMM1 to GMM3, this estimator is consistent for any positive definite \(W\). Letting \(C = \mathbb{E}[Z_i'X_i] = M_{ZX}\) and \(\Lambda = \mathbb{E}[Z_i'u_iu_i'Z_i]\), its asymptotic distribution is:
\[
\sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}_{GMM} - \beta\right) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, (C'WC)^{-1}C'W\Lambda WC(C'WC)^{-1}\right)
\]

title: Generalized Method of Moments Estimators
text:
The asymptotic variance above is minimized (in the positive semi-definite sense) when \(W = \Lambda^{-1}\). This gives the optimal GMM estimator:
\[
\sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}^{GMM*} - \beta\right) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, (C'\Lambda^{-1}C)^{-1}\right) = \mathcal{N}\left(0, \left(\mathbb{E}[Z_i'X_i]'\,\mathbb{E}[Z_i'u_iu_i'Z_i]^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}[Z_i'X_i]\right)^{-1}\right)
\]
To see that \(W = \Lambda^{-1}\) is optimal, note that for any positive definite \(W\):
\[
(C'WC)^{-1}C'W\Lambda WC(C'WC)^{-1} - (C'\Lambda^{-1}C)^{-1} \geq 0
\]
in the positive semi-definite sense, so \(\Lambda^{-1}\) yields the smallest asymptotic variance.

title: Generalized Method of Moments Estimators
text:
Since \(\Lambda = \mathbb{E}[Z_i'u_iu_i'Z_i]\) is unknown, the optimal estimator is implemented in two steps:

Step 1. Use \(\hat{W}_1 = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i Z_i'Z_i\right)^{-1}\) to compute the first-stage 2SLS estimator \(\hat{\beta}^{2SLS}\), and form residuals \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i = \mathbf{y}_i - X_i\hat{\beta}^{2SLS}\).
Step 2. Estimate \(\Lambda^{-1}\) using: \[
\hat{\Lambda}^{-1} = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i'Z_i\right)^{-1}
\] and compute the Feasible GMM (FGMM) estimator: \[
\hat{\beta}^{FGMM} = \left[\left(\sum_i X_i'Z_i\right)\hat{\Lambda}^{-1}\left(\sum_i Z_i'X_i\right)\right]^{-1}\left(\sum_i X_i'Z_i\right)\hat{\Lambda}^{-1}\left(\sum_i Z_i'\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]

This estimator is consistent and asymptotically equivalent to the infeasible optimal GMM. Its asymptotic variance is estimated by:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}^{FGMM}) = N\left[\left(\sum_i X_i'Z_i\right)\hat{\Lambda}^{-1}\left(\sum_i Z_i'X_i\right)\right]^{-1}
\]

title: Generalized Method of Moments Estimators
text:
When \(L > K\), we can test whether the additional \(r = L - K\) moment conditions (the overidentifying restrictions) are valid. The hypotheses are:
\[
H_0: \mathbb{E}[Z_i'\mathbf{u}_i] = 0 \quad \text{(all } L \text{ instruments valid)}
\] \[
H_1: \mathbb{E}[Z_i'\mathbf{u}_i] \neq 0 \quad \text{(some instruments invalid)}
\]
Under \(H_0\), the CLT gives \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_i Z_i'u_i \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbb{E}[Z_i'u_iu_i'Z_i])\). Using consistent estimates, the Sargan-Hansen test statistic is:
\[
S\left(\hat{\beta}_{GMM}\right) = \hat{\mathbf{u}}'Z\left(Z'\hat{\mathbf{u}}\hat{\mathbf{u}}'Z\right)^{-1}Z'\hat{\mathbf{u}} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{L-K} \quad \text{under } H_0
\]
where \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i = \mathbf{y}_i - X_i\hat{\beta}_{GMM}\) and \(L - K\) is the number of overidentifying restrictions.

Under homoskedasticity and no serial correlation, this is the Sargan statistic.
Under heteroskedastic or serially correlated errors, this is Hansen’s J statistic.

Rejection of \(H_0\) indicates at least one instrument fails the exclusion restriction. Note that in first-differences models, we replace \(\mathbf{u}\), \(y\), and \(X\) with \(\Delta\mathbf{u}\), \(\Delta y\), and \(\Delta X\) throughout.


When we wish to test whether a subset of instruments is valid, conditional on a baseline set of valid instruments being maintained, we use the C-statistic (difference-in-Sargan):

Let \(S_1\) be the Sargan-Hansen statistic using all \(r_1\) instruments.
Let \(S_0\) be the Sargan-Hansen statistic using only the restricted subset of \(r_0 < r_1\) instruments.

Then:
\[
C = S_1 - S_0 \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{r_1 - r_0} \quad \text{under } H_0
\]
The degrees of freedom equal the number of instruments being tested. A rejection implies that the additional instruments are not exogenous.

title: Arellano-Bond
text:
The Anderson-Hsiao estimator is consistent but uses at most one instrument per time period. For period \(t\), all lagged levels \(y_{i1}, y_{i2}, \ldots, y_{i,t-2}\) are valid instruments for \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\) under serially uncorrelated errors. Arellano and Bond (1991) propose exploiting all of these simultaneously in a GMM framework, yielding an estimator that is more efficient than Anderson-Hsiao.



Starting from the dynamic panel model:
\[
y_{it} = \alpha y_{i,t-1} + f_i + u_{it} \qquad i = 1, \ldots, N, \quad t = 1, \ldots, T
\]
First differencing to remove \(f_i\):
\[
\Delta y_{it} = \alpha \Delta y_{i,t-1} + \Delta u_{it}
\]
Under serially uncorrelated \(u_{it}\), the available orthogonality conditions for each period \(t\) are:
\[
E(y_{i,t-s} \cdot \Delta u_{it}) = 0 \quad \text{for } s \geq 2
\]



For each period \(t = 3, 4, \ldots, T\), there are \(t - 2\) valid instruments, giving a total of \(\frac{(T-2)(T-1)}{2}\) moment conditions. For \(T = 5\) as an example:







Period
Valid instruments




\(t = 3\)
\(E(y_{i1}\Delta u_{i3}) = 0\)


\(t = 4\)
\(E(y_{i1}\Delta u_{i4}) = 0\), \(\quad E(y_{i2}\Delta u_{i4}) = 0\)


\(t = 5\)
\(E(y_{i1}\Delta u_{i5}) = 0\), \(\quad E(y_{i2}\Delta u_{i5}) = 0\), \(\quad E(y_{i3}\Delta u_{i5}) = 0\)



These are organized into a block-diagonal instrument matrix \(Z_i\). For \(T = 5\):
\[
Z_i = \begin{bmatrix}
y_{i1} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & y_{i1} & y_{i2} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & y_{i1} & y_{i2} & y_{i3}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
where row \(t - 2\) (for \(t = 3, 4, 5\)) contains the valid lagged levels for that period. The stacked moment conditions are:
\[
E[Z_i'\Delta\mathbf{u}_i] = 0 \qquad \left(L \times 1\right), \quad L = \frac{(T-2)(T-1)}{2}
\]
In contrast, the Anderson-Hsiao estimator for the same \(T = 5\) panel uses only:
\[
Z_i^{AH} = \begin{bmatrix} y_{i1} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & y_{i2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & y_{i3} \end{bmatrix}
\]
exploiting just one instrument per period.



Since \(L > K\), we apply GMM. Let \(\Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}\) denote the vector of \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\) for \(t = 3, \ldots, T\).


The first-step weighting matrix uses the tridiagonal structure of \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta u_i \Delta u_i']\) under homoskedasticity and no serial correlation in \(u_{it}\):
\[
\hat{W}_1 = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i' H Z_i\right)^{-1}, \qquad H = D_T D_T' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & \cdots \\ -1 & 2 & -1 & \cdots \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & \cdots \\ \vdots & & & \ddots \end{bmatrix}
\]
where \(D_T\) is the \((T-1)\times T\) first-difference matrix. Under the homoskedasticity assumption, \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta u_i \Delta u_i'] = \sigma_u^2 H\), so \(\hat{W}_1\) is consistent for \(\Lambda^{-1}\) and the one-step estimator is already efficient. The one-step Arellano-Bond estimator is:
\[
\hat{\alpha}^{AB1} = \left[\left(\sum_i \Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}'Z_i\right)\hat{W}_1\left(\sum_i Z_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}\right)\right]^{-1}\left(\sum_i \Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}'Z_i\right)\hat{W}_1\left(\sum_i Z_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]



When homoskedasticity of \(u_{it}\) cannot be assumed, a second step improves efficiency. Using residuals from the first step \(\widehat{\Delta u}_i^{(1)} = \Delta\mathbf{y}_i - \hat{\alpha}^{AB1}\Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}\), we form:
\[
\hat{W}_2 = \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i'\widehat{\Delta u}_i^{(1)}\widehat{\Delta u}_i^{(1)'}Z_i\right)^{-1}
\]
The two-step Arellano-Bond estimator is:
\[
\hat{\alpha}^{AB2} = \left[\left(\sum_i \Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}'Z_i\right)\hat{W}_2\left(\sum_i Z_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}\right)\right]^{-1}\left(\sum_i \Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}'Z_i\right)\hat{W}_2\left(\sum_i Z_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]
Its asymptotic variance is consistently estimated by:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}\left(\hat{\alpha}^{AB2}\right) = \left[\left(\sum_i \Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}'Z_i\right)\left(\sum_i Z_i'\widehat{\Delta u}_i\widehat{\Delta u}_i'Z_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i Z_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_{i-}\right)\right]^{-1}
\]
\(\star\) Caution: FGMM estimators that use many overidentifying restrictions have poor finite-sample properties. In small samples, the two-step standard errors are typically biased downward relative to the true variance. The Windmeijer (2005) finite-sample correction is standard practice and addresses this bias.




The two-step Arellano-Bond estimator is:

Consistent: \(\hat{\alpha}^{AB2} \xrightarrow{p} \alpha\) as \(N \to \infty\) for fixed \(T\).
Asymptotically normal: \(\sqrt{N}(\hat{\alpha}^{AB2} - \alpha) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar})\).
Asymptotically efficient among GMM estimators using the \(L = \frac{(T-2)(T-1)}{2}\) moment conditions.






The validity of the \(r = L - K\) overidentifying restrictions is tested via:
\[
H_0: E[Z_i'\Delta\mathbf{u}_i] = 0 \qquad \text{(all instruments valid)}
\]
The test statistic is:
\[
S\left(\hat{\alpha}^{AB}\right) = \widehat{\Delta\mathbf{u}}'Z\left(Z'\widehat{\Delta\mathbf{u}}\widehat{\Delta\mathbf{u}}'Z\right)^{-1}Z'\widehat{\Delta\mathbf{u}} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{L-K} \quad \text{under } H_0
\]
Rejection implies at least one lagged level is not exogenous with respect to \(\Delta u_{it}\), i.e., the \(u_{it}\) are serially correlated at a lag that invalidates those instruments.



The moment conditions \(E[y_{i,t-2}\Delta u_{it}] = 0\) require \(u_{it}\) to be serially uncorrelated. Arellano and Bond propose directly testing for serial correlation in the first-differenced residuals \(\widehat{\Delta u}_{it}\):

\(m_1\) test: Tests for AR(1) in \(\widehat{\Delta u}_{it}\). Even when \(u_{it}\) is i.i.d., \(\Delta u_{it}\) and \(\Delta u_{i,t-1}\) share the \(u_{i,t-1}\) term, so \(\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\Delta u_{it}, \Delta u_{i,t-1}) = -\sigma_u^2 \neq 0\). A significant \(m_1\) is therefore expected and is not a concern on its own.
\(m_2\) test: Tests for AR(2) in \(\widehat{\Delta u}_{it}\). Under \(H_0\) that \(u_{it}\) is serially uncorrelated: \[
\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\Delta u_{it}, \Delta u_{i,t-2}) = \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(u_{it} - u_{i,t-1}, u_{i,t-2} - u_{i,t-3}) = 0
\] A significant \(m_2\) statistic indicates serial correlation in \(u_{it}\) itself, which invalidates \(y_{i,t-2}\) as an instrument (since \(y_{i,t-2}\) would then be correlated with \(u_{i,t-1}\) and hence with \(\Delta u_{it}\)). In that case, deeper lags (\(y_{i,t-3}\) or further) are required to restore validity.

title: Binary Choice Models
text:
We now want to consider models were our outcome variable takes on discrete values. For example, whether or not I decide to purchase a good at a store is a choice of \(m=2\) mutually exclusive categories, which can be modeled using a Bernoulli RV.
There are many such cases of this phenomena; perhaps our outcome variable can take \(m=j\) categories, such as the different choice of cities to vacation in. There even exists cases such that each category has a natural hierarchy structure, such that \(m=1\) is mild and \(m=10\) is extreme, and so forth. For now, we will begin by introducing the simplest of these cases in which we have two possible categories; i.e., where \(y_i\) can only take on two possible values.



In the case where our outcome variable \(y_i\) can only take on two values, we say that \(y \sim Bern\), such that:
\[
y =
\begin{cases}
  1 & \text{w/ Probability } p \\
  0 & \text{w/ Probability } (1-p)
\end{cases}
\]
When we take the unconditional expectation of a discrete random variable, we use the formula:
\[
\mathbb{E}[y] = \sum_{i=1}^m y_i \cdot \mathbb{P}(y_i)
\]
Since we have a binary model, we know that \(m=2\), such that:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[y] &= \sum_{i=1}^2 y_i \cdot \mathbb{P}(y_i) \\
&= y_i \mathbb{P}(y_i) + (1-y_i) (1-\mathbb{P}(y_i)) \\
&= 1 \mathbb{P}(y_i) + 0 (1-\mathbb{P}(y_i))  \\
&= \mathbb{P}(y_i)
\end{aligned}
\]
Similarly, for conditional expectations, we know that:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[y \mid x] &= \sum_{i=1}^2 y_i \cdot \mathbb{P}(y = i \mid x) \\
&= y_1 \mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid x) + (1-y_1) (1-\mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid x)) \\
&= 1 \cdot \mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid x) + 0 (1-\mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid x))  \\
&= \mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid x)
\end{aligned}
\]



In regression analysis, we write our model as:
\[
y_i = F(x_i,\beta) +\mu_i
\]
Where \(F(\cdot)\) is some function used to model the probability that \(y_i = 1 \mid x\). Our specification of \(F(\cdot)\) controls the characteristics of our binary choice models.
If we assumed that \(\mathbb{E}[\mu_i \mid x] = 0\) take conditional expectations of our model, we find the following relationship:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x] = F(x_i,\beta) + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\mu_i \mid x]}_{=0} \\
&\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x] = \mathbb{P}[y_i = 1 \mid x] = F(x_i,\beta)
\end{aligned}
\]


Suppose that we decide to give \(F(\cdot)\) a standard linear form, such that the regressors have a linear relationship with the outcome variable (think standard OLS model) After applying OLS, this is known as the Linear Probability Model.
\[
F(x_i,\beta) = x_i'\beta \quad \text{such that} \quad y_i = x_i'\beta + \mu_i
\] When we apply OLS, we get that:


\[
\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x] = \mathbb{P}[y_i = 1 \mid x] = x_i'\beta
\]



\[
\text{MEs:} \quad  \frac{\partial \mathbb{P}[y_i = 1 \mid x]}{\partial x_i} = \beta
\]




Although the LPM has nice interpretability such as the marginal effect simply being the beta coefficients, this is not a good choice to model our binary outcome variable. Specifically, there are three main reasons why linear modeling using OLS is a poor choice:

Discrete Variance of Errors

We know that \(y_i\) can take on values of either \(0\) or \(1\); this implies there exists two possible values for the errors:
(i). \(y_i = 1: \mu_i = 1 - x_i'\beta\) with probability \(x_i'\beta\) (ii). \(y_i = 0: \mu_i = - x_i'\beta\) with probability \(1 - x_i'\beta\)
This implies that the error term is a discrete random variable, only able to take on two values.

Unbounded Probability

We know that by definition, \(0 \leq \mathbb{P}[y_i =1 \mid x] \leq 1\); yet, we find that \(\mathbb{P}[y_i =1 \mid x] = x_i'\beta \in (-\infty, +\infty)\). Thus, we have an issue that our probabilities are bounded, yet our fitted values can lead to predictions outside of the \([0,1]\) range. This can lead to negative predicted probabilities and probabilities above 1, which are meaningless in this model.

Heteroskedastic Errors

The issue with the error term from (1) is that the variance of the error terms assume a heteroskedastic structure. To see this:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{V}\text{ar}( \mu_i \mid x) &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_i^2 \mid x] - \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\mu_i \mid x]^2}_\text{=0}  \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(\mu_i = -x_i'\beta)^2 \mid x ] \mathbb{P}[\mu_i = -x_i'\beta \mid x] + \mathbb{E}[(\mu_i = 1-x_i'\beta)^2 \mid x ] \mathbb{P}[\mu_i = 1-x_i'\beta \mid x]   \\
  &= (-x_i'\beta)^2(1-p_i) + (1 - x_i'\beta)^2 (p_i) \\
  &= (-x_i'\beta)^2(1-x_i'\beta) + (1-x_i'\beta)^2(x_i'\beta)\\
  &= (x_i'\beta)(1-x_i'\beta) \\
  &= \mathbb{P}[y_i = 1 \mid x] \mathbb{P}[y_i = 0 \mid x]
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, the variance of the \(\mu_i\) depends on the \(x_i'\beta\); in other words, if \(p_i\) is large, then the variance of the errors is tiny. If \(p_i \approx 0.5\), the variance of the errors is large. This means the variance is non-constant across observations.




The goal is to constrain the outcome \(F(x_i,\beta) \in [0,1]\). To do so, we seek to construct a “single index model” such that \(F(\cdot)\) maps the single index \(x_i'\beta\) to \(y_i\). The most popular models use the form:
\[
\mathbb{P}[y_i = 1 \mid x] = F(x_i'\beta)
\]
Where \(F(\cdot)\) is chosen as some cumulative distribution function; our choice of this distribution deteremines the properties of our model.
The two most popular choices are Logit and Probit.



\[
F(x_i'\beta) = \Lambda(x_i'\beta) = \frac{\exp(x_i'\beta)}{1 + \exp(x_i'\beta)}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
& F(x_i'\beta) = \Phi(x_i'\beta) = \int_{-\infty}^{x_i'\beta} \phi(t)dt \\
& \text{where } \phi(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}e^{(\frac{-t^2}{2})}
\end{aligned}
\]


Both models are very similar in shape, however logit has slightly fatter tails. Both are monotone and increasing functions of \(x_i'\beta\); thus, whenever \(\uparrow \beta, \uparrow F(x_i'\beta)\).
However, since both models are no longer linear in \(\beta\), we cannot use OLS. Instead, we must use maximum likelihood as our estimators.

title: Binary Choice Models
text:
We now want to consider models were our outcome variable takes on discrete values. For example, whether or not I decide to purchase a good at a store is a choice of \(m=2\) mutually exclusive categories, which can be modeled using a Bernoulli RV.
There are many such cases of this phenomena; perhaps our outcome variable can take \(m=j\) categories, such as the different choice of cities to vacation in. There even exists cases such that each category has a natural hierarchy structure, such that \(m=1\) is mild and \(m=10\) is extreme, and so forth. For now, we will begin by introducing the simplest of these cases in which we have two possible categories; i.e., where \(y_i\) can only take on two possible values.

title: Binary Choice Models
text:
In the case where our outcome variable \(y_i\) can only take on two values, we say that \(y \sim Bern\), such that:

\begin{cases}

\end{cases}
\]

\]

&= 1 \mathbb{P}(y_i) + 0 (1-\mathbb{P}(y_i))  \\
&= \mathbb{P}(y_i)
\end{aligned}

\end{aligned}

title: Nested Models
Nested Models
text:
Recall that from our multinomial models that they only hold under the IID alternatives assumption; this tells us that alternatives are completely independent of each other, each being drawn randomly with equal chance. Of course, we can think of immediate examples that would violate this assumption: cities such as Barcelona and Madrid are likely correlated; they share similar characteristics in language, culture, food, etc. Thus, deciding to move to one of these cities is surely influenced by each cities’ similarities.
Indirectly, this IID assumption leads to the “Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives” assumption, derived from the fact that relative probabilities for any two alternatives depend only on the attributes of those two alternatives. This implies that adding another alternative or changing the characteristics of a third does not affect the relative odds between any two alternatives \(j\) and \(\ell\).

title: Nested Models
Nested Models
text:
Similar motivations and logic as Nested Logit, with the only different being the form of the error distribution. As with regular probit regression, we assumed the errors to follow a normal distribution; more formally,
\[\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)\]
Where \(\varepsilon\) is a \((mx1)\) matrix, and
\[
\Sigma =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
    - & - \\
    - & -
  \end{bmatrix} & 0 \\
  0 & \begin{bmatrix}
    - & - \\
    - & -
  \end{bmatrix}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Such that the variance of the errors allows for a nesting structure: errors amongst same-branch observations are allowed to be correlated (diagonal), but NOT across limbs (off-diagonal). This is very similar to the clustering standard errors from the heteroskedasticity relaxation from our random/fixed effects models.
Issue: Multinomial Probit choice probability does not have a closed-form solution; for an \(m\) choice problem, we have to solve for a \(m-1\) fold integral; computationally very expensive as we move beyond 5 or so alternatives.

title: Tobit Model
text:
When working with panel or cross-sectional data, we often encounter situations where data is incompletely observed. It is crucial to distinguish between two types:



Censored Data: Information is lost on the dependent variable (\(y\)), but we have full information on the regressors (\(x\)) for the entire sample.

Example: Income surveys where high earners are recorded simply as “$100k+”. We know their age, education, etc., but their exact income is “right-censored.”
Key Feature: We have a representative sample of the population, but the outcome value is “stuck” at a threshold for some.

Truncated Data: We do not have the full sample. Data is lost on both the dependent variable and the regressors because the observation rule depends on \(y\).

Example: Studying determinants of poverty but only sampling people below the poverty line. We completely lack data (both \(y\) and \(x\)) for anyone above the line.
Key Feature: The sample is a non-representative sub-sample of the population.







To model these processes, we assume there is an underlying “Latent Variable” \(y^*\) that satisfies the classical linear assumptions:
\[
y_i^* = x_i' \beta + \varepsilon_i
\]
However, \(y^*\) is not perfectly observed.


1. Censoring from Below (Left-Censoring)
We observe \(y_i\) based on a threshold \(L\):
\[
y_i = \begin{cases}
y_i^* & \text{if } y_i^* > L \\
L & \text{if } y_i^* \leq L
\end{cases}
\]
Result: A “spike” (mass point) in the distribution of \(y\) at \(L\).
2. Censoring from Above (Right-Censoring)
\[
y_i = \begin{cases}
y_i^* & \text{if } y_i^* < U \\
U & \text{if } y_i^* \geq U
\end{cases}
\]
3. Truncation from Below
We only observe unit \(i\) if \(y_i^* > L\).
\[
\text{Sample Rule: Keep } i \text{ if } y_i^* > L
\]
Result: The distribution is “cut off.” The area under the curve must sum to 1, so the remaining probability density is scaled up.




If we run a standard OLS regression (\(y\) on \(x\)) using censored data, our estimates will be biased.


At low values of \(x\), many observations hit the lower bound \(L\). This flattens the slope of the observed relationship relative to the true latent relationship.



The expected value of the observed data is:
\[
E[y|x] = P(y^* \le L) \cdot L + P(y^* > L) \cdot E[y^* | y^* > L, x]
\]
This relationship is non-linear.

At high \(x\), \(E[y|x] \approx E[y^*|x]\) (convergence to true slope).
At low \(x\), data piles up at \(L\), dragging the expectation line flat.
Consequence: OLS will generally underestimate the slope coefficient \(\beta\).






Since OLS is inconsistent, we must use Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). We need to make parametric assumptions (usually Normality) about the error term: \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\).


The density of observed \(y\) is a mixture of a continuous part and a discrete probability mass.

Continuous part (\(y_i > L\)): We observe the actual value. The likelihood contribution is the PDF: \(f^*(y_i | x_i)\).
Censored part (\(y_i = L\)): We know only that \(y^* \le L\). The likelihood contribution is the probability (CDF): \(F^*(L | x_i)\).

We define a dummy indicator \(d_i\):
\[
d_i = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } y_i > L \quad (\text{Uncensored}) \\
0 & \text{if } y_i = L \quad (\text{Censored})
\end{cases}
\]
The Log-Likelihood Function:
\[
\ell(\beta, \sigma^2) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ d_i \ln \left( \frac{1}{\sigma} \Phi\left(\frac{y_i - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) \right) + (1-d_i) \ln \Phi\left(\frac{L - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) \right]
\]



Here, we do not observe anyone with \(y^* \le L\). We must re-normalize the probability density so it integrates to 1 over the range \((L, \infty)\).
\[
f(y_i | y_i > L, x_i) = \frac{f^*(y_i|x_i)}{P(y_i > L | x_i)} = \frac{\frac{1}{\sigma}\phi(\frac{y_i - x_i'\beta}{\sigma})}{1 - \Phi(\frac{L - x_i'\beta}{\sigma})}
\]
The Log-Likelihood Function:
\[
\ell = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ \ln \left( \frac{1}{\sigma}\Phi(\cdot) \right) - \ln \left( 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{L - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) \right) \right]
\]
Intuition: In the truncated case, the denominator \(1 - \Phi(\cdot)\) essentially tells the model: “Hey, we are missing the left tail of the bell curve, so inflate the probabilities of the data we do see to account for that missing mass.”




The Tobit model is the specific and most common case of censored regression where the threshold is zero (\(L=0\)) and censoring is from below.



Latent Variable: \(y_i^* = x_i'\beta + \varepsilon_i\), with \(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\).
Observation Rule:

\[
y_i = \max(0, y_i^*)
\]



A classic example is hours worked (\(H_i\)).

\(H_i^*\): Desired hours (latent utility). A person might desire “-5 hours” of work (meaning they need a high wage just to start working).
\(H_i\): Actual observed hours. Since you can’t work negative hours, we observe 0.




We split the sample into those working (\(H_i > 0\)) and those not working (\(H_i = 0\)).

For \(H_i > 0\) (Uncensored): Contribution is the density of the normal distribution:

\[
\frac{1}{\sigma} \Phi\left(\frac{y_i - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)
\]

For \(H_i = 0\) (Censored): Contribution is the probability that latent utility is negative:

\[
\mathbb{P}(y_i^* \le 0) = \mathbb{P}\left(\frac{y_i^* - x_i'\beta}{\sigma} \le \frac{-x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) = \Phi\left(-\frac{x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) = 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)
\]
Combined Log-Likelihood:
\[
\ell(\beta, \sigma) = \sum_{y_i = 0} \ln \left[ 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) \right] + \sum_{y_i > 0} \ln \left[ \frac{1}{\sigma} \phi\left(\frac{y_i - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) \right]
\]




Ideally, we estimate \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\) separately.
However, if there is high multicollinearity or little variation in the censored portion, it can be difficult to disentangle \(\beta\) from \(\sigma\).
Homoskedasticity Assumption: Crucial for Tobit. If \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon)\) varies with \(x\), the Tobit estimates are inconsistent (unlike OLS, where heteroskedasticity only affects standard errors).




In Tobit, there are two different marginal effects of interest:

Effect on the Latent Variable:

\[
\frac{\partial E[y^*|x]}{\partial x_k} = \beta_k
\]
Interpretation: How a change in \(x\) changes “desired” hours.

Effect on the Observed Variable:

\[
\frac{\partial E[y|x]}{\partial x_k} = \beta_k \cdot \Phi\left(\frac{x'\beta}{\sigma}\right)
\]
Interpretation: How a change in \(x\) changes actual hours worked.
Note: The effect on actual hours is always smaller than the effect on desired hours because \(0 \le \Phi(\cdot) \le 1\). This dampening factor \(\Phi\) represents the probability of being uncensored (actually working).
