Intuition: In the truncated case, the denominator \(1 - \Phi(\cdot)\) essentially tells the model: “Hey, we are missing the left tail of the bell curve, so inflate the probabilities of the data we do see to account for that missing mass.”

title: Tobit Model
text:
The Tobit model is the specific and most common case of censored regression where the threshold is zero (\(L=0\)) and censoring is from below.



Latent Variable: \(y_i^* = x_i'\beta + \varepsilon_i\), with \(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\).
Observation Rule:

\[
y_i = \max(0, y_i^*)
\]



A classic example is hours worked (\(H_i\)).

\(H_i^*\): Desired hours (latent utility). A person might desire “-5 hours” of work (meaning they need a high wage just to start working).
\(H_i\): Actual observed hours. Since you can’t work negative hours, we observe 0.




We split the sample into those working (\(H_i > 0\)) and those not working (\(H_i = 0\)).

For \(H_i > 0\) (Uncensored): Contribution is the density of the normal distribution:

\[
\frac{1}{\sigma} \Phi\left(\frac{y_i - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)
\]

For \(H_i = 0\) (Censored): Contribution is the probability that latent utility is negative:

\[
\mathbb{P}(y_i^* \le 0) = \mathbb{P}\left(\frac{y_i^* - x_i'\beta}{\sigma} \le \frac{-x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) = \Phi\left(-\frac{x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) = 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)
\]
Combined Log-Likelihood:
\[
\ell(\beta, \sigma) = \sum_{y_i = 0} \ln \left[ 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) \right] + \sum_{y_i > 0} \ln \left[ \frac{1}{\sigma} \phi\left(\frac{y_i - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) \right]
\]




Ideally, we estimate \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\) separately.
However, if there is high multicollinearity or little variation in the censored portion, it can be difficult to disentangle \(\beta\) from \(\sigma\).
Homoskedasticity Assumption: Crucial for Tobit. If \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon)\) varies with \(x\), the Tobit estimates are inconsistent (unlike OLS, where heteroskedasticity only affects standard errors).




In Tobit, there are two different marginal effects of interest:

Effect on the Latent Variable:

\[
\frac{\partial E[y^*|x]}{\partial x_k} = \beta_k
\]
Interpretation: How a change in \(x\) changes “desired” hours.

Effect on the Observed Variable:

\[
\frac{\partial E[y|x]}{\partial x_k} = \beta_k \cdot \Phi\left(\frac{x'\beta}{\sigma}\right)
\]
Interpretation: How a change in \(x\) changes actual hours worked.
Note: The effect on actual hours is always smaller than the effect on desired hours because \(0 \le \Phi(\cdot) \le 1\). This dampening factor \(\Phi\) represents the probability of being uncensored (actually working).

title: Intro to Causal Inference
text:
Causal inference is the process of drawing a conclusion about a cause-effect relationship between economic variables. It aims to provide credible quantitative answers to questions such as:

What is the impact of a deworming treatment for children on their long-term health and economic outcomes?
What is the impact of an extension of unemployment benefits on unemployment durations?
What is the impact of early childcare on children’s cognitive development and parents’ labor market participation?

The classic structural approach uses theory-based models of individual choice to conduct ex-ante and ex-post policy evaluation. The treatment effect approach has established itself as a key methodology for policy evaluation and the estimation of causal effects.
The main goal is to evaluate ex-post the impact of an existing policy by comparing the distribution of a chosen outcome among affected individuals (the “treatment group”) with the distribution among unaffected individuals (the “control group”).
The main challenge is to find a way to perform the comparison such that the distribution of outcomes for the control group serves as a good counterfactual for the distribution of outcomes in the treatment group in the absence of the treatment.
The main advantage relative to the structural approach is that it provides transparent and credible identification of the policy parameters of interest and does not rely on untestable functional form assumptions.
The main disadvantage is that the estimated parameters are “reduced forms” and are therefore only internally valid. They are generally not useful for welfare analysis and cannot be easily applied to different settings.
For a treatment effects analysis that aims at estimating causal effects, there are four crucial questions:

What is the causal relationship of interest?
What experiment could ideally be used to capture the causal effect of interest?
What is the identification strategy?
What is the method of inference? (the population studied, the sample used, the assumptions when constructing standard errors)




The fundamental problem of causal inference is that we can never observe a person’s counterfactual outcomes. We can never know what a person’s outcome would have been if her treatment had been different. Different empirical methods deal with the problem of the “missing counterfactual” by finding suitable control groups that can mimic such counterfactual situations. These methods include:

Randomized Controlled Trials
Regression Discontinuity Designs
Selection on Observables and Matching
Difference-in-Differences
Synthetic Control Methods

Each of these methods relies on different assumptions and identifies different types of causal policy parameters.



To formally study causal effects, we adopt the potential outcomes framework, also known as the Rubin Causal Model (RCM). Let \(Y_{1i}\) denote the outcome for individual \(i\) if exposed to the treatment (\(D_i = 1\)), and \(Y_{0i}\) the outcome for the same individual if not exposed (\(D_i = 0\)). The treatment effect for individual \(i\) is \(Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}\).
Since we only observe one of the two potential outcomes, the observed outcome is:
\[
Y_i = Y_{1i}D_i + Y_{0i}(1-D_i) = Y_{0i} + D_i(Y_{1i} - Y_{0i})
\]


Since individual-level treatment effects cannot be estimated, we focus on two population parameters. The average treatment effect (ATE):
\[
\alpha_{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}]
\]
and the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT):
\[
\alpha_{ATT} = \mathbb{E}[Y_{1i} - Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1]
\]
The ATE is the average treatment effect for the whole population. The ATT is the average treatment effect among the group of individuals that actually experienced the treatment.



Let \(\beta\) denote the naive difference in expected outcomes between treated and untreated individuals:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta &\equiv \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0] \\
&= \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y_{1i} - Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1]}_{\alpha_{ATT}} + \underbrace{(\mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 0])}_{\text{selection bias}}
\end{aligned}
\]
The second term is the selection bias: the difference in untreated potential outcomes between treated and untreated individuals. This is nonzero whenever, for instance, individuals with low \(Y_{0i}\) choose treatment more frequently than those with high \(Y_{0i}\). A simple comparison of average outcomes between treatment and control groups will generally not identify the ATT.
The sample analogs for \(\alpha_{ATE}\) and \(\alpha_{ATT}\) require observing both potential outcomes, which is infeasible. The sample analog of \(\beta\) is simply:
\[
\beta^S = \bar{Y}_T - \bar{Y}_C = \frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i D_i - \frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i=1}^N (1-D_i)Y_i
\]
where \(N_1 = \sum D_i\) and \(N_0 = N - N_1\).



Implicit in the potential outcomes framework is an important assumption maintained throughout: the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA).
SUTVA: the outcome of individual \(i\) depends only on the treatment of individual \(i\) and not on the treatments of other individuals.
SUTVA is a strong assumption as it rules out equilibrium or feedback effects as well as strategic interactions among agents. As a result, the potential outcomes framework is not well-suited to the evaluation of system-wide reforms that are likely to have substantial equilibrium effects.






The easiest case is when the distribution of potential outcomes is independent of the treatment:
\[
(Y_{1i}, Y_{0i}) \perp D_i
\]
This situation is typical in randomized experiments, where individuals are assigned to treatment or control groups randomly. In this case, \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 0]\), so the selection bias vanishes and \(\alpha_{ATE} = \alpha_{ATT} = \beta\). An unbiased estimate of \(\alpha_{ATE}\) is:
\[
\hat{\alpha}_{ATE} = \bar{Y}_T - \bar{Y}_C = \beta^S
\]



A less restrictive assumption is conditional independence:
\[
(Y_{1i}, Y_{0i}) \perp D_i \mid X_i
\]
where \(X_i\) is a vector of covariates. This is the basis for matching: for each “type” of individual (each value of covariates) we can match treated and control individuals, so that the latter act as counterfactuals for the former. Conditional independence implies:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_{ATE} &= \mathbb{E}[Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}] = \int \left(\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1, X_i] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0, X_i]\right) dF(X_i)
\end{aligned}
\]
Similarly, the ATT integrates over the distribution of \(X_i\) among the treated.



When conditional independence fails, we need an instrument \(Z_i\) that provides exogenous variation in the treatment:
\[
(Y_{1i}, Y_{0i}) \perp Z_i \mid X_i \qquad \text{and} \qquad \text{Cov}(Z_i, D_i \mid X_i) \neq 0
\]
In this context we can only identify an average treatment effect for a subgroup of individuals; the resulting parameter is the local average treatment effect, \(\alpha_{LATE}\).






Rearranging the potential outcomes equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_i &= Y_{0i} + D_i(Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}) \\
&= \mathbb{E}(Y_{0i}) + (Y_{1i} - Y_{0i})D_i + (Y_{0i} - \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i}]) \\
&\equiv \beta_0 + \beta_i D_i + U_i
\end{aligned}
\]
Assume initially that \(\beta_i = \beta\) for all \(i\) (homogeneous treatment effects). Then \(\beta\) is the coefficient in a linear regression of \(Y_i\) on \(D_i\), \(Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}\) is a constant, and \(\alpha_{ATE} = \alpha_{ATT} = \beta\). Consistently estimating \(\beta\) requires that \(U_i = Y_{0i} - \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i}]\) is independent of \(D_i\), i.e. no selection bias.



When \(\beta_i\) is not constant (heterogeneous treatment effects), the OLS estimator from the regression \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \check{\beta} D_i + U_i\) converges to:
\[
\check{\beta} = \mathbb{E}[Y_{1i} - Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1] + (\mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 0]) = \alpha_{ATT} + \text{selection bias}
\]
In the absence of selection bias (e.g. under random assignment), a linear regression of \(Y_i\) on \(D_i\) identifies the ATT. Under random assignment, \(\alpha_{ATE} = \alpha_{ATT}\).






Consider the true data generating process:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + X_i'\beta_1 + W_i'\gamma + U_i \qquad \text{where} \quad \mathbb{E}[U_i \mid X_i, W_i] = 0
\]
Suppose we exclude \(W_i\) and estimate the short regression \(Y_i = \beta_0 + X_i'\beta_1 + \tilde{U}_i\), where \(\tilde{U}_i = W_i'\gamma + U_i\). For the case where both \(X\) and \(W\) are one-dimensional:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_1^S = \beta_1 + \gamma \frac{\text{Cov}(W_i, X_i)}{\text{Var}(X_i)}
\]
The second term is the omitted variable bias. For there to be OVB, the omitted variable \(W_i\) must be both correlated with the included variable \(X_i\) and a determinant of \(Y_i\) (i.e. \(\gamma \neq 0\)). The sign and magnitude of the bias depends on the sign and magnitude of \(\text{Cov}(W_i, X_i)\) and how important \(W_i\) is in determining \(Y_i\).



Suppose \(Y_i\) causes \(X_i\), but we are interested in the causal effect of \(X_i\) on \(Y_i\). If the true relationships are:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + U_i \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_i = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 Y_i + V_i
\]
with \(\text{Cov}(V_i, U_i) = 0\), then OLS estimation of the outcome equation yields:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_1^S = \beta_1 + \frac{\gamma_1}{1 - \gamma_1\beta_1}\frac{\text{Var}(U_i)}{\text{Var}(X_i)}
\]
which is only consistent for \(\beta_1\) if \(\gamma_1 = 0\). Addressing reverse causality requires exogenous variation in \(X_i\), either through random assignment or a suitable instrumental variable that shifts \(X_i\) but has no direct impact on \(Y_i\).



Suppose the true model is \(Y_i^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i^* + U_i\) with \(\text{Cov}(U_i, X_i^*) = 0\), but we only observe \(X_i = X_i^* + \mu_i\), where \(\mu_i\) is uncorrelated with \(X_i^*\) (classical measurement error). Then:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1 \left(\frac{\text{Var}(X_i^*)}{\text{Var}(X_i^*) + \text{Var}(\mu_i)}\right)
\]
Since the term in parentheses is between 0 and 1, classical measurement error in the regressor produces attenuation bias towards zero. If the signal-to-noise ratio \(\text{Var}(X_i^*)/\text{Var}(\mu_i)\) is very small, the slope estimate will be close to zero.
Note that attenuation bias is not a general result: it depends on the specific structure of the measurement error. If measurement error is in the outcome \(Y_i^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i^* + (U_i + \mu_i)\), consistency is unaffected (the variance of the estimate increases but the estimate remains consistent).

title: Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
Natural or quasi-experiments try to mimic the situation of randomized controlled trials by exploiting variation that is arguably as good as randomly assigned. A special case arises when assignment to treatment is based on a cutoff in an observable variable.
The key ingredients of a regression discontinuity design (RDD) are: at least one observable covariate (the “running” or “assignment” variable) and at least one cutoff that determines assignment to treatment. The key intuition is that units just below and just above the cutoff should be similar in all respects except treatment status. Hence, differences in outcomes at the cutoff can be attributed to the treatment.
RD designs come in two varieties:

Sharp RD (SRD): treatment status is a deterministic function of the assignment variable at the cutoff. \(D_i = \mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c]\).
Fuzzy RD (FRD): treatment status is a discontinuous stochastic function of the assignment variable at the cutoff. Crossing the cutoff makes it more likely that the unit is treated, but the jump in \(P(D_i = 1)\) is not from 0 to 1. This is analogous to imperfect compliance in an RCT, with cutoff crossing \(Z_i = \mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c]\) serving as the instrument for \(D_i\).




Define the following notation:

\(Y_i\): outcome
\(X_i\): assignment (running) variable
\(D_i = \mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c]\): binary treatment status
\(\beta_i\): individual treatment effect
\(c\): cutoff
\(U_i\): unobservables, other factors that affect \(Y_i\)

We make two assumptions:
A1. Homogeneous treatment effect: \(\beta_i = \beta_D\)
A2. Continuity: \(\mathbb{E}[U_i \mid X_i = x]\) is continuous in \(x\)
Under A1 and A2, the RD gap identifies \(\beta_D\). To see this, write the linear regression model \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_D D_i + \delta X_i + U_i\). Then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] \\
&= \lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_D D_i + \delta X_i + U_i \mid X_i = x) - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_D D_i + \delta X_i + U_i \mid X_i = x) \\
&= \beta_D + \delta c + \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid X_i = c) - \beta_D \cdot 0 - \delta c - \lim_{x \uparrow c}\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid X_i = x) \\
&= \beta_D
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality uses A2. Without A1 (heterogeneous effects), the RD gap identifies the conditional average treatment effect at the cutoff:
\[
\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid X_i = c)
\]
Note that under A2, \(\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid X_i = c, D_i = 0) = \mathbb{E}(U_i \mid X_i = c, D_i = 1)\), so \(U_i\) is mean-independent of \(D_i\) at \(c\). This means we can test A2 indirectly by checking whether observed covariates \(W_i\) satisfy \(\mathbb{E}(W_i \mid X_i = x)\) continuous at \(c\) – analogous to balance checks in RCTs.


A2 is implied by an alternative assumption A2’ (imprecise control): \(P(X_i = x \mid U_i = u)\) is continuous in \(x\) for all \(u\). This states that the density of \(X_i\) must be smooth for all “types” of agents. It allows for different agents to have different levels of control over \(X_i\), as long as none of them can control \(X_i\) completely or make sure it is always above the cutoff. Under A2’, A2 follows from Bayes’ rule:
\[
\mathbb{E}(U_i \mid X_i = x) = \sum_u \frac{P(X_i = x \mid U_i = u)P(U_i = u)}{\sum_u P(X_i = x \mid U_i = u) P(U_i = u)} u
\]
A practical implication of A2’ is that the density of the running variable should be smooth at the cutoff. A manipulation test (McCrary density test) checks for a discontinuity in the density of \(X_i\) at \(c\).




RDD estimates are local: they identify treatment effects only for units with \(X_i \approx c\). In the absence of additional assumptions, they are not informative about treatment effects at other values of the score. This is a fundamental external validity limitation of the design.





When treatment status is influenced by factors beyond \(X_i\), so \(D_i \neq \mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c]\), there must be a first stage: a discontinuity in the likelihood of treatment at the cutoff.
A3. First stage: \(\lim_{x \downarrow c} P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x) - \lim_{x \uparrow c} P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i = x) > 0\)
A4. Exclusion restriction: \(\beta_Z = 0\) (crossing the cutoff affects outcomes only through treatment, not directly)
The data generating process is:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_D D_i + \delta X_i + \beta_Z Z_i + U_i \qquad D_i = \pi_0 + \pi_Z Z_i + \pi_X X_i + V_i
\]
Under A1-A4, the ratio of RD gaps in \(Y_i\) and \(D_i\) at the cutoff identifies \(\beta_D\):
\[
\frac{\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x]}{\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x]} = \beta_D
\]
Proof: The numerator (reduced form / ITT at the cutoff):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] \\
&= \beta_D [E(D_i \mid X_i = c^+) - E(D_i \mid X_i = c^-)] + \beta_Z \quad \text{under A1, A2} \\
&= \beta_D \pi_Z + \beta_Z \\
&= \beta_D \pi_Z \quad \text{under A4}
\end{aligned}
\]
Dividing by the first stage \(\pi_Z\) gives \(\beta_D\). \(\blacksquare\)
The RD gap in \(Y_i\) alone (the reduced form) is also referred to as the intention-to-treat effect at the cutoff. It does not depend on the validity of the exclusion restriction and is sometimes policy-relevant in its own right.



Once we drop A1 and allow for heterogeneous effects \(\beta_i\) and heterogeneous compliance \(\pi_i\), the data generating process is:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_i D_i + \delta X_i + \beta_Z Z_i + U_i \qquad D_i = \pi_0 + \pi_i Z_i + \pi_X X_i + V_i
\]
Under A2-A4 with no cross-overs (one-sided non-compliance), the ratio of reduced forms identifies the ATT at the cutoff:
\[
\frac{\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x]}{\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x]} = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_i = 1, X_i = c)
\]
Under A2-A4 with two-sided non-compliance, the ratio identifies a weighted average treatment effect at the cutoff:
\[
\frac{\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x]}{\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x]} = \mathbb{E}\left(\beta_i \frac{\pi_i}{\mathbb{E}(\pi_i)} \,\Big|\, X_i = c\right)
\]
Under A2-A5 (monotonicity: \(P(\pi_i = -1 \mid X_i = c) = 0\), ruling out defiers at the cutoff), the ratio identifies the local average treatment effect (LATE) for compliers at the cutoff:
\[
\frac{\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x]}{\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x]} = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid X_i = c, \pi_i = 1)
\]
The proportion of compliers at the cutoff is given by the first stage: \(P(\pi_i = 1 \mid X_i = c) = \lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x]\).




The RD estimand is the gap in \(Y_i\) at the cutoff:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{SRD} = \lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] = \mu_+ - \mu_-
\]
In practice there are often few observations right around the cutoff. A natural solution is to include observations further away and fit a local polynomial on each side. The pooled specification within a \(\pm h\) bandwidth is:
\[
Y_i = \mu_- + (\mu_+ - \mu_-)\mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c] + \mu_{-,1}(X_i - c) + (\mu_{+,1} - \mu_{-,1})(X_i - c)\mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c] + U_i'
\]
The coefficient on \(\mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c]\) is the RD point estimate \(\hat{\mu}_+ - \hat{\mu}_-\).


While the true regression function might be approximately linear close to the cutoff, a larger bandwidth \(h\) makes it more likely that the function exhibits curvature. Local polynomial methods implement polynomial regression fits using only observations near the cutoff, within a bandwidth \(h\):
For observations with \(X_i \geq c\):
\[
Y_i = \mu_+ + \mu_{+,1}(X_i - c) + \mu_{+,2}(X_i - c)^2 + \ldots + \mu_{+,p}(X_i - c)^p + \varepsilon_i
\]
using \(K\!\left(\frac{X_i - c}{h}\right)\) as a weight for each observation. Symmetrically for \(X_i < c\). The intercept estimates \(\hat{\mu}_+\) and \(\hat{\mu}_-\) are estimates of \(\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x]\) and \(\lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x]\).
The three key choices are:

Kernel function \(K(\cdot)\): assigns non-negative weights based on distance to \(c\). The recommended choice is the triangular kernel \(K(u) = (1-|u|)\mathbf{1}(|u| \leq 1)\), which assigns maximum weight at \(X_i = c\) and declines linearly. In practice results are not sensitive to the kernel choice.
Bandwidth \(h\): controls the width of the neighborhood. Smaller \(h\) reduces misspecification bias but increases variance (fewer observations). There is a fundamental bias-variance trade-off. The optimal bandwidth minimizes the asymptotic MSE:

\[
AMSE_{\hat{\tau}_p}(h) = \underbrace{h^{2(p+1)} B_p^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{nh} V_p}_{\text{Variance}}
\]
The optimal bandwidth is:
\[
h_{opt} = \left(\frac{V_p}{2(p+1)B_p^2}\right)^{1/(2p+3)} \cdot n^{-1/(2p+3)}
\]
The Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014) procedure estimates \(h_{opt}\) by estimating the unknown bias \(B_p\) using a local polynomial of order \(q = p+1\) with a pilot bandwidth \(b\).

Polynomial order \(p\): higher order reduces bias for a given bandwidth but increases variance. The AMSE formula can be used to select the optimal order.




Since the optimal bandwidth is chosen to minimize AMSE, there is a residual bias term \(\mathcal{B}\) that should be accounted for in inference. The robust bias-corrected confidence interval is:
\[
\text{CI}_{rbc} = \left[(\hat{\tau} - \hat{\mathcal{B}}) \pm 1.96 \cdot \sqrt{\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{bc}}\right]
\]
where \(\hat{\mathcal{B}}\) is the estimated bias and \(\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{bc}\) is a bias-corrected variance estimator (larger than the conventional standard error to account for the variability of \(\hat{\mathcal{B}}\)).




In fuzzy RDD, we additionally need to estimate the RD gap in \(D_i\):
\[
\lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[D_i \mid X_i = x] = \alpha_+ - \alpha_-
\]

\[

\]
The fuzzy RD point estimate is the ratio:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{FRD} = \frac{\hat{\mu}_+ - \hat{\mu}_-}{\hat{\alpha}_+ - \hat{\alpha}_-}
\]
In practice, the LATE estimate is obtained by using the IV estimator, instrumenting \(D_i\) with \(Z_i = \mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c]\) and including \((X_i - c)\) and \((X_i - c)\mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c]\) as regressors within the bandwidth.
The recommended procedure is to use robust local polynomial methods, analogous to the sharp RD setting. Optimal bandwidth selection for the LATE typically relies on a single bandwidth for both numerator and denominator.

title: Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
Natural or quasi-experiments try to mimic the situation of randomized controlled trials by exploiting variation that is arguably as good as randomly assigned. A special case arises when assignment to treatment is based on a cutoff in an observable variable.
The key ingredients of a regression discontinuity design (RDD) are: at least one observable covariate (the “running” or “assignment” variable) and at least one cutoff that determines assignment to treatment. The key intuition is that units just below and just above the cutoff should be similar in all respects except treatment status. Hence, differences in outcomes at the cutoff can be attributed to the treatment.
RD designs come in two varieties:

Sharp RD (SRD): treatment status is a deterministic function of the assignment variable at the cutoff. \(D_i = \mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c]\).
Fuzzy RD (FRD): treatment status is a discontinuous stochastic function of the assignment variable at the cutoff. Crossing the cutoff makes it more likely that the unit is treated, but the jump in \(P(D_i = 1)\) is not from 0 to 1. This is analogous to imperfect compliance in an RCT, with cutoff crossing \(Z_i = \mathbf{1}[X_i \geq c]\) serving as the instrument for \(D_i\).

title: Difference in Differences
text:
With data from a randomized experiment, comparing mean outcomes in treatment and control groups gives an unbiased estimate of the causal effect. In observational settings, matching methods try to find comparable units conditional on observed covariates, but the conditional independence assumption is hard to defend when economic models are all about self-selection. A third route is difference-in-differences (DiD), which exploits panel data on units observed before and after treatment. The key idea is that even if treated and control units differ systematically in unobserved ways, those differences may be constant over time. If so, they cancel out when we compare the change in outcomes across groups.



Consider the following panel data regression model:
\[
Y_{it} = \beta_{it} D_{it} + \mu_i + \delta_t + U_{it}
\]
where \(\delta_t\) are time effects common across units, \(\mu_i\) are time-invariant confounders (so \(\mu_i\) and \(D_{it}\) are not independent), and \(U_{it}\) are causes of the outcome unrelated to selection into treatment, \(\mathbb{E}(U_{it} \mid D_{it}) = \mathbb{E}(U_{it})\). The causal mapping gives potential outcomes:
\[
Y_{0it} = \mu_i + \delta_t + U_{it} \qquad Y_{1it} = \beta_{it} + \mu_i + \delta_t + U_{it}
\]
so individual treatment effects are \(\beta_{it} = Y_{1it} - Y_{0it}\).
To simplify, assume there are only two periods. Period \(t = 0\) is the pre-treatment period (\(D_{i0} = 0\) for all \(i\)) and period \(t = 1\) is the post-treatment period (\(D_{i1} = 1\) for some units). The regression model becomes:
\[
Y_{it} = \beta_i D_{it} + \mu_i + \gamma t + U_{it}
\]
Computing expectations by treatment status and period:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}(Y_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 1) &= \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_{i1} = 1) + \mathbb{E}(\mu_i \mid D_{i1} = 1) + \gamma + \mathbb{E}(U_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 1) \\
\mathbb{E}(Y_{i0} \mid D_{i1} = 1) &= \mathbb{E}(\mu_i \mid D_{i1} = 1) + \mathbb{E}(U_{i0} \mid D_{i1} = 1)
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the difference within the treatment group and subtracting the analogous difference for the control group:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 1) - \mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 0) \\
&= \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_{i1} = 1) + \mathbb{E}(\Delta U_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 1) - \mathbb{E}(\Delta U_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 0)
\end{aligned}
\]
The DiD estimator identifies the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) under the common trends assumption:
\[
\mathbb{E}(\Delta U_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 1) = \mathbb{E}(\Delta U_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 0)
\]
which is equivalent to saying that, in the absence of treatment, the average outcomes for treated and untreated units would have evolved the same way over time:
\[
\mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{0i1} \mid D_{i1} = 1) = \mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{0i1} \mid D_{i1} = 0)
\]
This assumption is fundamentally untestable – it is a claim about a counterfactual. With more than two periods, however, one can check whether trends were parallel in pre-treatment periods as a diagnostic.
Also note that common trends is not invariant to monotone transformations of the outcome. If it holds for wages measured in levels, it will not generally hold for wages in logs.



With unit-level panel data, the ATT is estimated from the first-differenced OLS regression:
\[
\Delta Y_{i1} = \gamma + \beta_i D_{i1} + \Delta U_{i1}
\]
The OLS estimator converges to:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D = \frac{\text{Cov}(\Delta Y_{i1}, D_{i1})}{\text{Var}(D_{i1})} = \mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 1) - \mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 0) = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_{i1} = 1)
\]
With only repeated cross-sectional data (where units in one period may differ from those in another), the ATT is recovered from the pooled OLS regression:
\[
Y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_{i1} + \beta_2 t + \beta_i(D_{i1} \times t) + U_{it}
\]
where \(t\) is a post-period dummy. One can show that under common trends, plim \(\hat{\beta}_i = \mathbb{E}(\beta_i \mid D_{i1} = 1)\) by expanding and collecting expectations in each cell of the 2x2 DiD table.



The simple two-period model generalizes to the multi-period, staggered timing case using the static two-way fixed effects (TWFE) specification:
\[
Y_{it} = \mu_i + \gamma_t + \beta_D D_{it} + U_{it}
\]
where \(\gamma_t\) is a time fixed effect for each period and \(\mu_i\) is a time-invariant unit fixed effect.
The identifying assumption is strict exogeneity: conditional on individual and time effects, unobserved factors are mean-independent of \(D_{it}\) in all periods:
\[
\mathbb{E}(U_{it} \mid D_{i1}, \ldots, D_{iT}, \mu_i, t) = \mu_i + \gamma_t \quad \text{for } t = 0, \ldots, T
\]
Under strict exogeneity and homogeneous treatment effects \(\beta_i = \beta_D\), the proof that OLS on the TWFE specification is consistent uses the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem (demeaning within units and then within time periods) and the strict exogeneity condition:
\[
\text{plim}\; \hat{\beta}_D = \frac{\mathbb{E}[\text{Cov}(D_{it} - \bar{D}_i, Y_{it} - \bar{Y}_i \mid \lambda_t)]}{\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(D_{it} - \bar{D}_i \mid \lambda_t)]} = \beta_D
\]
When \(t = 0, 1\) and \(D_{i0} = 0\) for all \(i\), the TWFE and DiD estimands are identical:
\[
\frac{\mathbb{E}[\text{Cov}(D_{it} - \bar{D}_i, Y_{it} - \bar{Y}_i \mid \lambda_t)]}{\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(D_{it} - \bar{D}_i \mid \lambda_t)]} = \mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{it} \mid D_{it} = 1) - \mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{it} \mid D_{it} = 0) = \beta_D
\]



The static TWFE specification yields a sensible estimand under homogeneous effects. But recent work by de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfoeuille (2020), Goodman-Bacon (2021), and Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2022) has shown that the static specification no longer yields interpretable estimands when treatment effects are heterogeneous either across units or over time.
Goodman-Bacon (2021) shows that the OLS estimate \(\hat{\beta}_D\) from a TWFE regression is a variance-weighted average of all possible 2x2 DiD estimators. For illustration, suppose there are three groups: never-treated (\(y^U\)), early-treated (\(y^k\)), and late-treated (\(y^l\)). There are four distinct 2x2 DiD comparisons that the TWFE OLS estimator combines into a single \(\hat{\beta}_D\):

Early-treated vs. never-treated (pre/post the early date \(k\))
Late-treated vs. never-treated (pre/post the late date \(l\))
Early-treated as treated, late-treated as control (before \(l\))
Late-treated as treated, early-treated as control (after \(k\))

The weight on each 2x2 DiD is a positive function of the size of the subsample and the variance of the treatment variable within the subsample. Variance is higher when the two groups are closer in size and when treatment occurs near the middle of the time window. Changing the number or spacing of time periods changes the weights and thus the obtained estimate, even if all the underlying 2x2 DiDs stay constant.
The core problem is comparisons 3 and 4, which use already-treated units as controls. These introduce forbidden comparisons: changes in the treatment effect on already-treated units get subtracted out, which can produce negative 2x2 DiD estimates even when all true treatment effects are positive.
When effects are constant, \(\hat{\beta}_D\) identifies the ATT. When effects vary across units but not over time, \(\hat{\beta}_D\) identifies a variance-weighted average treatment effect on the treated (VWATT), which differs from both the sample ATT (weighted by group share) and the average effect in the treated period (weighted by time spent treated). When effects also vary over time, the TWFE estimand can have the wrong sign.



A popular way to assess TWFE estimates is to estimate separate impact estimates for pre- and post-treatment periods using the dynamic TWFE specification:
\[
Y_{it} = \mu_i + \gamma_t + \sum_{k,\, k \neq -1} \beta_k \mathbf{1}[t - E_i = k] + U_{it}
\]
where \(E_i\) is the period in which unit \(i\) first receives treatment and \(k = t - E_i\) is time relative to treatment. Units are categorized into adoption cohorts based on initial treatment timing. Relative times typically exclude \(k = -1\) as the base category and pool observations at the extremes.
In an event study, treatment is expected to affect outcomes only after it occurs, not before. Finding pre-treatment \(\hat{\beta}_k \approx 0\) is reassuring; significant pre-treatment effects suggest other factors are driving outcomes.
The dynamic specification yields sensible estimates only when there is heterogeneity in time since treatment but not across cohorts (Borusyak and Jaravel, 2018; Sun and Abraham, 2021). If all units have treatment effect \(\tau_s\) in the \(s\)-th period after treatment, then \(\hat{\beta}_s = \tau_s\). But with heterogeneous effects across adoption cohorts, the coefficients from the dynamic TWFE specification are once again difficult to interpret and include the same forbidden comparisons as the static case.





Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) propose an approach that uses never-treated or not-yet-treated units as controls and avoids forbidden comparisons. Their approach relies on two assumptions:
Assumption 1 (Parallel trends for staggered settings): For all \(t \neq t'\) and \(g \neq g'\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y_{it}(\infty) - Y_{it'}(\infty) \mid G_i = g] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{it}(\infty) - Y_{it'}(\infty) \mid G_i = g']
\]
where \(G_i\) is the earliest period at which unit \(i\) received treatment, \(g\) is the first treatment date, and \(Y_{it}(\infty)\) are “never-treated” potential outcomes. In the counterfactual where treatment had not occurred, all adoption cohorts would have evolved in parallel.
Assumption 2 (Staggered no anticipation): \(Y_{it}(g) = Y_{it}(\infty)\) for all \(t < g\).
The building block is the group-time average treatment effect on the treated:
\[
ATT(g, t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_{it}(g) - Y_{it}(\infty) \mid G_i = g]
\]
which gives the average treatment effect at time \(t\) for the cohort first treated at time \(g\). Under Assumption 1, one can identify:
\[
ATT(g, t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_{it} - Y_{i,g-1} \mid G_i = g] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{it} - Y_{i,g-1} \mid G_i = g']
\]
for any comparison group \(g' > t\). Since this holds for any \(g' \in \mathcal{G}\) with \(g' > t\), one can average over comparison groups:
\[
ATT(g, t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_{it} - Y_{i,g-1} \mid G_i = g] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{it} - Y_{i,g-1} \mid G_i = \mathcal{G}]
\]
The sample estimator replaces expectations with sample analogs:
\[
\widehat{ATT}(g, t) = \frac{1}{N_g} \sum_{i:\, G_i = g} [Y_{it} - Y_{i,g-1}] - \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{G}}} \sum_{i:\, G_i \in \mathcal{G}} [Y_{it} - Y_{i,g-1}]
\]
Two natural choices for the comparison group \(\mathcal{G}\):

Never-treated units (\(\mathcal{G} = \{\infty\}\))
Not-yet-treated units (\(\mathcal{G} = \{g' : g' > t\}\))

With many periods or cohorts, reporting all \(\widehat{ATT}(g, t)\) is cumbersome and individual estimates may be imprecise. The method extends to weighted averages. The event-study parameter giving the average effect \(\ell\) periods after adoption across cohorts is:
\[
ATT_\ell^w = \sum_g w_g\, ATT(g, g + \ell)
\]
where \(w_g\) can weight cohorts equally or by their relative frequency in the treated population. Inference is via bootstrap.
Advantages over standard TWFE: (1) the approach provides sensible estimands under arbitrary treatment effect heterogeneity, and (2) it is transparent about which units serve as the control group.



Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2022) propose an imputation estimator based on the TWFE model:

Fit the TWFE regression \(Y_{it}(\infty) = \mu_i + \gamma_t + U_{it}\) using only not-yet-treated observations.
Impute the never-treated potential outcome for each treated unit as the predicted value \(\hat{Y}_{it}(\infty)\).
Estimate the individual treatment effect as \(Y_{it} - \hat{Y}_{it}(\infty)\) and aggregate to form \(ATT(g, t)\).

This differs from the Callaway-Sant’Anna estimator in that it uses the average pre-treatment outcome across all periods before \(g\) rather than just the outcome in period \(g - 1\).




The staggered DiD literature is rapidly evolving. Some notable extensions:

Non-absorbing treatments: when treatment can turn on and off, one can impose a “no carryover” assumption where potential outcomes depend only on current treatment status (de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfoeuille, 2020; Imai and Kim, 2021), or relax it to allow potential outcomes to depend on the full treatment path (de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfoeuille, 2024).
Multivalued or continuous treatments: Callaway et al. (2024) and de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfoeuille (2024).




The parallel trends assumption is untestable by construction. But with multiple pre-treatment periods, one can check whether trends were the same pre-treatment using the dynamic TWFE specification. If pre-treatment leads are all insignificant, an event-study plot supports the research design. In the staggered setting, the Callaway-Sant’Anna approach provides an analogous pre-trends check.
Several important limitations apply:
1. Parallel pre-trends do not imply parallel post-trends. The test only checks the identifying assumption in the pre-period. Even if pre-trends are parallel, post-treatment trends may diverge for reasons unrelated to treatment.
2. Low power. The test may fail to reject even when parallel trends is violated (Bilinski and Hatfield, 2018; Dette and Schumann, 2020). Pre-treatment periods are few and estimates are noisy, so even substantial violations may not be detectable. Note that in the staggered setting, dynamic TWFE specifications may reject even when parallel pre-trends hold, since they are biased under heterogeneous treatment effects.
3. Pre-testing induces selection bias (Roth, 2022). When parallel trends is violated, draws of data in which we happen not to find a significant pre-trend form a selected sample. In that selected sample, we tend to underestimate the treatment-control gap at \(t = 0\), which makes the post-period DiD look particularly large conditional on passing the pre-test. This is pre-test bias.
Formally: suppose in the population there is a linear difference in trend with slope 3. In draws where the pre-trend coefficient happens to be insignificant, the pre-period DiD is around 1.4 rather than 3, while the post-period DiD inflates to around 3.8 rather than 3. Analyzing only the draws that pass the pre-test thus produces inflated post-period estimates.
What to do: diagnostics of the power and distortions from pre-testing (Roth, 2022, “Pre-Test with Caution”) and formal sensitivity analyses that bound inference under smooth violations of parallel trends (Rambachan and Roth, 2023, “A More Credible Approach”).



1. Is everyone treated at the same time?

If YES: static or dynamic standard TWFE are fine.
If NO: use TWFE only if confident about treatment effect homogeneity.
If not confident: use a heterogeneity-robust estimator for staggered treatment timing.

2. Are you sure about the validity of parallel trends?

If YES: explain why (e.g., quasi-random treatment timing).
If NO: consider a method that conditions on covariates.
If NO: show an event-study plot with diagnostics of the power of the pre-test plus formal sensitivity analyses.

3. Do you have many clusters sampled from a super-population?

If YES: use cluster-robust methods.
If few treated clusters: consider alternative inference methods.

title: Difference in Differences
text: With data from a randomized experiment, comparing mean outcomes in treatment and control groups gives an unbiased estimate of the causal effect. In observational settings, matching methods try to find comparable units conditional on observed covariates, but the conditional independence assumption is hard to defend when economic models are all about self-selection. A third route is difference-in-differences (DiD), which exploits panel data on units observed before and after treatment. The key idea is that even if treated and control units differ systematically in unobserved ways, those differences may be constant over time. If so, they cancel out when we compare the change in outcomes across groups.

title: Difference in Differences
text:

\[
Y_{it} = \beta_{it} D_{it} + \mu_i + \delta_t + U_{it}
\]

\[

\]

\[
Y_{it} = \beta_i D_{it} + \mu_i + \gamma t + U_{it}
\]

\[

\end{aligned}

\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\mathbb{E}(\Delta U_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 1) = \mathbb{E}(\Delta U_{i1} \mid D_{i1} = 0)
\]
which is equivalent to saying that, in the absence of treatment, the average outcomes for treated and untreated units would have evolved the same way over time:
\[
\mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{0i1} \mid D_{i1} = 1) = \mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{0i1} \mid D_{i1} = 0)
\]
This assumption is fundamentally untestable – it is a claim about a counterfactual. With more than two periods, however, one can check whether trends were parallel in pre-treatment periods as a diagnostic.
Also note that common trends is not invariant to monotone transformations of the outcome. If it holds for wages measured in levels, it will not generally hold for wages in logs.

text:
The parallel trends assumption is untestable by construction. But with multiple pre-treatment periods, one can check whether trends were the same pre-treatment using the dynamic TWFE specification. If pre-treatment leads are all insignificant, an event-study plot supports the research design. In the staggered setting, the Callaway-Sant’Anna approach provides an analogous pre-trends check.
Several important limitations apply:
1. Parallel pre-trends do not imply parallel post-trends. The test only checks the identifying assumption in the pre-period. Even if pre-trends are parallel, post-treatment trends may diverge for reasons unrelated to treatment.
2. Low power. The test may fail to reject even when parallel trends is violated (Bilinski and Hatfield, 2018; Dette and Schumann, 2020). Pre-treatment periods are few and estimates are noisy, so even substantial violations may not be detectable. Note that in the staggered setting, dynamic TWFE specifications may reject even when parallel pre-trends hold, since they are biased under heterogeneous treatment effects.
3. Pre-testing induces selection bias (Roth, 2022). When parallel trends is violated, draws of data in which we happen not to find a significant pre-trend form a selected sample. In that selected sample, we tend to underestimate the treatment-control gap at \(t = 0\), which makes the post-period DiD look particularly large conditional on passing the pre-test. This is pre-test bias.
Formally: suppose in the population there is a linear difference in trend with slope 3. In draws where the pre-trend coefficient happens to be insignificant, the pre-period DiD is around 1.4 rather than 3, while the post-period DiD inflates to around 3.8 rather than 3. Analyzing only the draws that pass the pre-test thus produces inflated post-period estimates.
What to do: diagnostics of the power and distortions from pre-testing (Roth, 2022, “Pre-Test with Caution”) and formal sensitivity analyses that bound inference under smooth violations of parallel trends (Rambachan and Roth, 2023, “A More Credible Approach”).

title: Difference in Differences
text:
1. Is everyone treated at the same time?

If YES: static or dynamic standard TWFE are fine.
If NO: use TWFE only if confident about treatment effect homogeneity.
If not confident: use a heterogeneity-robust estimator for staggered treatment timing.

2. Are you sure about the validity of parallel trends?

If YES: explain why (e.g., quasi-random treatment timing).
If NO: consider a method that conditions on covariates.
If NO: show an event-study plot with diagnostics of the power of the pre-test plus formal sensitivity analyses.

3. Do you have many clusters sampled from a super-population?

If YES: use cluster-robust methods.
If few treated clusters: consider alternative inference methods.

title: Problem Set 01
text:
Consider the model with a single regressor \(x_{it}\):
\[
y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{it} + \alpha_i + u_{it}
\]
where \(\alpha_i\) represents an unobserved effect fixed over time and \(u_{it}\) is a homoskedastic error term which is independent over time \(t\) and individuals \(i\). There are \(N\) randomly sampled individuals, each observed for \(T = 4\) time periods. Assume that \(E(u_{it} \mid X_i, \alpha_i) = 0\) for all \(i\) and that \(E(u_{it}u_{is} \mid X_i, \alpha_i) = 0\) for any \(t\) and \(s : t \neq s\), where \(X_i\) represents the \(T \times 2\) data matrix for individual \(i\).


To estimate a random effects model we need the following assumptions:

RE1: \(E[\alpha_i \mid X_i] = 0\)
RE2: \(E[u_{it} \mid X_i, \alpha_i] = 0\)
RE3: Homoskedasticity and no serial correlation:

\(\text{Var}(u_{it} \mid X_i, \alpha_i) = \sigma_u^2\)
\(\text{Var}(\alpha_i \mid X_i) = \sigma_\alpha^2\)
\(\text{Cov}(u_{is}, u_{it} \mid X_i, \alpha_i) = 0\) for \(s \neq t\)

RE4: \(\text{plim}_{N \to \infty} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i = E[X_i'V^{-1}X_i]\) has rank \(K\)

Let the composite error be \(v_i = \alpha_i + u_i\) and define the variance-covariance matrix of the error as \(V = E[v_iv_i' \mid X_i]\). Consider the matrix \(B\) such that \(B'B = V^{-1}\) and transform the initial model:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y &= X\beta + v \\
By &= BX\beta + Bv \\
y^* &= X^*\beta + v^*
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(y^* = By\), \(X^* = BX\), and \(v^* = Bv\). Applying OLS to the transformed model by minimizing the SSR:
\[
\text{SSR} = (y^* - X^*\beta)'(y^* - X^*\beta) = y^{*'}y^* - 2\beta'X^{*'}y^* + \beta'X^{*'}X^*\beta
\]
Taking the FOC with respect to \(\beta\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \text{SSR}}{\partial \beta} &= -2X^{*'}y^* + 2X^{*'}X^*\beta = 0 \\
(BX)'(BX)\beta &= (BX)'(By) \\
X'B'BX\beta &= X'B'By
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting \(B'B = V^{-1}\), we obtain the Random Effects estimator:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{RE} = (X'V^{-1}X)^{-1}X'V^{-1}y
\]
To prove consistency, substitute \(y = X\beta + v\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{RE} &= \beta + (X'V^{-1}X)^{-1}X'V^{-1}v \\
&= \beta + \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i\right)
\end{aligned}
\]
Note that:

\(\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} E[X_i'V^{-1}X_i]^{-1}\) by LLN and CMT
\(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i X_i'V^{-1}v_i \xrightarrow{p} E[X_i'V^{-1}v_i]\) by LLN

By LIE:
\[
E[X_i'V^{-1}v_i] = E\left[E[X_i'V^{-1}v_i \mid X_i]\right] = E\left[X_i'V^{-1}\underbrace{E[v_i \mid X_i]}_{=0}\right] = 0
\]
Thus, by Slutsky:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{RE} \xrightarrow{p} \beta + E[X_i'V^{-1}X_i]^{-1} \cdot 0 = \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\]



Multiplying the sampling error by \(\sqrt{N}\):
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta) = \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_i X_i'V^{-1}v_i\right)}_{(2)}
\]

\((1) \xrightarrow{p} E[X_i'V^{-1}X_i]^{-1}\) by LLN and CMT
\((2) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(X_i'V^{-1}v_i))\) by CLT

The variance term is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(X_i'V^{-1}v_i) &= E[X_i'V^{-1}v_iv_i'V^{-1}X_i] \\
&= E\left[X_i'V^{-1}\underbrace{E[v_iv_i' \mid X_i]}_{=V}V^{-1}X_i\right] \quad \text{by LIE} \\
&= E[X_i'V^{-1}VV^{-1}X_i] \\
&= E[X_i'V^{-1}X_i]
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, by Slutsky:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, E[X_i'V^{-1}X_i]^{-1}\underbrace{E[X_i'V^{-1}X_i]}_{}\,E[X_i'V^{-1}X_i]^{-1}\right) = \mathcal{N}\left(0, E[X_i'V^{-1}X_i]^{-1}\right)
\]
Thus, the asymptotic variance of \(\hat{\beta}_{RE}\) is:
\[
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE}) = \frac{1}{N}E[X_i'V^{-1}X_i]^{-1}
\]



Since \(\hat{\beta}_{RE}\) depends on \(V = E[v_iv_i' \mid X_i]\), which depends on the residuals \(v_i\), we need a consistent estimate \(\hat{V}\) to make the estimator feasible. We use Pooled OLS to get first-stage residuals, since it is consistent and does not depend on \(V\).
Step 1. Estimate by Pooled OLS:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{POLS} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'y_i\right)
\]
and compute residuals \(\hat{v}_{it} = y_{it} - x_{it}'\hat{\beta}_{POLS}\).
Step 2. Estimate the variance of \(v_{it}\):
\[
\widehat{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\alpha^2} = \frac{1}{NT - K}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^T \hat{v}_{it}^2
\]
Step 3. Estimate the covariance between \(v_{it}\) and \(v_{is}\) for \(t \neq s\):
\[
\hat{\sigma}_\alpha^2 = \frac{1}{NT(T-1)/2 - K}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\sum_{s=t+1}^T \hat{v}_{it}\hat{v}_{is}
\]
Step 4. Recover \(\hat{\sigma}_u^2 = \widehat{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\alpha^2} - \hat{\sigma}_\alpha^2\) and construct:
\[
\hat{V}_i = \hat{\sigma}_u^2 I_T + \hat{\sigma}_\alpha^2 \ell_T\ell_T'
\]
Step 5. Compute the feasible GLS estimator:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{RE} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'\hat{V}_i^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'\hat{V}_i^{-1}y_i\right)
\]

title: Problem Set 01
text:
Coefficient Equivalence
After applying the within and first-difference transformations, we have:
\[
\text{FE: } \tilde{y}_{it} = \tilde{x}_{it}\beta + \tilde{u}_{it} \qquad \text{FD: } \Delta y_{it} = \Delta x_{it}\beta + \Delta u_{it}
\]
When \(T = 2\), the demeaned FE variables for each individual are:
\[
\tilde{x}_{i1} = x_{i1} - \frac{x_{i1}+x_{i2}}{2} = -\frac{\Delta x_{i2}}{2}, \qquad \tilde{x}_{i2} = x_{i2} - \frac{x_{i1}+x_{i2}}{2} = \frac{\Delta x_{i2}}{2}
\]
and similarly for \(\tilde{y}\) and \(\tilde{u}\). The OLS estimators are:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{FE} = \frac{\sum_i\sum_t \tilde{x}_{it}\tilde{y}_{it}}{\sum_i\sum_t \tilde{x}_{it}^2}, \qquad \hat{\beta}_{FD} = \frac{\sum_i \Delta x_{i2}\Delta y_{i2}}{\sum_i \Delta x_{i2}^2}
\]
Substituting the FE variables in terms of FD quantities:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{FE} = \frac{\sum_i\left[\left(-\frac{\Delta x_{i2}}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{\Delta y_{i2}}{2}\right) + \left(\frac{\Delta x_{i2}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{\Delta y_{i2}}{2}\right)\right]}{\sum_i\left[\left(-\frac{\Delta x_{i2}}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\Delta x_{i2}}{2}\right)^2\right]} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\sum_i \Delta x_{i2}\Delta y_{i2}}{\frac{1}{2}\sum_i \Delta x_{i2}^2} = \hat{\beta}_{FD} \qquad \blacksquare
\]

title: Problem Set 01
text:
Variance Equivalence
The variance of each estimator takes the form \(\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}) = \sigma_u^2 / S_{xx}\). The variance of the errors for both models is estimated by:
\[
\text{FE: } \hat{\sigma}_{\tilde{u}}^2 = \frac{1}{N(T-1)-K}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^T \hat{\tilde{u}}_{it}^2 \qquad \text{FD: } \hat{\sigma}_e^2 = \frac{1}{N(T-1)-K}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=2}^T \Delta\hat{u}_{it}^2
\]
Note the degrees of freedom are equal for both. Expanding the FE numerator for \(T = 2\):
\[
\sum_i\sum_{t=1}^2 \hat{\tilde{u}}_{it}^2 = \sum_i\left[\left(-\frac{\Delta\hat{u}_{i2}}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\Delta\hat{u}_{i2}}{2}\right)^2\right] = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i\Delta\hat{u}_{i2}^2
\]
so \(\hat{\sigma}_{\tilde{u}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}\hat{\sigma}_e^2\). For the denominators:
\[
S_{xx, \text{FE}} = \sum_i\sum_{t=1}^2 \tilde{x}_{it}^2 = \sum_i\frac{\Delta x_{i2}^2}{2} = \frac{1}{2}S_{xx, \text{FD}}
\]
Thus:
\[
\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{FE}) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_{\tilde{u}}^2}{S_{xx, \text{FE}}} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\hat{\sigma}_e^2}{\frac{1}{2}S_{xx, \text{FD}}} = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_e^2}{S_{xx, \text{FD}}} = \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{FD}) \qquad \blacksquare
\]

title: Problem Set 01
text:
(a) Pooled OLS vs. Fixed Effects
The Pooled OLS estimate shows a statistically significant negative effect of having children on life satisfaction: the coefficient on has_kids is \(-0.131\) (\(p < 0.001\)). This suggests that, on average, individuals with children report lower life satisfaction than those without.
In the Fixed Effects specification, the coefficient on has_kids becomes small and statistically insignificant (\(0.017\), \(p = 0.648\)). Once unobserved individual effects are accounted for, changes in parental status are not associated with statistically significant changes in life satisfaction.
The substantial difference between the two estimates suggests that \(f_i\) is correlated with has_kids. The negative POLS estimate likely reflects self-selection into parenthood based on time-invariant characteristics (preferences, personality traits, or baseline well-being) that are negatively correlated with life satisfaction and positively correlated with having children. As a result, POLS is biased and FE is the more appropriate estimator.

title: Problem Set 01
text:
(b) Gender and Children Interaction
The coefficient on sex disappears in the FE regression because sex is time-invariant at the individual level. The within transformation subtracts each individual’s time mean, so \(\tilde{z}_i = z_i - z_i = 0\) for any time-constant covariate; the coefficient \(\gamma\) on \(\mathbf{z}_i\) is not identified.
Since has_kids is time-varying, its interaction with sex is also time-varying and therefore identified.
Re-running FE with the interaction term:

Coefficient on has_kids: \(0.048\) (\(p = 0.386\)) — the effect of children for men (\(\text{sex} = 0\)).
Coefficient on has_kids \(\times\) sex: \(-0.060\) (\(p = 0.436\)) — the differential effect for women relative to men.
Implied effect for women: \(0.048 - 0.060 = -0.012\).

Neither effect is statistically significant, and the differential between men and women is also not significant at conventional levels.

title: Problem Set 01
text:
(c) Random Effects
The RE model is able to include time-invariant variables (such as sex) since it transforms the model via a decomposition of the variance-covariance matrix rather than demeaning.
In the RE model, the estimated coefficient on has_kids is \(-0.041\) (\(p = 0.233\)), compared to \(+0.048\) (\(p = 0.386\)) under FE. Although neither is statistically significant, the difference in sign and magnitude suggests the two estimators are capturing different sources of variation. This discrepancy is consistent with a violation of RE1: \(\mathbb{E}[\alpha_i \mid X_{it}] = 0\) likely does not hold, i.e., the unobserved individual effect \(\alpha_i\) is correlated with the regressors.

title: Problem Set 01
text:
(d) Hausman Test
The Hausman test comparing FE and RE yields \(\chi^2(8) = 136.60\) (\(p < 0.001\)). We reject \(H_0\) at all conventional significance levels.
\(H_0\) is that the difference in coefficients between FE and RE is not systematic — i.e., that RE1 holds and both estimators are consistent. Rejection implies that \(\mathbb{E}[\alpha_i \mid X_i] \neq 0\): the unobserved effects are correlated with the regressors. The RE estimator is therefore inconsistent here, and FE is preferred.

title: Problem Set 03
text:
Let \(y_i = 1\) if traveller \(i\) chooses air transport and \(y_i = 0\) if she chooses train. Let \(x_i\) be a \(K\)-element vector of traveller and trip characteristics. We observe \(N\) independent realisations of \((y_i, x_i)\).


Since \(y_i\) is Bernoulli, its conditional distribution is:
\[
y_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{with probability } P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i) \\ 0 & \text{with probability } 1 - P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i) \end{cases}
\]
We model \(P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i) = F(x_i'\beta)\), so the regression is \(y_i = F(x_i'\beta) + u_i\) with \(\mathbb{E}[u_i \mid x_i] = 0\). Choosing \(F\) to be the logistic CDF \(\Lambda\) restricts fitted probabilities to \((0,1)\) and gives the logit model:
\[
P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i) = \Lambda(x_i'\beta) = \frac{e^{x_i'\beta}}{1 + e^{x_i'\beta}}
\]
Under random sampling, the likelihood is:
\[
L = \prod_{i=1}^N \left[\Lambda(x_i'\beta)\right]^{y_i}\left[1 - \Lambda(x_i'\beta)\right]^{1-y_i}
\]
Taking logs:
\[
\ell = \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{ y_i \ln\Lambda(x_i'\beta) + (1-y_i)\ln\left[1 - \Lambda(x_i'\beta)\right] \right\}
\]
The FOC \(\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta} = 0\) gives:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{y_i - \Lambda(x_i'\beta)}{\Lambda(x_i'\beta)(1-\Lambda(x_i'\beta))} \Lambda'(x_i'\beta)\, x_i = 0
\]
For the logistic CDF, \(\Lambda'(x_i'\beta) = \Lambda(x_i'\beta)(1 - \Lambda(x_i'\beta))\), so the FOCs simplify to:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N \left(y_i - \Lambda(x_i'\beta)\right)x_i = 0
\]
This is nonlinear in \(\beta\) and has no closed-form solution. In practice \(\hat{\beta}\) is found via numerical optimization (Newton-Raphson or BFGS).
Asymptotic variance. Using a mean value expansion of the score around the true \(\beta_0\):
\[
0 = \ell_\beta(\hat{\beta}) = \ell_\beta(\beta_0) + \ell_{\beta\beta'}(\beta^*)(\hat{\beta} - \beta_0)
\]
where \(\beta^*\) lies between \(\hat{\beta}\) and \(\beta_0\). Rearranging and scaling by \(\sqrt{N}\):
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta} - \beta_0) = -\left[\frac{1}{N}\ell_{\beta\beta'}(\beta^*)\right]^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\ell_\beta(\beta_0)\right]
\]

By consistency of \(\hat{\beta}\) and the LLN and CMT: \(-\left(\frac{1}{N}\ell_{\beta\beta'}(\beta^*)\right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} (-A_0)^{-1}\), where \(A_0 = \mathbb{E}[\ell_{i,\beta\beta'}(\beta_0)]\).
By the CLT: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\ell_\beta(\beta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, B_0)\), where \(B_0 = \mathbb{E}[\ell_{i,\beta}(\beta_0)\ell_{i,\beta}(\beta_0)']\).

By Slutsky’s theorem:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta} - \beta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,\, A_0^{-1}B_0A_0^{-1})
\]
Under correct model specification, the Information Matrix Equality holds: \(-A_0 = B_0\), so the variance simplifies to \((-A_0)^{-1} = B_0^{-1}\):
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta} - \beta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,\, B_0^{-1})
\]
Estimation. A consistent estimator of \(B_0^{-1}\) is the outer product of gradients (OPG):
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}) = \frac{1}{N}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left(y_i - \Lambda(x_i'\hat{\beta})\right)^2 x_ix_i'\right]^{-1}
\]
The OPG estimator is always positive semi-definite in finite samples, unlike the Hessian-based alternative which can fail to be so.



The index is \(x_i'\beta = \beta_0 + \beta_1\Delta c_i + \beta_2\Delta t_i + \beta_3\text{hinc}_i\), where \(\Delta c_i = c_{\text{air}} - c_{\text{train}}\) and \(\Delta t_i = t_{\text{air}} - t_{\text{train}}\).
The marginal effect of \(x_{ij}\) on the choice probability is:
\[
\frac{\partial P(y_i=1 \mid x_i)}{\partial x_{ij}} = \underbrace{\Lambda(x_i'\beta)(1-\Lambda(x_i'\beta))}_{\geq 0} \cdot \beta_j
\]
so the sign of \(\beta_j\) determines the direction of the effect.


Both \(\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.961\) and \(\hat{\beta}_2 = -0.131\) are negative. This is plausible: as air travel becomes more expensive or slower relative to train, the probability of choosing air decreases. An increase in relative air cost or time reduces the utility of air travel and shifts choices toward train.
To keep the choice probability unchanged when \(\Delta(\Delta t_i) = +1\) hour:
\[
\beta_1\,\Delta(\Delta c_i) + \beta_2\,\Delta(\Delta t_i) = 0
\]
\[
-0.961\,\Delta(\Delta c_i) - 0.131\,(1) = 0 \implies \Delta(\Delta c_i) = -\frac{0.131}{0.961} \approx -0.1363
\]
Since \(\Delta c_i\) is measured in hundreds of dollars, the air fare must fall by approximately $13.63 to offset a one-hour increase in travel time.



\[
\hat{\beta}_2 \pm z_{0.025} \cdot \widehat{SE}(\hat{\beta}_2) = -0.131 \pm 1.96 \times 0.055 = [-0.239,\ -0.023]
\]
The interval is “approximate” in two senses: (1) the asymptotic normality of \(\hat{\beta}\) is a large-sample result, and (2) the standard error is itself estimated from the data. With only 121 observations the normal approximation may be unreliable.



\[
z = \frac{\hat{\beta}_1 - 0}{\widehat{SE}(\hat{\beta}_1)} = \frac{-0.961}{0.765} = -1.256
\]
At size \(\alpha = 0.05\), the one-sided critical value is \(z_{0.05} = -1.645\). Since \(-1.256 > -1.645\), the test statistic does not fall in the rejection region. We fail to reject \(H_0\): there is no statistically significant evidence that \(\beta_1 < 0\) at the 5% level.



Model 3 imposes \(\beta_1 = 0\) relative to the unrestricted Model 2. The LR statistic is:
\[
LR = 2(\ell_{\text{unrestricted}} - \ell_{\text{restricted}}) = 2(-270.53 - (-270.85)) = 2(0.32) = 0.64
\]
Under \(H_0\), \(LR \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_1\). The 5% critical value is \(\chi^2_{1,0.05} = 3.84\). Since \(0.64 < 3.84\), we fail to reject \(H_0\). The restricted Model 3 is preferred: once income and travel time are controlled for, the cost differential adds no significant explanatory power.

title: Problem Set 03
text:
Since \(y_i\) is Bernoulli, its conditional distribution is:
\[
y_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{with probability } P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i) \\ 0 & \text{with probability } 1 - P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i) \end{cases}
\]
We model \(P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i) = F(x_i'\beta)\), so the regression is \(y_i = F(x_i'\beta) + u_i\) with \(\mathbb{E}[u_i \mid x_i] = 0\). Choosing \(F\) to be the logistic CDF \(\Lambda\) restricts fitted probabilities to \((0,1)\) and gives the logit model:
\[
P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i) = \Lambda(x_i'\beta) = \frac{e^{x_i'\beta}}{1 + e^{x_i'\beta}}
\]
Under random sampling, the likelihood is:
\[
L = \prod_{i=1}^N \left[\Lambda(x_i'\beta)\right]^{y_i}\left[1 - \Lambda(x_i'\beta)\right]^{1-y_i}
\]
Taking logs:
\[
\ell = \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{ y_i \ln\Lambda(x_i'\beta) + (1-y_i)\ln\left[1 - \Lambda(x_i'\beta)\right] \right\}
\]
The FOC \(\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta} = 0\) gives:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{y_i - \Lambda(x_i'\beta)}{\Lambda(x_i'\beta)(1-\Lambda(x_i'\beta))} \Lambda'(x_i'\beta)\, x_i = 0
\]
For the logistic CDF, \(\Lambda'(x_i'\beta) = \Lambda(x_i'\beta)(1 - \Lambda(x_i'\beta))\), so the FOCs simplify to:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N \left(y_i - \Lambda(x_i'\beta)\right)x_i = 0
\]
This is nonlinear in \(\beta\) and has no closed-form solution. In practice \(\hat{\beta}\) is found via numerical optimization (Newton-Raphson or BFGS).
Asymptotic variance. Using a mean value expansion of the score around the true \(\beta_0\):
\[
0 = \ell_\beta(\hat{\beta}) = \ell_\beta(\beta_0) + \ell_{\beta\beta'}(\beta^*)(\hat{\beta} - \beta_0)
\]
where \(\beta^*\) lies between \(\hat{\beta}\) and \(\beta_0\). Rearranging and scaling by \(\sqrt{N}\):
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta} - \beta_0) = -\left[\frac{1}{N}\ell_{\beta\beta'}(\beta^*)\right]^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\ell_\beta(\beta_0)\right]
\]

By consistency of \(\hat{\beta}\) and the LLN and CMT: \(-\left(\frac{1}{N}\ell_{\beta\beta'}(\beta^*)\right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} (-A_0)^{-1}\), where \(A_0 = \mathbb{E}[\ell_{i,\beta\beta'}(\beta_0)]\).
By the CLT: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\ell_\beta(\beta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, B_0)\), where \(B_0 = \mathbb{E}[\ell_{i,\beta}(\beta_0)\ell_{i,\beta}(\beta_0)']\).

By Slutsky’s theorem:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta} - \beta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,\, A_0^{-1}B_0A_0^{-1})
\]
Under correct model specification, the Information Matrix Equality holds: \(-A_0 = B_0\), so the variance simplifies to \((-A_0)^{-1} = B_0^{-1}\):
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta} - \beta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,\, B_0^{-1})
\]
Estimation. A consistent estimator of \(B_0^{-1}\) is the outer product of gradients (OPG):
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}) = \frac{1}{N}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left(y_i - \Lambda(x_i'\hat{\beta})\right)^2 x_ix_i'\right]^{-1}
\]
The OPG estimator is always positive semi-definite in finite samples, unlike the Hessian-based alternative which can fail to be so.

title: Problem Set 03
text:
(a) Log-Likelihood
Define \(d_i = \mathbf{1}[y_i < U]\). The contributions to the likelihood are:

Uncensored (\(d_i = 1\), \(y_i < U\)): \(y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(x_i'\beta, \sigma^2)\), so the density is \(\frac{1}{\sigma}\phi\!\left(\frac{y_i - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)\).
Censored (\(d_i = 0\), \(y_i = U\)): \(P(y_i^* \geq U \mid x_i) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)\).

Under random sampling:
\[
L = \prod_{i=1}^N \left[\frac{1}{\sigma}\phi\!\left(\frac{y_i - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)\right]^{d_i} \left[1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)\right]^{1-d_i}
\]
Taking logs:
\[
\ell = \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{ d_i\left[-\frac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi) - \ln\sigma - \frac{(y_i - x_i'\beta)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right] + (1-d_i)\ln\left[1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)\right] \right\}
\]

title: Problem Set 03
text:
(b) Truncated Mean \(\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x_i, y_i < U]\)
\[
\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x_i, y_i < U] = \mathbb{E}[x_i'\beta + \epsilon_i \mid \epsilon_i < U - x_i'\beta]
= x_i'\beta + \mathbb{E}[\epsilon_i \mid \epsilon_i < U - x_i'\beta]
\]
Multiplying through by \(\sigma/\sigma\) and using the standard normal truncation formula:
\[
\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x_i, y_i < U] = x_i'\beta + \sigma\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\epsilon_i}{\sigma} \;\Big|\; \frac{\epsilon_i}{\sigma} < \frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right] = x_i'\beta - \sigma\,\frac{\phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)}{\Phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)}
\]
Letting \(\lambda_i = \frac{\phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)}{\Phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)}\) denote the (upper-censored) inverse Mills ratio:
\[
\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x_i, y_i < U] = x_i'\beta - \sigma\lambda_i
\]

title: Problem Set 03
text:
(c) Heckman’s Two-Step Estimator
Step 1. Model the censoring indicator with Probit. Since \(P(d_i = 1 \mid x_i) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right) = \Phi(x_i'\gamma)\) where \(\gamma = -\beta/\sigma\) (up to a sign convention), estimate \(\hat{\gamma}\) by MLE. Use \(\hat{\gamma}\) to compute the estimated inverse Mills ratio \(\hat{\lambda}_i\) for each observation.
Step 2. Using only the uncensored observations (\(y_i < U\)), run OLS of \(y_i\) on \(x_i\) and \(\hat{\lambda}_i\):
\[
y_i = x_i'\beta - \sigma\hat{\lambda}_i + v_i
\]
This gives consistent estimates of \(\beta\) and \(\sigma\) in large samples. One practical issue: the inverse Mills ratio can be nearly linear in \(x_i'\hat{\gamma}\) over a limited range of covariate values, causing near-multicollinearity with \(x_i\) and inflating standard errors. The standard errors from Step 2 OLS also need to be corrected for the first-stage estimation, since \(\hat{\lambda}_i\) is a generated regressor.

title: Problem Set 03
text:
(d) Censored Mean \(\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x_i]\)
The censored mean weights the uncensored and censored parts by their respective probabilities:
\[
\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x_i] = P(d_i = 0 \mid x_i)\cdot U + P(d_i = 1 \mid x_i)\cdot\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x_i, y_i < U]
\]
Substituting \(P(d_i = 1) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)\), \(P(d_i = 0) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)\), and the truncated mean from (b):
\[
\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid x_i] = U\left[1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)\right] + \Phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)x_i'\beta - \sigma\,\phi\!\left(\frac{U - x_i'\beta}{\sigma}\right)
\]

title: Problem Set 03
text:
(a) Multinomial Logit
We use a multinomial logit rather than a conditional logit. The regressor of interest, education, varies across individuals but is the same regardless of which fertility outcome we are considering; it is individual-specific and alternative-invariant. Conditional logit is designed for regressors that vary across alternatives (e.g., the price of each alternative), which is not the case here.
Stata normalizes the lowest outcome category, which here is 0 children (zero kids), as the base. All coefficients are interpreted relative to this base.
A coefficient of \(0.0484\) on education for the “2 children” outcome means that one additional year of education increases the log-odds of having two children versus zero by \(0.0484\). For 12 versus 0 years of education, the log-odds difference is \(0.0484 \times 12 = 0.5808\), corresponding to a relative risk ratio of \(\exp(0.5808) \approx 1.787\). So a person with 12 years of education is approximately 1.79 times more likely to have two children than zero, relative to a person with no education.

title: Problem Set 03
text:
(b) Average Marginal Effects
The average marginal effect (AME) of education on outcome \(j\) is:
\[
\text{AME}_j = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\partial P(y_i = j \mid x_i)}{\partial \text{education}_i}
\]
In practice, we compute the predicted probabilities for each individual, increment education by a small amount \(h = 0.0001\), recompute the predicted probabilities, and take the numerical derivative \((p^{\text{new}} - p)/h\) averaged across all individuals.
A key constraint is that the four AMEs must sum to zero across all outcomes for each individual:
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{3} \frac{\partial P(y_i = j \mid x_i)}{\partial x_i} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\sum_{j=0}^{3} P(y_i = j \mid x_i) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}(1) = 0
\]
An increase in the probability of any one outcome must be offset by decreases elsewhere. The table below confirms this: the four AMEs sum to essentially zero.

title: Problem Set 03
text:
(c) Ordered Probit
An ordered probit is more appropriate here than multinomial logit. The number of children is ordinal: 0, 1, 2, 3 are naturally ordered, and imposing this structure gives more efficient estimates and imposes meaningful restrictions (the IIA assumption of multinomial logit is also avoided).
The latent variable is \(y_i^* = \beta\,\text{educ}_i + u_i\) with \(u_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\). The observed outcome is determined by three estimated thresholds \(\hat{\alpha}_1 < \hat{\alpha}_2 < \hat{\alpha}_3\):
\[
y_i = \begin{cases} 0 & y_i^* \leq \alpha_1 \\ 1 & \alpha_1 < y_i^* \leq \alpha_2 \\ 2 & \alpha_2 < y_i^* \leq \alpha_3 \\ 3 & y_i^* > \alpha_3 \end{cases}
\]
The implied probabilities are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(y_i = 0 \mid x_i) &= \Phi(\alpha_1 - x_i'\beta) \\
P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i) &= \Phi(\alpha_2 - x_i'\beta) - \Phi(\alpha_1 - x_i'\beta) \\
P(y_i = 2 \mid x_i) &= \Phi(\alpha_3 - x_i'\beta) - \Phi(\alpha_2 - x_i'\beta) \\
P(y_i = 3 \mid x_i) &= 1 - \Phi(\alpha_3 - x_i'\beta)
\end{aligned}
\]
Threshold interpretation. With \(\hat{\alpha}_1 = 0.386\), \(\hat{\alpha}_2 = 0.913\), \(\hat{\alpha}_3 = 1.690\):

\(\hat{\alpha}_1 = 0.386\): the cutpoint separating 0 and 1 child. Individuals whose latent index \(y_i^*\) falls at or below 0.386 are predicted to have no children.
\(\hat{\alpha}_2 = 0.913\): the cutpoint separating 1 and 2 children. A latent index between 0.386 and 0.913 corresponds to one child.
\(\hat{\alpha}_3 = 1.690\): the cutpoint separating 2 and 3 children. A latent index between 0.913 and 1.690 corresponds to two children, and above 1.690 to three or more.

Education coefficient. Since \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{educ}} = 0.0119 > 0\), higher education shifts \(y_i^*\) upward. This decreases the probability of lower outcomes (zero or one child) and increases the probability of higher outcomes (two or three children), without requiring a separate coefficient for each outcome transition.
Marginal effect at education = 12. The marginal effect on \(P(y_i = 2)\) evaluated at \(\text{educ}_i = 12\) is:
\[
\frac{\partial P(y_i = 2 \mid \text{educ}_i = 12)}{\partial\,\text{educ}_i} = \left[\phi(\hat{\alpha}_2 - 12\hat{\beta}) - \phi(\hat{\alpha}_3 - 12\hat{\beta})\right]\hat{\beta} \approx 0.00209
\]
One additional year of education at the 12-year level increases the probability of having two children by approximately 0.209 percentage points.
